knowledge_statements.statement_title: T-Join Polyhedron
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the dominant polyhedron generated by incidence vectors of T-joins.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph and let \(T\subseteq V(G)\) have even cardinality. The \(T\)-join polyhedron is \[TJ(G,T):=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^J:J\text{ is a }T\text{-join of }G\}+\mathbb R_+^{E(G)}.\] Equivalently, \(x\in TJ(G,T)\) if and only if \(x\) componentwise majorizes a convex combination of incidence vectors of \(T\)-joins.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an even vertex set T, the T-join polyhedron is the convex hull of T-join incidence vectors plus the nonnegative orthant; equivalently, its vectors componentwise dominate convex combinations of T-join incidence vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: TJ(G,T)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^J:J\text{ is a }T\text{-join}\}+\mathbb R_+^{E(G)}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cut Description of the T-Join Polyhedron
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact description of the T-join dominant by nonnegativity and T-cut inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph and let \(T\subseteq V(G)\) have even cardinality. If a \(T\)-cut is a cut \(\delta(S)\) satisfying \(|S\cap T|\) odd, then \[TJ(G,T)=\{x\in\mathbb R^{E(G)}:x\ge0,\ x(C)\ge1\text{ for every }T\text{-cut }C\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The T-join polyhedron is exactly the set of nonnegative edge vectors having value at least one on every cut whose shore contains an odd number of vertices from T.
assumptions_latex: C=\delta(S)\text{ is a }T\text{-cut when }|S\cap T|\text{ is odd}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: TJ(G,T)=\{x\ge0:x(C)\ge1\ \forall T\text{-cuts }C\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bipartite Graph and Bipartition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of a bipartite graph and its associated color classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A graph \(G\) is bipartite if its vertex set can be partitioned as \(V(G)=A\mathbin{\dot\cup}B\) so that every edge has one endpoint in \(A\) and the other in \(B\). The sets \(A\) and \(B\) are called the color classes of \(G\), and \((A,B)\) is called a bipartition of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph is bipartite if its vertices can be partitioned into two color classes such that every edge joins the two different classes. The pair of classes is a bipartition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is bipartite}\iff \exists A,B:\ V(G)=A\mathbin{\dot\cup}B\ \land\ \forall uv\in E(G),\ ((u\in A\land v\in B)\lor(u\in B\land v\in A))

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted Stable-Set–Edge-Cover Min–Max Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted integral covering duality for bipartite graphs without isolated vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a bipartite graph without isolated vertices and let \(w:V\to\mathbb Z_+\). If \(\alpha_w(G)=\max\{\sum_{v\in S}w_v:S\subseteq V\text{ is stable}\}\), then
\[
\alpha_w(G)=\min\left\{\sum_{e\in E}x_e:x\in\mathbb Z_+^E,\ \sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e\ge w_v\ \forall v\in V\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every bipartite graph without isolated vertices and every nonnegative integer vertex-weight function, the maximum weight of a stable set equals the minimum total multiplicity of a nonnegative integer edge multicover meeting each vertex's weight requirement.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is bipartite and has no isolated vertices}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \alpha_w(G)=\min\left\{\sum_{e\in E}x_e:\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e\ge w_v\ \forall v\in V\right\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complementary Matching and Point Cover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A point cover is a vertex cover, and a line is an edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every possibly infinite bipartite graph \(G\), there exist a matching \(M\) and a vertex cover \(P\) such that \(|e\cap P|=1\) for every \(e\in M\), and every \(v\in P\) is incident with exactly one edge of \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every bipartite graph, possibly infinite, has a matching and a vertex cover such that each matching edge contains exactly one cover vertex and each cover vertex lies on exactly one matching edge.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is a possibly infinite bipartite graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists M,P\;\bigl[M\text{ is a matching},\ P\text{ is a vertex cover},\ (\forall e\in M)\ |e\cap P|=1,\ (\forall v\in P)\ \deg_M(v)=1\bigr]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bipartite Supply–Demand Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient neighborhood conditions for fractional supply-demand feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be bipartite with color classes \(S,T\), let \(d:S\to\mathbb R_+\), and let \(b:T\to\mathbb R_+\). There exists \(y:E\to\mathbb R_+\) such that
\[
\sum_{e\ni s}y_e=d(s)\quad\forall s\in S,
\qquad
\sum_{e\ni t}y_e\le b(t)\quad\forall t\in T
\]
if and only if
\[
d(U)\le b(\Gamma(U))\quad\forall U\subseteq S,
\]
where \(d(U)=\sum_{s\in U}d(s)\), \(b(\Gamma(U))=\sum_{t\in\Gamma(U)}b(t)\), and \(\Gamma(U)\) is the set of vertices in \(T\) adjacent to \(U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative demand on one side of a bipartite graph can be exactly met using nonnegative edge shipments without exceeding supply capacities on the other side if and only if every subset of demand vertices has total demand at most the total supply in its neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is bipartite with color classes }S\text{ and }T
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists y\in\mathbb R_+^E:\ \sum_{e\ni s}y_e=d(s)\ \forall s\in S,\ \sum_{e\ni t}y_e\le b(t)\ \forall t\in T\iff d(U)\le b(\Gamma(U))\ \forall U\subseteq S

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Successive Shortest-Path Complexity for Assignment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Assignment specialization of successive shortest-path minimum-cost flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an assignment instance with $n_1=|N_1|$, each successive shortest-path iteration computes residual shortest-path distances from a supply node, updates node potentials, and augments one unit of flow to a demand node. Each iteration assigns one additional vertex of $N_1$; therefore the algorithm terminates within $n_1$ iterations and runs in $O(n_1S(n,m,C))$ time, where $S(n,m,C)$ is the time required to solve a shortest-path problem with nonnegative arc lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On an assignment instance, successive shortest path assigns one additional first-side vertex per unit-flow augmentation. It therefore terminates within n1 iterations and runs in O(n1 S(n,m,C)) time.
assumptions_latex: S(n,m,C)\text{ is the time for a shortest-path problem with nonnegative arc lengths}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{iterations}\le n_1,\qquad T(n,m,C)=O(n_1S(n,m,C)).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complexity equivalence of bipartite matching and disjoint s-t paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bidirectional equivalence preserving an arbitrary asymptotic running-time bound in the vertex and edge-or-arc parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every function \phi(n,m), the bipartite matching problem with n vertices and m edges is solvable in time O\!\left(\phi(n,m)\right) if and only if the disjoint s\!\!-\!t paths problem with n vertices and m arcs is solvable in time O\!\left(\phi(n,m)\right).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every function phi(n,m), bipartite matching on n vertices and m edges has an O(phi(n,m)) algorithm if and only if the disjoint s-t paths problem on n vertices and m arcs has an O(phi(n,m)) algorithm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{BipartiteMatching}(n,m)\in O\!\left(\phi(n,m)\right)\iff \operatorname{DisjointSTPaths}(n,m)\in O\!\left(\phi(n,m)\right).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimum Antichain Partition Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The height-versus-antichain-partition equality for finite posets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every finite partially ordered set \(P\), the maximum cardinality of a chain equals the minimum number of antichains in a partition of \(P\): \[\max\{|C|:C\subseteq P\text{ is a chain}\}=\min\{|\mathcal A|:\mathcal A\text{ is a partition of }P\text{ into antichains}\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In every finite poset, the size of a longest chain equals the smallest number of antichains needed to partition the poset.
assumptions_latex: P\text{ is a finite partially ordered set}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max\{|C|:C\subseteq P\text{ is a chain}\}=\min\{|\mathcal A|:\mathcal A\text{ partitions }P\text{ into antichains}\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Shortest-augmenting-path Hungarian method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic Hungarian method for maximum-weight matching with rational edge weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(U\mathbin{\dot\cup}W,E)$ be bipartite with $w:E\to\mathbb{Q}$, and start with $M=\varnothing$. Given $M$, form $D_M$ by directing each matched edge from $W$ to $U$ with length $w_e$ and each unmatched edge from $U$ to $W$ with length $-w_e$. Let $U_M$ and $W_M$ be the vertices missed by $M$. If a directed $U_M$--$W_M$ path exists, choose a shortest such path $P$ and replace $M$ by $M\triangle E(P)$. Iterate until no such path exists. The terminal matching has maximum cardinality, and a maximum-weight matching among the generated matchings has maximum weight among all matchings in $G$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from the empty matching, orient matched and unmatched edges in opposite directions with lengths w and −w. Repeatedly augment along a shortest path between unmatched vertices in the two color classes. When no such path remains, the matching has maximum size, and the heaviest generated matching is globally maximum-weight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M_{\mathrm{terminal}}\text{ has maximum cardinality, and }\max_{M'\text{ generated}}w(M')=\max_{N\text{ matching in }G}w(N)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Forest-Representative System Criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hall-type characterization for forest-representative systems of finite hypergraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite hypergraph \(H\) has a forest-representative system if and only if, for every integer \(k>0\), the union of any \(k\) hyperedges of \(H\) has cardinality strictly greater than \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite hypergraph has a forest-representative system exactly when every collection of k hyperedges, for k greater than zero, has a union containing more than k vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H\text{ has a forest-representative system}\iff \forall \mathcal L\subseteq E(H),\ |\mathcal L|>0\Rightarrow\left|\bigcup_{L\in\mathcal L}L\right|>|\mathcal L|.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Partial Systems of Distinct Representatives Form a Matroid
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matroid structure induced on the ground set by a family of subsets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\) be a family of subsets of a finite set \(S\). The subsets of \(S\) that occur as partial systems of distinct representatives of \(\mathcal F\) are the independent sets of a matroid on \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a family of subsets of a finite ground set S, its partial systems of distinct representatives form the independent-set family of a matroid on S.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{X\subseteq S:X\text{ is a partial SDR of }\mathcal F\}\text{ is the independent-set system of a matroid on }S.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Induced-edge criterion for a bipartite k-factor
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A necessary-and-sufficient condition for a bipartite graph to contain a spanning k-regular subgraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be bipartite and let \(k\in\mathbb Z_{+}\). Then \(G\) has a \(k\)-factor if and only if every \(X\subseteq V\) satisfies \[|E(G[X])|\geq k\left(|X|-\frac{|V|}{2}\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bipartite graph has a k-factor exactly when every vertex subset X spans at least k(|X|-|V|/2) edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\exists F\subseteq E:\ (V,F)\text{ is }k\text{-regular}\bigr)\iff\bigl(\forall X\subseteq V,\ |E(G[X])|\geq k(|X|-|V|/2)\bigr)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vertex Cover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covering graph edges by incident vertices; distinct from covering vertices by edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph $G=(V,E)$, a set $C\subseteq V$ is a vertex cover if every edge has at least one endpoint in $C$, equivalently, $C\cap e\neq\varnothing$ for every $e\in E$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertex cover is a set of vertices incident to every edge of the graph. It is not the same as an edge cover, which covers vertices using edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\text{ is a vertex cover}\iff \forall e\in E,\ C\cap e\neq\varnothing.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted Dilworth Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted chain-covering min-max theorem for a poset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((P,\preccurlyeq)\) be a partially ordered set and let \(w:P\to\mathbf Z_+\). The minimum cardinality of a family of chains that covers every \(p\in P\) at least \(w(p)\) times equals \(\max\{\sum_{p\in A}w(p):A\subseteq P\text{ is an antichain}\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an integer-valued nonnegative weight on a poset, the fewest chains needed to cover every element p at least w(p) times equals the maximum total weight of an antichain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{\mathcal C}\{|\mathcal C|:\#\{C\in\mathcal C:p\in C\}\ge w(p)\ \forall p\in P\}=\max_{A\text{ antichain}}\sum_{p\in A}w(p).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equitable matching decomposition of a bipartite graph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An equitable form of bipartite edge-coloring.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be bipartite and let \(k\in\mathbb Z_{+}\) satisfy \(k\geq\Delta(G)\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Criterion for a Two-Size Matching Partition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes a prescribed partition of a bipartite edge set into matching classes of two cardinalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be bipartite and let \(k_1,k_2,p_1,p_2\in\mathbb Z_+\) satisfy \(k_1+k_2\geq\Delta(G)\), \(k_1p_1+k_2p_2=|E|\), and \(p_1\geq p_2\). Then \(E\) can be partitioned into \(k_1\) matchings of size \(p_1\) and \(k_2\) matchings of size \(p_2\) if and only if every \(X\subseteq V\) satisfies \(|E(G[X])|\geq k_1(p_1+|X|-|V|)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated degree, edge-count, and size-order assumptions, the edges admit the prescribed partition into matchings of two sizes exactly when every vertex subset X spans at least k1(p1+|X|-|V|) edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: E\text{ has the prescribed matching partition}\iff \forall X\subseteq V,\ |E(G[X])|\geq k_1(p_1+|X|-|V|)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Edge coloring and chromatic index
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines edge colorings and records the universal degree lower bound and its possible strictness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph \(G=(V,E)\), a \(k\)-edge-coloring is a partition \(\Pi=(M_1,\ldots,M_k)\) of \(E\) into matchings; an edge in \(M_i\) has color \(i\). The edge-coloring number is \(\chi(G):=\min\{k:E\text{ admits a }k\text{-edge-coloring}\}\). Every graph satisfies \(\chi(G)\geq\Delta(G)\), and the inequality can be strict; for example, \(\chi(K_3)>\Delta(K_3)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An edge coloring partitions a graph's edges into matchings, and the chromatic index is the minimum number of such color classes. It is at least the maximum vertex degree, with strict inequality possible, as for a triangle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \chi(G)\geq\Delta(G),\qquad \chi(K_3)>\Delta(K_3).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence criterion for a bipartite forest with prescribed degrees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes exact degree realization on one side by an acyclic subgraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(S,T;E)$ be bipartite and let $m:S\to\mathbf Z_+$. Writing $\widetilde m(X)=\sum_{s\in X}m(s)$, there exists a forest $F\subseteq E$ with $d_F(s)=m(s)$ for every $s\in S$ if and only if $|\Gamma_G(X)|\ge \widetilde m(X)-|X|+1$ for every nonempty $X\subseteq S$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bipartite graph contains a forest realizing the prescribed degree m(s) at every vertex s on the S side exactly when each nonempty X contained in S has at least the sum of the prescribed degrees on X minus |X| plus one neighbors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists F\subseteq E\text{ a forest with }d_F(s)=m(s)\ (\forall s\in S)\iff |\Gamma_G(X)|\ge\widetilde m(X)-|X|+1\ (\forall\varnothing\ne X\subseteq S)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Criterion for a Common System of Distinct Representatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient intersection condition for two equally sized indexed set families to have a common SDR.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F_1\) and \(\mathcal F_2\) be indexed families of subsets of a finite set \(S\), with \(|\mathcal F_1|=|\mathcal F_2|=n\). They have a common system of distinct representatives if and only if, for every pair of subfamilies \(\mathcal G_1\subseteq\mathcal F_1\) and \(\mathcal G_2\subseteq\mathcal F_2\), \[\left|\left(\bigcup_{A\in\mathcal G_1}A\right)\cap\left(\bigcup_{A\in\mathcal G_2}A\right)\right|\ge |\mathcal G_1|+|\mathcal G_2|-n.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two indexed families of n subsets of a finite set have a common system of distinct representatives exactly when, for every pair of subfamilies, the intersection of their unions has size at least the sum of the subfamily sizes minus n.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F_1\) and \(\mathcal F_2\) are indexed families of subsets of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F_1\text{ and }\mathcal F_2\text{ have a CSDR}\iff \forall\mathcal G_i\subseteq\mathcal F_i,\ \left|\left(\bigcup_{A\in\mathcal G_1}A\right)\cap\left(\bigcup_{A\in\mathcal G_2}A\right)\right|\ge |\mathcal G_1|+|\mathcal G_2|-n.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integral-multiplicity b-matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition occurs in a section on bipartite graphs; edge variables are nonnegative integers rather than merely binary selectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be bipartite and let $b\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}^{V}$. A $b$-matching is a vector $x\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}^{E}$ satisfying
\[
\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e\le b_v\qquad\text{for every }v\in V.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A b-matching assigns nonnegative integral multiplicities to edges so that the total multiplicity incident to each vertex does not exceed that vertex's nonnegative integral capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ is a }b\text{-matching}\iff x\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}^{E}\text{ and }\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e\le b_v\ \forall v\in V.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unstable matching and blocking pair
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete one-to-one matching of men and women with preference rankings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A complete matching \(\mu\) is called unstable if there exist \(m\) and \(w\) with \(\mu(m)\ne w\) such that \(m\) prefers \(w\) to \(\mu(m)\), and \(w\) prefers \(m\) to \(\mu^{-1}(w)\). Such a pair \((m,w)\) is a blocking pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complete matching is unstable when an unmatched man and woman each prefer the other to their assigned mate; they form a blocking pair.
assumptions_latex: \(\mu\) is a complete one-to-one matching between men and women.
Each participant has a preference ranking over potential mates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists m,w:\ \mu(m)\ne w,\ w\succ_m\mu(m),\ m\succ_w\mu^{-1}(w)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Prescribed Colour Classes and Disjoint Matchings

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted bipartite b-matching–multicover duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The extracted phrase “t-matching” is interpreted as “b-matching” from the immediately preceding definition and the theorem's vertex-capacity vector b. A collection of vertices is represented by nonnegative integral multiplicities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be bipartite, $w\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}^{E}$, and $b\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}^{V}$. Then
\[
\max\left\{\sum_{e\in E}w_ex_e:x\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}^{E},\ \sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e\le b_v\ \forall v\in V\right\}
=
\min\left\{\sum_{v\in V}b_vy_v:y\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}^{V},\ y_u+y_v\ge w_{uv}\ \forall uv\in E\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a bipartite graph with nonnegative integral edge weights and vertex capacities, the maximum weight of an integral b-matching equals the minimum b-weight of a vertex multiset whose endpoint multiplicities cover every edge to at least its edge weight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max\left\{\sum_{e\in E}w_ex_e:x\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}^{E},\ \sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e\le b_v\ \forall v\in V\right\}=\min\left\{\sum_{v\in V}b_vy_v:y\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}^{V},\ y_u+y_v\ge w_{uv}\ \forall uv\in E\right\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vertex-Coverage Edge Partition Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence of a k-class edge partition attaining the degree-limited coverage count at every vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be bipartite and let \(k\in\mathbb Z_{+}\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fixed-cardinality bottleneck-matching min-max theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to every feasible positive matching cardinality; the corresponding quantity for the empty matching is undefined.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(S,T,A)\) be a weighted bipartite graph, and let \(k\ge 1\) be such that a \(k\)-edge matching exists. If \(X_k\) ranges over all \(k\)-edge matchings and \(H_{k-1}\) ranges over all subgraphs obtained from \(G\) by deleting \(k-1\) vertices, then
\[
\max_{X_k}\min\{w_{ij}:(i,j)\in X_k\}
=
\min_{H_{k-1}}\max\{w_{ij}:(i,j)\in E(H_{k-1})\}.
\]
The dual quantity for the empty matching is undefined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every feasible positive cardinality k, the greatest attainable minimum edge weight of a k-edge bipartite matching equals the least possible maximum remaining edge weight after deleting k−1 vertices. The empty-matching case is undefined.
assumptions_latex: G=(S,T,A)\text{ is a weighted bipartite graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max_{X_k}\min_{(i,j)\in X_k}w_{ij}=\min_{H_{k-1}}\max_{(i,j)\in E(H_{k-1})}w_{ij}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Kőnig–Ore Deficiency Formula and Hall Criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum exposed-vertex characterization and the resulting criterion for saturating one side of a bipartite graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(S,T;E)\) be bipartite. Define \(\varphi(G)\) as the minimum number of vertices of \(S\) left exposed by a matching and \(\mu(G)=\max_{X\subseteq S}(|X|-|\Gamma_G(X)|)\). Then \(\varphi(G)=\mu(G)\). Consequently, a matching covering all of \(S\) exists if and only if \[|\Gamma_G(X)|\ge |X|\qquad\text{for every }X\subseteq S.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a bipartite graph, the minimum number of S-side vertices left unmatched equals the maximum neighborhood deficiency over subsets of S. Hence a matching covers all of S exactly when every subset of S has at least as many neighbors as vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \varphi(G)=\mu(G),\qquad \bigl(\exists M\text{ covering }S\bigr)\iff\bigl(\forall X\subseteq S,\ |\Gamma_G(X)|\ge |X|\bigr)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relabel and Saturating-Push Bounds for Bipartite Preflow–Push
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operation bounds for the bipartite preflow–push algorithm on partitions of sizes \(n_1,n_2\) and a network with \(m\) arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Each distance label increases at most \(O(n_1)\) times. Hence the total number of relabel operations is \(O\!\left(n_1(n_1+n_2)\right)=O(n_1n_2)\), and the number of saturating pushes is \(O(n_1m)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Folkman–Fulkerson Criterion for Disjoint Matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Induced-edge inequality characterizing the existence of multiple equal-cardinality, edge-disjoint bipartite matchings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(S,T;E)\) be bipartite, let \(U=S\cup T\), and let \(k,\ell\) be nonnegative integers. There exist \(\ell\) pairwise edge-disjoint matchings, each of size \(k\), if and only if \[i_G(Z)\ge \ell\bigl(k+|Z|-|U|\bigr)\] for every \(Z\subseteq U\), where \(i_G(Z)\) is the number of edges of \(G\) with both endpoints in \(Z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bipartite graph contains the prescribed number of pairwise edge-disjoint matchings of the prescribed size exactly when every vertex subset induces at least the stated number of edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\ \ell\text{ pairwise edge-disjoint matchings of size \(k\)}\iff \forall Z\subseteq U,\ i_G(Z)\ge\ell(k+|Z|-|U|)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Greedy Maximum-Cardinality Matching Algorithm for Convex Bipartite Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The source's selection key \(\pi_i\) is an evident notation error: \(\pi\) is defined for vertices \(j\in T\), so the comparison must use \(\pi_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(S,T,A)\) be convex with respect to the ordering \(S=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), and define \(\pi_j=\max\{i\in S:(i,j)\in A\}\) for each nonisolated \(j\in T\). Start with \(M=\varnothing\). For \(i=1,\ldots,m\), if \(i\) has an exposed neighbor, choose an exposed neighbor \(j\) minimizing \(\pi_j\) and add \((i,j)\) to \(M\); otherwise make no change. This procedure produces a maximum-cardinality matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Process the ordered side from left to right. If the current vertex has an unmatched neighbor, match it to one whose rightmost neighbor occurs earliest. The resulting matching has maximum cardinality.
assumptions_latex: G=(S,T,A)\text{ is convex with respect to }S=\{1,\ldots,m\}
\pi_j=\max\{i\in S:(i,j)\in A\}\text{ for every nonisolated }j\in T
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\text{ produced by the procedure is a maximum-cardinality matching of }G.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matroid-Constrained Bipartite Matching Min–Max Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum matching cardinality under endpoint-independence constraints and its minimum rank-weighted point-cover characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $G$ be a bipartite graph with bipartition $(A,B)$, and let $(A,r_A)$ and $(B,r_B)$ be matroids. The maximum cardinality of a matching whose met vertices in $A$ and in $B$ are independent in their respective matroids equals
\[\min_{T\text{ a point cover of }G}\bigl(r_A(T\cap A)+r_B(T\cap B)\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The largest bipartite matching whose matched vertices are independent in the two side matroids equals the minimum rank-weight of a vertex cover, with each side measured by its matroid rank.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max\{|M|:M\text{ is a matching meeting independent sets on both sides}\}=\min_{T\text{ a point cover}}\bigl(r_A(T\cap A)+r_B(T\cap B)\bigr).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bipartite Graphs and Matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational definitions used by maximum-cardinality bipartite matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A graph \(G\) is bipartite if \(V(G)=V_1(G)\mathbin{\dot\cup}V_2(G)\) and \(E(G[V_1(G)])=E(G[V_2(G)])=\varnothing\), equivalently every edge has one endpoint in each part. A matching is a set \(M\subseteq E(G)\) such that every vertex is incident to at most one edge of \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph is bipartite when its vertices can be partitioned into two sets with every edge running between the sets. A matching is a set of edges in which no vertex occurs more than once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is bipartite}\iff \exists V_1,V_2:\ V(G)=V_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}V_2,\ E(G[V_1])=E(G[V_2])=\varnothing;\quad M\text{ is a matching}\iff \forall v\in V(G),\ |\{e\in M:v\in e\}|\le1.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Auxiliary-Graph Bipartite Matching Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stage-based augmenting algorithm using mate, exposed-neighbor, predecessor-label, and queue data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(B=(V,U,E)\), initialize \(\operatorname{mate}[x]=0\) for all \(x\in V\cup U\). At each stage, record for each \(v\in V\) an unmatched neighbor \(\operatorname{exposed}[v]\), when one is encountered, and construct an auxiliary digraph on \(V\) with an arc \((v,\operatorname{mate}[u])\) for each \([v,u]\in E\) such that \(u\) is matched and \(\operatorname{mate}[u]\ne v\). Search this digraph from the unmatched vertices of \(V\), recording predecessor labels. If a reached vertex \(v\) satisfies \(\operatorname{exposed}[v]\ne0\), augment recursively along the labeled alternating path and begin a new stage. If the queue becomes empty, terminate and return \(\operatorname{mate}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Begin with the empty matching. In each stage, form an auxiliary directed graph on the V side through matched U vertices and search from every unmatched V vertex while recording predecessors. Upon reaching a V vertex adjacent to an unmatched U vertex, flip the matching along the resulting augmenting path and restart. If the search finds no such path, terminate and return mate.
assumptions_latex: B=(V,U,E)\text{ is a bipartite graph with bipartition }(V,U).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{mate}\text{ is the matching returned when the search queue becomes empty.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Augmenting-Path Algorithm for Bipartite Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed-reachability formulation of one augmentation step for a bipartite matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(U\mathbin{\dot\cup}W,E)$ be bipartite and let $M$ be a matching. Form $D_M$ by orienting each edge $uw\in M$ from $w$ to $u$ and each edge $uw\notin M$ from $u$ to $w$. Let $U_M$ and $W_M$ be the vertices of $U$ and $W$, respectively, missed by $M$. An $M$-augmenting path can be found by finding a directed path in $D_M$ from $U_M$ to $W_M$; augmenting along such a path produces a matching $M'$ with $|M'|>|M|$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Orient matched edges from W to U and unmatched edges from U to W. Searching for a directed path from an unmatched U-vertex to an unmatched W-vertex finds an augmenting path, whose edges can be toggled to obtain a larger matching.
assumptions_latex: U_M=\{u\in U:u\text{ is missed by }M\},\quad W_M=\{w\in W:w\text{ is missed by }M\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{A directed }U_M\text{-to-}W_M\text{ path yields an }M\text{-augmenting path and a matching }M'\text{ with }|M'|>|M|.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integral weights of perfect bipartite matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes edge weights whose total is integral on every perfect matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a bipartite graph and let \(w\in\mathbb{R}^{E}\). Every perfect matching of \(G\) has integer weight if and only if there exists \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\) such that \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\) and \(w_{uv}-b_u-b_v\in\mathbb{Z}\) for every edge \(uv\in E\) contained in at least one perfect matching.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimum-Weight Perfect-Matching Algorithm for Bipartite Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Retains the source's equality-graph, reduced-cost, and numbered-formulation notation. Initialization at an exposed root applies when the current matching is not already perfect.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be bipartite, let \(y\) be feasible for \((5.9)\), and let \(M\) be a nonperfect matching in the equality graph \(G_=\). Root an \(M\)-alternating tree \(T\) at an \(M\)-exposed vertex. Extend \(T\) along equality edges from \(B(T)\) to vertices outside \(V(T)\). If such an edge reaches an exposed vertex, augment \(M\); return when \(M\) is perfect, and otherwise restart from another exposed vertex. If every edge from \(B(T)\) ends in \(A(T)\), stop and report that \(G\) has no perfect matching. Otherwise set \(\varepsilon=\min\{\bar c_{vw}:v\in B(T),\ w\notin V(T)\}\), increase \(y_v\) by \(\varepsilon\) on \(B(T)\), decrease it by \(\varepsilon\) on \(A(T)\), and continue.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a bipartite graph, start with a dual-feasible labeling and a nonperfect equality-edge matching. Grow an alternating tree, augment upon reaching an exposed vertex, certify nonexistence when no edge can leave the tree appropriately, and otherwise adjust the labels by the smallest reduced cost that creates a new equality edge.
assumptions_latex: M\text{ is not already perfect when an exposed root is selected}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure returns a perfect matching }M\text{ or reports that }G\text{ has no perfect matching.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertex-incidence definitions and the cardinality consequence for perfect bipartite matchings.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Degree bound for edge-minimal perfect-matching resilience
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounds the number of vertices of degree at least three in a bipartite graph that is edge-minimal for retaining perfect matchings after each prescribed vertex-set deletion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a set and let \(X_1,\ldots,X_t\subseteq X\) satisfy \(|X_i|\le r\) for \(i=1,\ldots,t\). Let \(G\) be a bipartite graph with \(X\subseteq V(G)\). Suppose that \(G-X_i\) has a perfect matching for every \(i\), and that for every \(e\in E(G)\), property \(\forall i,\,(G-e)-X_i\text{ has a perfect matching}\) fails. Then \(\bigl|\{v\in V(G):\deg_G(v)\ge 3\}\bigr|\le r^3\binom{t}{3}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Let X1 through Xt be subsets of X, each having at most r elements. If G is bipartite, contains X among its vertices, every G minus Xi has a perfect matching, and deleting any edge makes this family-wide property fail, then G has at most r cubed times t choose three vertices of degree at least three.
assumptions_latex: \forall e\in E(G),\;\exists i\in\{1,\ldots,t\}\text{ such that }(G-e)-X_i\text{ has no perfect matching}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left|\{v\in V(G):\deg_G(v)\ge 3\}\right|\le r^3\binom{t}{3}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Kuhn Primal-Dual Assignment Algorithm and Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sign-consistent reading of the extract: because dual feasibility requires transformed weights to remain nonpositive, the crossing update uses the minimum positive slack. The displayed maximum and the later claim that transformed weights remain nonnegative are internal inconsistencies in the extract. For a noncomplete graph, adding sufficiently negative-weight missing edges preserves the original optimum only when an original perfect matching exists and the artificial weights are chosen below every competitive matching value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(V_1\cup V_2,E)=K_{n,n}$ and $c:E\to\mathbb R$. The assignment LP is $\max\{\sum_{e\in E}c_ex_e:\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e=1\ (v\in V),\ x\ge0\}$, and its bipartite incidence matrix is totally unimodular, so the feasible polytope is integral. Its dual is $\min\{\sum_{v\in V}y_v:y_v+y_w\ge c_{vw}\ ((v,w)\in E)\}$. For dual-feasible $y$, define $\bar c_{vw}=c_{vw}-y_v-y_w\le0$ and let $G_=(y)$ contain the edges with $\bar c_{vw}=0$. Every perfect matching in $G_=(y)$ is maximum-weight. Starting with dual-feasible $y$, repeatedly find a maximum-cardinality matching $F$ in $G_=(y)$. If $F$ is not perfect, grow a maximal $F$-alternating forest $H$ rooted at exposed vertices of $V_1$, set $\Delta=\min\{-\bar c_{vw}:v\in V_1\cap V(H),\ w\in V_2\setminus V(H)\}>0$, and update $y_v\leftarrow y_v-\Delta$ for $v\in V_1\cap V(H)$ and $y_v\leftarrow y_v+\Delta$ for $v\in V_2\cap V(H)$. The update preserves dual feasibility and permits the alternating forest or matching to grow. The algorithm terminates with a maximum-weight perfect matching, uses at most $n^2$ dual updates, and runs in $O(n^4)$ time under the stated $O(n^2)$ work bound between updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a complete balanced bipartite graph with real edge weights, the assignment polytope is integral. Kuhn's primal-dual algorithm maintains feasible vertex potentials and a maximum-cardinality matching in the zero-transformed-weight equality graph. When the matching is imperfect, it grows an alternating forest and updates the potentials by the minimum crossing slack. This preserves dual feasibility and enables the forest or matching to grow. The algorithm returns a maximum-weight perfect matching after at most n squared dual updates and runs in O(n to the fourth) time under the stated implementation bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ terminates as a maximum-weight perfect matching, with at most }n^2\text{ dual updates and total time }O(n^4).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Alternating-tree algorithm for perfect bipartite matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Repeated tree extension and augmentation with explicit positive and negative termination outcomes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a bipartite graph G, initialize M=\varnothing. Choose an M-exposed vertex r and initialize T to the one-vertex tree rooted at r. While there is an edge vw with v\in B(T) and w\notin V(T), augment M along the resulting augmenting path when w is M-exposed, restarting from an exposed root if one remains; otherwise extend T through w and the matching edge covering w. Return M when no M-exposed vertex remains. If no eligible edge leaves B(T), conclude that G has no perfect matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start with the empty matching and grow an alternating tree from an exposed vertex. Reaching an exposed outside vertex produces an augmentation and restart; reaching a covered outside vertex extends the tree through its matched partner. The procedure returns a perfect matching when all vertices are covered and otherwise reports nonexistence when the tree can neither extend nor augment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure returns a perfect matching of }G\text{ or concludes that }G\text{ has none.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unique-min condition for an auxiliary exchange graph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the exchange graph, its matching value, and the stated bound and equality condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x,y\in\mathbf Z^V\) with \(x\in\operatorname{dom}_{\mathbf Z}f\) and \(\|x-y\|_\infty=1\), set \(V^+=\operatorname{supp}^+(x-y)\), \(V^-=\operatorname{supp}^-(x-y)\), \(E=\{(u,v)\mid u\in V^+,\ v\in V^-,\ x-\chi_u+\chi_v\in\operatorname{dom}_{\mathbf Z}f\}\), and \(c(u,v)=\Delta f(x;v,u)\). The pair \((x,y)\) satisfies the unique-min condition if this weighted bipartite graph has exactly one minimum-weight perfect matching. Let \(\check f(x,y)\) be the minimum perfect-matching weight, with \(\check f(x,y)=+\infty\) if no perfect matching exists. Then \(f(y)-f(x)\geq\check f(x,y)\), and the unique-min condition is sufficient for equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The auxiliary exchange graph has positive- and negative-support vertices and feasible unit exchanges as edges, weighted by exchange differences of f. The unique-min condition means that it has exactly one minimum-weight perfect matching. Its matching value is positive infinity when no perfect matching exists, lower-bounds the function difference, and equals that difference under the unique-min condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(y)-f(x)\geq\check f(x,y),\qquad \text{unique-min}\Longrightarrow f(y)-f(x)=\check f(x,y).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Potential characterization of a unique minimum-weight perfect matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes uniqueness in a balanced weighted bipartite graph through an ordering and reduced-cost sign pattern.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V^+,V^-;E)\) be bipartite with \(|V^+|=|V^-|=m\), and let \(c:V^+\times V^-\to\mathbf R\cup\{+\infty\}\) satisfy \(c(u,v)<+\infty\iff (u,v)\in E\). A unique minimum-weight perfect matching exists if and only if there are a potential \(\widehat p:V^+\cup V^-\to\mathbf R\) and orderings \(V^+=\{u_1,\ldots,u_m\}\), \(V^-=\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}\) such that \(c(u_i,v_j)+\widehat p(u_i)-\widehat p(v_j)=0\) for \(i=j\), is nonnegative for \(j<i\), and is strictly positive for \(i<j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A balanced weighted bipartite graph has a unique minimum-weight perfect matching exactly when its two vertex classes can be ordered and assigned potentials so that diagonal reduced costs are zero, reduced costs below the diagonal are nonnegative, and those above the diagonal are strictly positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists!\text{ minimum-weight perfect matching}\iff\exists\widehat p,(u_i)_{i=1}^m,(v_i)_{i=1}^m:\ c(u_i,v_j)+\widehat p(u_i)-\widehat p(v_j)\begin{cases}=0&i=j,\\ \geq0&j<i,\\ >0&i<j.\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual-potential certificate for a minimum-weight perfect bipartite matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes an optimal perfect matching through nonnegative reduced costs that vanish on its edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V^+,V^-;E)\) be a bipartite graph admitting a perfect matching, with \(|V^+|=|V^-|=m\), and let \(c:V^+\times V^-\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) satisfy \(c(u,v)<+\infty\iff (u,v)\in E\). Then there exist a potential \(\widehat p:V^+\cup V^-\to\mathbb R\) and enumerations \(V^+=\{u_1,\ldots,u_m\}\), \(V^-=\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}\) such that \(c(u_i,v_j)+\widehat p(u_i)-\widehat p(v_j)\ge 0\) for all \(i,j\), with equality when \(i=j\). Consequently, \(\{(u_i,v_i):1\le i\le m\}\) is a minimum-weight perfect matching and its weight is \(\sum_{i=1}^m(\widehat p(v_i)-\widehat p(u_i))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every bipartite graph having a perfect matching and every real edge-cost function extended by positive infinity to nonedges, one can order both vertex classes and assign real vertex potentials so that every reduced cost is nonnegative and the paired edges have zero reduced cost. Those paired edges form a minimum-weight perfect matching, whose weight equals the corresponding dual-potential sum.
assumptions_latex: G=(V^+,V^-;E)\text{ is bipartite and admits a perfect matching}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\widehat p,\,(u_1,\ldots,u_m),\,(v_1,\ldots,v_m):\ c(u_i,v_j)+\widehat p(u_i)-\widehat p(v_j)\ge0\ \forall i,j,\quad c(u_i,v_i)+\widehat p(u_i)-\widehat p(v_i)=0\ \forall i;\quad \{(u_i,v_i)\}_{i=1}^m\text{ is minimum-weight and }\operatorname{OPT}=\sum_{i=1}^m(\widehat p(v_i)-\widehat p(u_i)).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(S,T;E)$ be bipartite. There exists a forest $F\subseteq E$ such that $d_F(s)=2$ for every $s\in S$ if and only if $|\Gamma_G(X)|\ge |X|+1$ for every nonempty $X\subseteq S$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bipartite graph contains a forest in which every vertex of one shore has degree exactly two if and only if every nonempty subset of that shore has at least one more neighbor than its cardinality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\exists F\subseteq E:\ (S\cup T,F)\text{ is a forest and }d_F(s)=2\ \forall s\in S\bigr)\iff\bigl(\forall\varnothing\ne X\subseteq S,\ |\Gamma_G(X)|\ge |X|+1\bigr)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extension of a Matching-Covered Subset to Maximum Cardinality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extension property for subsets of one side of a bipartite graph that can be saturated by a matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(S,T;E)\) be bipartite. If \(X\subseteq S\) is covered by some matching, then there is a set \(X'\subseteq S\), covered by some matching, such that \(X\subseteq X'\) and \(|X'|=\nu(G)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every subset of the S-side that can be covered by a matching is contained in another matching-coverable subset of S whose size equals the maximum matching cardinality.
assumptions_latex: X\text{ is covered by a matching}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists X'\subseteq S:\ X\subseteq X',\ |X'|=\nu(G),\text{ and }X'\text{ is covered by a matching}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hall's Criterion for Covering One Colour Class
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes when a bipartite matching covers one specified colour class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(V,E)$ be a bipartite graph with colour classes $U$ and $W$. Then $G$ has a matching covering $U$ if and only if $|N(S)|\geq |S|$ for every $S\subseteq U$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bipartite graph has a matching covering U if and only if every subset S of U has at least |S| neighbors.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\exists\text{ a matching covering }U\bigr)\iff\bigl(\forall S\subseteq U,\ |N(S)|\geq |S|\bigr).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hall's Theorem for Systems of Distinct Representatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence criterion for a system of distinct representatives of a finite indexed set family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite indexed family \(\mathcal F=(S_1,\ldots,S_n)\) has a system of distinct representatives if and only if, for every \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \[\left|\bigcup_{i\in I}S_i\right|\ge |I|.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite indexed family has a system of distinct representatives exactly when the union of every subfamily contains at least as many elements as that subfamily has members.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F=(S_1,\ldots,S_n)\) is a finite indexed family of sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F\text{ has an SDR}\iff \forall I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\},\ \left|\bigcup_{i\in I}S_i\right|\ge |I|.\)

children.title: Matching Deficiency Regimes
children.top_down_role: Coverage shortfalls measured through unmatched vertices or neighborhood deficits.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(L\dot\cup R,E)\) is a finite bipartite graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nu(G)=|L|-\delta_L(G)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The deficiency of \(L\) is \[\delta_L(G):=\max_{X\subseteq L}\bigl(|X|-|N_G(X)|\bigr).\] The deficiency form of the bipartite matching theorem states \[\nu(G)=|L|-\delta_L(G).\] Thus every matching leaves at least \(\delta_L(G)\) vertices of \(L\) uncovered, and some maximum matching leaves exactly that many uncovered.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Left-side deficiency is the largest neighborhood shortfall, and it exactly equals the minimum number of left vertices left unmatched.

children.title: Neighborhood Surplus Regimes
children.top_down_role: Positive neighborhood margins supporting robust matchability.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(L\dot\cup R,E)\) is a finite bipartite graph with \(L\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) has left neighborhood surplus at least \(k\) if and only if \(|N_G(X)|-|X|\ge k\) for every nonempty \(X\subseteq L\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform additive Hall surplus on a nonempty designated color class.

source_refs.locator: Section 10.1. Bipartite Matching p. 246

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(L\ne\varnothing\), define \[\sigma_L(G):=\min_{\varnothing\ne X\subseteq L}\bigl(|N_G(X)|-|X|\bigr).\] The neighborhood-surplus-\(k\) regime is the condition \(\sigma_L(G)\ge k\), equivalently \[|N_G(X)|\ge |X|+k\qquad\text{for every nonempty }X\subseteq L.\] For \(k=0\), this is Hall's condition for a matching saturating \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty left color class, neighborhood surplus at least k means every nonempty left subset has at least k more neighbors than its own size.
knowledge_statements.title: Neighborhood Surplus Regimes

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Augmentation Characterization of Bipartite Surplus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of surplus by robustness to duplicating a left-side vertex neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(A,B;E)\) be a bipartite graph with \(\operatorname{def}(G)=0\). Then \(\sigma(G)\) is the largest integer \(s\) such that, for every \(x\in A\), adding \(s\) new vertices to \(A\), each adjacent to all vertices of \(\Gamma(x)\), yields a bipartite graph with nonnegative surplus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a deficiency-zero bipartite graph, its surplus is the largest integer s such that duplicating the neighborhood of any left-side vertex on s new left-side vertices preserves nonnegative surplus.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sigma(G)=\max\left\{s\in\mathbb Z:\forall x\in A,\text{ the stated }s\text{-vertex augmentation has surplus }\ge 0\right\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Neighborhood Surplus and Surplus-Tight Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines set and graph surplus, records its sign relation to deficiency and its submodularity, and defines surplus-tight sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(A,B;E)\) be bipartite. For \(X\subseteq A\), define \(\sigma_G(X)=|\Gamma_G(X)|-|X|=-\operatorname{def}_G(X)\), and define \(\sigma(G)=\min_{\varnothing\neq Z\subseteq A}\sigma_G(Z)\). Then \(\operatorname{def}(G)=\max\{0,-\sigma(G)\}\). Moreover, for all \(X,Y\subseteq A\), \[\sigma_G(X\cup Y)+\sigma_G(X\cap Y)\leq \sigma_G(X)+\sigma_G(Y).\] A set \(X\subseteq A\) is \(\sigma\)-tight if \(\sigma_G(X)=\sigma(G)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set's surplus is its number of neighbors minus its size, while graph surplus is the minimum over nonempty subsets of side A. It is the negative of set deficiency, determines graph deficiency after truncation at zero, is submodular, and its minimizers are called sigma-tight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sigma_G(X)=-\operatorname{def}_G(X),\quad \operatorname{def}(G)=\max\{0,-\sigma(G)\},\quad \sigma_G(X\cup Y)+\sigma_G(X\cap Y)\leq\sigma_G(X)+\sigma_G(Y),\quad X\text{ is }\sigma\text{-tight}\iff\sigma_G(X)=\sigma(G).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: König–Egerváry Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bipartite matching–vertex-cover min–max equality, together with its equivalent binary-matrix formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every bipartite graph $G$, the maximum cardinality $\nu(G)$ of a matching equals the minimum cardinality $\tau(G)$ of a vertex cover. Equivalently, for every $A\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}$, the maximum number of $1$-entries with no two in a common row or column equals the minimum number of rows and columns whose union contains every $1$-entry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a bipartite graph, maximum matching size equals minimum vertex-cover size. Equivalently, in a binary matrix, the largest collection of 1s sharing no row or column has the same size as the smallest collection of rows and columns covering all 1s.
assumptions_latex: For the equivalent matrix formulation, $A\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}$.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nu(G)=\tau(G);\qquad \max\{|S|:S\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(A),\ S\text{ contains at most one entry from each row and column}\}=\min\{|L|:L\text{ is a collection of rows and columns covering }\operatorname{supp}(A)\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mendelsohn–Dulmage Matching Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coverage-preserving amalgamation of two matchings on opposite vertex classes of a bipartite graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G=(S,T,A) be a bipartite graph, and let X_1 and X_2 be matchings in G. Then there exists a matching X\subseteq X_1\cup X_2 such that X covers every vertex of S covered by X_1 and every vertex of T covered by X_2.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given two matchings in a bipartite graph, one can select a matching from their combined edges that preserves the first matching's covered vertices on the S side and the second matching's covered vertices on the T side.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists X\subseteq X_1\cup X_2\text{ such that }X\text{ is a matching, }V(X_1)\cap S\subseteq V(X)\cap S,\text{ and }V(X_2)\cap T\subseteq V(X)\cap T.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Frobenius Marriage Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence characterization for perfect matchings in bipartite graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be bipartite with bipartition \(V=A\mathbin{\dot\cup}B\). Then \(G\) has a perfect matching if and only if \(|A|=|B|\) and \(|N(X)|\ge |X|\) for every \(X\subseteq A\), where \(N(X)\subseteq B\) is the neighbor set of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bipartite graph with parts A and B has a perfect matching exactly when the parts have equal size and every subset of A has at least as many neighbors in B as vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ has a perfect matching}\iff \bigl(|A|=|B|\land\forall X\subseteq A,\ |N(X)|\ge |X|\bigr)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Egerváry’s weighted matching–cover theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted bipartite matching duality, including integral optimal covers for integral weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be bipartite and let $w:E\to\mathbb{R}_+$. Then
\[
\max\left\{\sum_{e\in M}w_e:M\text{ is a matching in }G\right\}
=
\min\left\{\sum_{v\in V}y_v:y\in\mathbb{R}_+^V,\ y_u+y_v\geq w_{uv}\ \forall uv\in E\right\}.
\]
If $w\in\mathbb{Z}_+^E$, the minimum admits an optimal solution in $\mathbb{Z}_+^V$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a bipartite graph with nonnegative edge weights, the maximum weight of a matching equals the minimum total nonnegative vertex weight whose endpoint sums dominate the edge weights. Integral edge weights admit an integral optimal vertex weighting.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max_{M\text{ matching}}\sum_{e\in M}w_e=\min_{\substack{y\in\mathbb{R}_+^V\\y_u+y_v\geq w_{uv}\ \forall uv\in E}}\sum_{v\in V}y_v,\quad w\in\mathbb{Z}_+^E\Rightarrow\operatorname*{argmin}_{\substack{y\in\mathbb{R}_+^V\\y_u+y_v\geq w_{uv}}}\sum_{v\in V}y_v\cap\mathbb{Z}_+^V\neq\varnothing

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximum-weight bipartite matching–covering duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Min-max duality for arbitrary matchings with nonnegative edge weights in a bipartite graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G'=(S',T';E')\) be a bipartite graph and let \(c:E'\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\). If \(\nu'_c\) is the maximum \(c\)-weight of a matching and \(\tau'_c\) is the minimum of \(\sum_{v\in S'\cup T'}\pi(v)\) over all nonnegative functions \(\pi:S'\cup T'\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) satisfying \(\pi(u)+\pi(v)\ge c(uv)\) for every \(uv\in E'\), then \(\nu'_c=\tau'_c\). If \(c\) is integer-valued, an optimal \(\pi\) can be chosen integer-valued.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a bipartite graph with nonnegative edge weights, the maximum weight of any matching equals the minimum total value of a nonnegative weighted vertex covering. With integer edge weights, an optimal nonnegative covering can be chosen integer-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nu'_c=\tau'_c;\qquad c(E')\subseteq\mathbb Z\Rightarrow\exists\pi^*\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{S'\cup T'}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted perfect-matching and vertex-potential covering duality in bipartite graphs, including integrality and nonnegativity refinements.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integral weighted vertex cover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The integral cover object used on the cover side of weighted matching–cover duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(V,E)$ be a graph and $w\in\mathbb{Z}_+^E$. A $w$-vertex cover is a vector $y\in\mathbb{Z}_+^V$ such that $y_u+y_v\geq w_{uv}$ for every edge $uv\in E$. For any $y\in\mathbb{R}^V$, its size is $y(V):=\sum_{v\in V}y_v$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A w-vertex cover assigns nonnegative integers to vertices so that the values at the endpoints of each edge sum to at least the edge's integral weight. The size of a vector is the sum of its components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y\text{ is a }w\text{-vertex cover}\iff y\in\mathbb{Z}_+^V\text{ and }y_u+y_v\geq w_{uv}\ \forall uv\in E;\qquad y(V)=\sum_{v\in V}y_v

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matching Number, Vertex-Cover Number, and Weak Inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions of the two cardinality parameters, their universal weak inequality, and the failure of equality for general graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A vertex cover of a graph \(G\) is a set \(C\subseteq V(G)\) meeting every edge. Define \(
u(G)=\max\{|M|:M	ext{ is a matching in }G\}\) and \(	au(G)=\min\{|C|:C	ext{ is a vertex cover of }G\}\). For every graph \(G\), \(
u(G)\leq	au(G)\); equality need not hold, since \(
u(K_3)<	au(K_3)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertex cover meets every edge. The matching number is the maximum matching size, and the vertex-cover number is the minimum cover size. Every graph has matching number at most its vertex-cover number, and the triangle shows that equality can fail.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nu(G)\leq\tau(G),\qquad \nu(K_3)<\tau(K_3).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(S,T;E)\) be a bipartite graph having a perfect matching and let \(c:E\to\mathbb R\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Allowed-edge components and their contracted bipartite graph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction used to decompose a bipartite graph with a perfect matching into elementary components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(U,W)\) be a bipartite graph with a perfect matching, and let \(L_1,\ldots,L_k\), where \(k\ge 1\), be the components of the subgraph consisting of all allowed edges of \(G\). Each \(L_i\) is elementary. Define \(S_i=U\cap V(L_i)\) and \(T_i=W\cap V(L_i)\). The graph \(G_0\) is obtained by shrinking every \(S_i\) and every \(T_i\) to a vertex and replacing each resulting set of parallel edges by one edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a bipartite graph with a perfect matching, the allowed-edge subgraph has elementary components. Contracting the two color-class portions of each component separately and suppressing parallel edges produces a bipartite quotient graph.
assumptions_latex: G=(U,W)\text{ is a bipartite graph with a perfect matching.}
L_1,\ldots,L_k\text{ are the components of the subgraph consisting of all allowed edges of }G.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall i\in\{1,\ldots,k\},\ L_i\text{ is elementary};\quad S_i=U\cap V(L_i),\ T_i=W\cap V(L_i),\text{ and }G_0\text{ is obtained by contracting all }S_i,T_i\text{ separately and suppressing parallel edges.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Characterizations of Elementary Bipartite Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes elementary bipartite graphs through minimum vertex covers, strict Hall expansion, opposite-color vertex deletion, and allowed edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a bipartite graph with bipartition \((U,W)\). The following are equivalent: (i) \(G\) is elementary; (ii) \(G\) has exactly two minimum vertex covers, namely \(U\) and \(W\); (iii) \(|U|=|W|\) and \(|\Gamma(X)|\ge |X|+1\) for every nonempty proper subset \(X\subset U\); (iv) either \(G=K_2\), or \(|V(G)|\ge4\) and \(G-u-w\) has a perfect matching for every \(u\in U\) and \(w\in W\); (v) \(G\) is connected and every edge of \(G\) is allowed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a bipartite graph, being elementary is equivalent to having only its two color classes as minimum vertex covers, satisfying strict Hall expansion on every nonempty proper subset of one class, retaining a perfect matching after deletion of any opposite-color pair except for the stated K2 case, and being connected with every edge allowed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Conditions (i)--(v) are equivalent.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mace Matroids and the Parameter m_{p,k}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of the (m,n)-mace and an associated prime-power parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For integers $m\le n$, the $(m,n)$-mace is the matroid obtained by freely adding one point to the cycle matroid $M(K_{m,n})$. For a prime $p$ and an integer $k>1$, define
\[
m_{p,k}=\begin{cases}(k-1)(p-1)+1,&p\ge 3,\\ k-1,&p=2.\end{cases}
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For m≤n, the (m,n)-mace is obtained by freely adding a point to the cycle matroid of the complete bipartite graph K_{m,n}. For prime p and integer k>1, m_{p,k} equals (k−1)(p−1)+1 when p≥3 and k−1 when p=2.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bipartite Ear Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the iterative odd-ear construction for bipartite graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Begin with an edge \(x\), and join its endpoints by an odd-length path \(P_1\). notation.meaning: Set of allowed edges of G

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the perfect-matching sense of allowed edges in a factorizable bipartite graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An edge \(e\in E\) is allowed if some perfect matching \(M\) of \(G\) contains \(e\). Let \(E_{\mathrm{al}}=\{e\in E:e\in M\text{ for some perfect matching }M\}\). The allowed-edge components of \(G\) are the vertex sets of the connected components of the spanning subgraph \((U,V;E_{\mathrm{al}})\). Thus two vertices lie in the same allowed-edge component exactly when they are joined by a path consisting entirely of allowed edges.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an exposed vertex \(u\in U\), initialize \(\operatorname{seen}(x)=0\) for every \(x\in U\). Define \(\operatorname{search}(x)\) to fail if \(\operatorname{seen}(x)=1\); otherwise set \(\operatorname{seen}(x)=1\) and inspect each \(y\in N(x)\). If \(y\) is exposed, match \(x\) to \(y\) and return success. If \(y\) is matched to \(z\) and \(\operatorname{search}(z)\) succeeds, replace \(zy\) by \(xy\) and return success. knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the one-path-per-success regime of the Kuhn algorithm family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Because an \(M\)-augmenting path \(P\) begins and ends with unmatched edges and alternates between edges outside and inside \(M\), it contains exactly one more unmatched than matched edge. knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard unweighted bipartite Hopcroft–Karp algorithm and adjacency-list bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(M=\varnothing\). In each phase, breadth-first search the alternating graph from all exposed vertices of \(U\), retaining layers through the first exposed vertices of \(V\); let \(\ell\) be their common shortest augmenting-path length. Using depth-first searches restricted to consecutive layers, find a maximal family \(\mathcal P\) of pairwise vertex-disjoint augmenting paths of length \(\ell\), and set \(M\leftarrow M\triangle\bigcup_{P\in\mathcal P}E(P)\). Stop when breadth-first search reaches no exposed vertex of \(V\), and output \(M\). With adjacency lists, the total running time is \(O(m\sqrt n)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructive minimum-cover certificate obtained from a maximum matching search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Form the alternating orientation relative to \(M\), and let \(Z\) be the vertices reachable from exposed vertices of \(U\). If no exposed vertex of \(V\) is reachable, define \(C=(U\setminus Z)\cup(V\cap Z)\). Every edge has an endpoint in \(C\), so \(C\) is a vertex cover. Moreover each edge of \(M\) has exactly one endpoint in \(C\), while every vertex of \(C\) is incident with an edge of \(M\). Hence \(|C|=|M|\), and the pair \((M,C)\) is directly verifiable as a maximum-matching and minimum-cover certificate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted coverings and tight edges
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual covering terminology for weighted perfect matching in a bipartite graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(S,T;E)\) be a bipartite graph having a perfect matching and let \(c:E\to\mathbb R\). A function \(\pi:S\cup T\to\mathbb R\) is a weighted covering of \(c\) if \(\pi(u)+\pi(v)\ge c(uv)\) for every \(uv\in E\). An edge \(uv\) is tight with respect to \(\pi\) if \(\pi(u)+\pi(v)=c(uv)\). The total value of \(\pi\) is \(\widetilde\pi(V)=\sum_{v\in V}\pi(v)\), where \(V=S\cup T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a bipartite graph with a perfect matching and edge weights c, a weighted covering assigns real values to the vertices so that the sum at the endpoints of every edge is at least its weight. An edge is tight when equality holds, and the covering's total value is the sum of all vertex values.
assumptions_latex: G=(S,T;E)\text{ is bipartite and has a perfect matching}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \pi\text{ is a weighted covering}\iff (\forall uv\in E)\;\pi(u)+\pi(v)\ge c(uv);\quad uv\text{ is tight}\iff\pi(u)+\pi(v)=c(uv);\quad\widetilde\pi(V)=\sum_{v\in V}\pi(v).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Balanced Minimum-Cost Assignment and Its Transportation LP Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formulates balanced minimum-cost assignment and states the integrality guarantee of its unit-supply, unit-demand transportation relaxation, including the solver-output boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let |\mathcal S|=|\mathcal D|=m, with assignment costs c_{ij}. The balanced assignment problem is \(\min \sum_{i\in\mathcal S}\sum_{j\in\mathcal D}c_{ij}x_{ij}\), subject to \(\sum_{j\in\mathcal D}x_{ij}=1\) for every \(i\in\mathcal S\), \(\sum_{i\in\mathcal S}x_{ij}=1\) for every \(j\in\mathcal D\), and \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\). Replacing \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) by \(x_{ij}\ge 0\) yields a Hitchcock transportation LP with unit supplies and demands. Every assignment is feasible for the relaxation, and every integral relaxation-feasible point is an assignment. Network simplex produces an integral optimal solution of this relaxation and therefore solves the assignment problem. Without a unique optimum, an interior-point method is not guaranteed to return an integral optimal point; if the optimum is unique, every LP solver returns that integral optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For equal-sized sets of people and tasks, balanced minimum-cost assignment assigns each person to exactly one task and covers each task exactly once. Dropping binary restrictions gives a transportation LP with unit supplies and demands. Network simplex returns an integral optimum and thus solves the assignment problem. When alternate optima exist, an interior-point method is not guaranteed to return an integral optimum; a unique optimum is integral and common to all LP solvers.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Network simplex obtains an integral optimum of the assignment LP relaxation; interior-point output is not guaranteed integral when the optimal face is non-singleton.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Classical square assignment formulation and polyhedral structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded representation and structural properties of the classical square minimum-cost assignment problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(P_m=\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{m\times m}:\sum_jx_{ij}=1\ \forall i,\ \sum_ix_{ij}=1\ \forall j\}\). The classical assignment problem minimizes \(\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}x_{ij}\) over binary \(x\), but total unimodularity of its bipartite incidence matrix permits replacement of \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) by \(x\ge 0\). The vertices of \(P_m\) are exactly the \(m!\) permutation matrices. In a transportation-basis representation, each vertex has \(m\) positive unit variables and \(m-1\) zero basic variables, and is represented by \(2^{m-1}m^{m-2}\) bases. Any balanced transportation problem with nonnegative integral supplies and demands can be expanded into an assignment problem by making one copy per unit of supply and demand. Moreover, any two distinct vertices are adjacent or have a third vertex adjacent to both.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The square assignment problem is a unit-supply, unit-demand transportation model. Its nonnegative LP relaxation is integral, and its vertices are precisely the permutation matrices. Transportation bases representing these vertices contain m positive unit arcs and m−1 degenerate zero arcs. Integral balanced transportation problems can be expanded into assignment problems by copying supply and demand units.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{vert}(P_m)=\{\text{permutation matrices of order }m\},\qquad |\operatorname{vert}(P_m)|=m!.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Square Minimum-Cost Assignment Formulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the balanced one-to-one minimum-cost assignment problem, its binary-matrix formulation, and the associated doubly stochastic and permutation matrix classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For costs \(c_{ij}\) on \(n\) persons and \(n\) jobs, a feasible assignment is a permutation \((p_1,\ldots,p_n)\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with cost \(\sum_{i=1}^n c_{i p_i}\). Equivalently, it is represented by \(X=(x_{ij})\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) satisfying \(\sum_{j=1}^n x_{ij}=1\) for every \(i\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^n x_{ij}=1\) for every \(j\), and minimizes \(\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}x_{ij}\). A nonnegative square matrix whose row and column sums are all one is doubly stochastic; such a matrix is a permutation matrix when all entries are binary. The permutation formulation has \(n!\) feasible assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A square minimum-cost assignment pairs each of n persons with exactly one of n jobs and minimizes total selected cost. Feasible assignments are permutations, equivalently binary matrices with every row and column sum equal to one. Nonnegative matrices with these sums are doubly stochastic, and binary ones are permutation matrices. There are n! possible assignments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{X\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n c_{ij}x_{ij}:\sum_{j=1}^n x_{ij}=1\ \forall i,\ \sum_{i=1}^n x_{ij}=1\ \forall j\right\}

children.title: Objective-Convention Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Transformations connecting reward-maximization with cost-minimization formulations.

assumptions_latex: There are \(n\) assigned edges in every feasible assignment.
Weights \(w_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}\) are converted to costs by \(c_{ij}=K-w_{ij}\), where \(K\in\mathbb{R}\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maximum-weight and transformed minimum-cost problems have identical optimal assignments, with \(C^*=nK-W^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine conversion for fixed-cardinality perfect assignments.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.1 The Minimum Cost Flow Problem p. 9

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every feasible assignment \(\pi\in S_n\), define \(W(\pi)=\sum_iw_{i,\pi(i)}\) and \(C(\pi)=\sum_ic_{i,\pi(i)}\). If \(c_{ij}=K-w_{ij}\), then
\[
C(\pi)=nK-W(\pi).
\]
Consequently, \(W(\pi)\geq W(\sigma)\) if and only if \(C(\pi)\leq C(\sigma)\) for all \(\pi,\sigma\in S_n\). Thus the maximizers of \(W\) are exactly the minimizers of \(C\), and their optimal values satisfy \(C^*=nK-W^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtracting every weight from one fixed constant converts maximization to minimization without changing the optimal perfect assignments.

children.title: Bottleneck Assignment
children.top_down_role: Assignment quality governed by the worst selected edge value.

assumptions_latex: The bipartite graph is complete and balanced, with finite edge costs \(c_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A bottleneck-optimal assignment minimizes \(\max_i c_{i,\pi(i)}\) over \(\pi\in S_n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization form of the bottleneck assignment problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an assignment \(\pi\in S_n\), its bottleneck cost is
\[
b(\pi)=\max_{1\leq i\leq n}c_{i,\pi(i)}.
\]
The bottleneck assignment problem seeks
\[
b^*=\min_{\pi\in S_n}b(\pi).
\]
An assignment \(\pi^*\) is bottleneck-optimal precisely when \(b(\pi^*)=b^*\). Unlike the ordinary minimum-cost assignment, this objective depends only on the largest selected edge cost and does not distinguish assignments having the same largest cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize the largest edge cost appearing in a perfect assignment, without regard to the sum of its selected costs.
knowledge_statements.title: Bottleneck Assignment

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The minimax definition is precise and standard, but the record supplies no citation supporting the selected minimization convention for bottleneck assignment.

children.title: Lexicographic Assignment
children.top_down_role: Assignment quality governed by an ordered hierarchy of selected values.

assumptions_latex: The bipartite graph is complete and balanced, with finite edge costs \(c_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}\).
Selected costs are sorted in nonincreasing order before comparison.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A lexicographically optimal assignment minimizes its nonincreasing sorted cost vector in lexicographic order.

notation.meaning: nonincreasing rearrangement of the costs selected by \(\pi\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lexicographic bottleneck minimization of sorted selected costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\pi\in S_n\), let \(s(\pi)=(s_1(\pi),\ldots,s_n(\pi))\) be the costs \(c_{i,\pi(i)}\) sorted so that \(s_1(\pi)\geq\cdots\geq s_n(\pi)\). An assignment \(\pi^*\) is lexicographically optimal when
\[
s(\pi^*)\leq_{\mathrm{lex}}s(\pi)\qquad\text{for every }\pi\in S_n.
\]
Thus it first minimizes the largest selected cost; subject to that, it minimizes the second largest selected cost, and continues through all coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sort each assignment's selected costs from largest to smallest, then minimize the resulting vector lexicographically.
knowledge_statements.title: Lexicographic Assignment

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nonincreasing-vector lexicographic minimization variant is internally correct, but no source supports this specific assignment convention.

children.title: Bottleneck–Lexicographic Refinement
children.top_down_role: Refinement relationships between worst-value optimization plus lexicographic comparison.

assumptions_latex: Assignments are compared through their selected costs sorted in nonincreasing order.
The bottleneck objective minimizes the first coordinate of that sorted vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every lexicographically optimal assignment is bottleneck-optimal, and subsequent coordinates refine ties successively.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relation between bottleneck and lexicographic minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Because \(s_1(\pi)=\max_i c_{i,\pi(i)}\), any assignment minimizing \(s(\pi)\) lexicographically also minimizes the bottleneck value. More precisely, let \(\mathcal{P}_0=S_n\) and recursively define
\[
\alpha_k=\min_{\pi\in\mathcal{P}_{k-1}}s_k(\pi),\qquad
\mathcal{P}_k=\{\pi\in\mathcal{P}_{k-1}:s_k(\pi)=\alpha_k\}.
\]
Then \(\alpha_1=b^*\), \(\mathcal{P}_1\) is the set of bottleneck-optimal assignments, and \(\mathcal{P}_n\) is exactly the set of lexicographically optimal assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lexicographic optimization first solves the bottleneck problem, then successively breaks ties using the next-largest selected costs.
knowledge_statements.title: Bottleneck–Lexicographic Refinement

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The refinement relation is correct under the preceding nonincreasing minimization convention, but neither that convention nor the refinement claim has cited support.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hungarian primal-dual augmentation algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithmic specification for balanced minimum-cost assignment using dual potentials, tight edges, slack values, and augmentations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a nonnegative integer cost matrix \(C=(c_{ij})\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^{n\times n}\), initialize an empty matching and dual potentials \(\alpha_i=0\), \(\beta_j=\min_i c_{ij}\). At each of \(n\) stages, search the tight-edge structure \(\alpha_i+\beta_j=c_{ij}\) for an augmenting path. If none is available, update the potentials using the minimum positive slack, activate newly tight edges, resume the search, and augment. After the \(n\) stages, return the resulting complete matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonnegative integer n-by-n cost matrix, the Hungarian method starts with an empty matching and feasible vertex potentials. Each stage searches tight edges for an augmenting path; when the search stalls, it changes the potentials by the minimum positive slack to create new tight edges and continues. After n augmentations it returns an optimal complete matching.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The algorithm returns an optimal complete matching of }B\text{ under costs }c_{ij}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The linear-programming dual of the maximum-weight assignment problem is
\[
\min\left\{\sum_{i\in L}u_i+\sum_{j\in R}v_j: u_i+v_j\geq w_{ij}\text{ for all }(i,j)\in L\times R\right\},
\]
where \(u_i,v_j\in\mathbb{R}\) are unrestricted. Every feasible pair \((u,v)\) gives an upper bound on every assignment weight. A feasible assignment and feasible potentials are simultaneously optimal when each assigned edge satisfies \(u_i+v_j=w_{ij}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vertex potentials dominate every edge weight; minimizing their total gives the dual assignment problem, with equality on optimally assigned edges.
