knowledge_statements.statement_title: Assignment Complementary Slackness Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Establishes simultaneous primal and dual optimality and equality of values for a feasible assignment-price pair satisfying complementary slackness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a feasible assignment and prices $p=(p_1,\ldots,p_n)$ satisfy complementary slackness for every assigned person $i$. Then the assignment is optimal, $p$ minimizes $D(p)=\sum_{i=1}^n q_i(p)+\sum_{j=1}^n p_j$, where $q_i(p)=\max_{j\in A(i)}\{a_{ij}-p_j\}$, and the optimal assignment value equals the optimal dual cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a feasible assignment and its prices satisfy complementary slackness for every person, both are optimal for their respective primal and dual problems, and their optimal values are equal.
assumptions_latex: \text{The assignment is feasible and complementary slackness holds for every assigned person.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The assignment is primal optimal, }p\in\arg\min D(p),\text{ and }\operatorname{OPT}_{\rm primal}=\min_p D(p).

children.title: Reduced-Cost Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometric structure induced by reduced edge costs.

assumptions_latex: Potentials \((u,v)\) satisfy \(u_i+v_j\geq w_{ij}\) for every edge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every reduced cost \(r_{ij}=u_i+v_j-w_{ij}\) is nonnegative, and zero reduced cost identifies the equality graph.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-slack geometry under the maximum-weight convention.

source_refs.locator: 1.3.2 Dual Cost Improvement p. 24

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For feasible dual potentials, define the reduced-cost slack of edge \((i,j)\) by
\[
r_{ij}=u_i+v_j-w_{ij}\geq0.
\]
The equality graph is
\[
E_0(u,v)=\{(i,j)\in L\times R:r_{ij}=0\}.
\]
Thus dual feasibility places every weighted edge on or below the additive potential surface \(u_i+v_j\); equality edges lie on that surface. For any assignment \(\pi\), its duality gap equals \(\sum_i r_{i,\pi(i)}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reduced costs are nonnegative dual slacks; zero-slack edges form the equality graph, and assigned slacks sum to the duality gap.

children.title: Tight-Edge Structure
children.top_down_role: Edges selected by equality between primal costs plus dual potentials.

assumptions_latex: An assignment \(\pi\) and dual potentials \((u,v)\) are feasible for the maximum-weight primal-dual pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair is optimal exactly when every assigned edge is tight; hence any perfect matching contained in the equality graph is optimal.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complementary-slackness certificate for assignment optimality.

source_refs.locator: 1.3.2 Dual Cost Improvement p. 24

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every feasible assignment \(\pi\),
\[
\sum_i u_i+\sum_jv_j-\sum_iw_{i,\pi(i)}=
\sum_i\bigl(u_i+v_{\pi(i)}-w_{i,\pi(i)}\bigr)=\sum_i r_{i,\pi(i)}.
\]
All terms are nonnegative. Therefore the primal and dual objectives agree exactly when \(r_{i,\pi(i)}=0\) for every \(i\). Consequently, feasible potentials together with a perfect matching wholly contained in \(E_0(u,v)\) form a directly checkable optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible perfect matching is optimal exactly when all its edges have zero reduced cost under feasible dual potentials.

children.top_down_role: Alternating search restricted to tight edges of the assignment instance.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(S\) with the unmatched vertices of \(L\) and set \(T=\varnothing\). Repeatedly traverse an equality edge \((i,j)\in E_0(u,v)\setminus M\) from \(i\in S\) to \(j\notin T\), add \(j\) to \(T\), and record its predecessor. If \(j\) is unmatched, output the resulting alternating augmenting path. Otherwise, if \((i',j)\in M\), add \(i'\) to \(S\). Stop with boundary \((S,T)\) when no further equality edge leaves \(S\) toward \(R\setminus T\).

children.title: Equality-Graph Augmentation
children.top_down_role: Matching enlargement supported by paths in the equality graph.

assumptions_latex: The current matching \(M\) consists only of equality edges.
An alternating path \(P\) begins and ends at unmatched vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Replacing \(M\) by \(M\triangle P\) increases its cardinality by one and preserves containment in the equality graph.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given an equality-graph augmenting path \(P\), update the matching by
\[
M' = M\triangle E(P).
\]
That is, remove from \(M\) the matched edges of \(P\) and insert the previously unmatched edges of \(P\). Because \(P\) alternates and both endpoints are unmatched, \(M'\) is a matching with \(|M'|=|M|+1\). Every edge of \(P\) is tight, so \(M'\subseteq E_0(u,v)\); the potentials remain unchanged. Stop when the matching is perfect, otherwise restart equality-graph search.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Flip matching status along a tight augmenting path; the matching grows by one while every matched edge remains tight.
knowledge_statements.title: Equality-Graph Augmentation

children.title: Stalled-Search Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Search configurations requiring a change to the current tight-edge structure.

assumptions_latex: The graph is complete bipartite, potentials are dual feasible, and \(M\) is a nonperfect matching of equality edges.
Equality-graph search stalls with reachable sets \(S\subseteq L\) and \(T\subseteq R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minimum boundary slack is positive, and the stated potential update preserves feasibility while creating a new equality edge from \(S\) to \(R\setminus T\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At a stalled search, no equality edge joins \(S\) to \(R\setminus T\). Set
\[
\delta=\min\{r_{ij}:i\in S,\ j\in R\setminus T\}>0.
\]
Update potentials by \(u'_i=u_i-\delta\) for \(i\in S\), \(v'_j=v_j+\delta\) for \(j\in T\), and leave all other potentials unchanged. Then every dual inequality remains feasible: slacks across \(S\times(R\setminus T)\) decrease by \(\delta\), while no other slack becomes negative. At least one boundary edge becomes tight, so equality-graph search can resume.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When tight-edge search stalls, shift reachable potentials by the smallest boundary slack, preserving feasibility and exposing a new tight edge.
knowledge_statements.title: Stalled-Search Boundaries

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\operatorname{OPT}=\max_{\pi}\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i,\pi(i)}\), where the maximum is over all permutations \(\pi\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Initialize prices \(p_j=0\) and leave all bidders unassigned. While some bidder \(i\) is unassigned, choose an object \(j^*\) maximizing \(a_{ij}-p_j\), let \(w_i\) be the second-largest value in \(\{a_{ij}-p_j:j=1,\ldots,n\}\), and replace \(p_{j^*}\) by \(p_{j^*}+a_{ij^*}-p_{j^*}-w_i+\varepsilon\). Assign \(j^*\) to \(i\), displacing its previous bidder if necessary. Stop when every bidder is assigned and output the resulting permutation \(\sigma\). The output obeys \(\varepsilon\)-complementary slackness and therefore has benefit at least \(\operatorname{OPT}-n\varepsilon\). If all \(a_{ij}\) are integers and \(\varepsilon<1/n\), the output is optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly raise the price of an unassigned bidder's best object and displace its owner. For at least two bidders and objects, the final assignment is within n epsilon of optimal and is exact when benefits are integral and epsilon is less than 1/n.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Auction iteration for the assignment problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies initialization, bidding, object-price updates, reassignment, and the singleton-admissible-set convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Start an iteration with a partial assignment $S$ and prices $p$ satisfying $\epsilon$-CS; $S=\varnothing$ with arbitrary prices is a valid initialization. Choose a nonempty set $I$ of unassigned persons. For each $i\in I$, choose
\[
 j_i\in\arg\max_{j\in A(i)}(a_{ij}-p_j),\qquad v_i=\max_{j\in A(i)}(a_{ij}-p_j),
\]
define
\[
 w_i=\max_{j\in A(i),\,j\ne j_i}(a_{ij}-p_j),\qquad b_{ij_i}=p_{j_i}+v_i-w_i+\epsilon=a_{ij_i}-w_i+\epsilon,
\]
where $w_i=-\infty$, or a sufficiently small computational surrogate, if $A(i)=\{j_i\}$. For every object $j$ receiving bids from the nonempty set $P(j)$, set
\[
 p_j:=\max_{i\in P(j)}b_{ij},
\]
remove the previous pair incident to $j$ if one exists, and add $(i_j,j)$ for a bidder $i_j\in P(j)$ attaining the maximum. Iterate until the assignment is complete.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Selected unassigned persons bid for their best benefit-minus-price objects, raising each bid enough to exceed the second-best value by epsilon. Each object adopts its highest bid as its new price, evicts any former assignee, and is assigned to a highest bidder.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_j\leftarrow\max_{i\in P(j)}b_{ij},\qquad S\leftarrow\bigl(S\setminus\{(h,j)\in S\}\bigr)\cup\{(i_j,j)\}\quad\text{for every }P(j)\ne\varnothing

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epsilon-Auction Algorithm and Termination Guarantee
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perturbed forward-auction bidding that prevents zero increments, preserves epsilon-complementary slackness, and terminates when a feasible assignment exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix $\epsilon>0$. In each iteration, an unassigned person $i$ selects a best object $j_i$ and raises its price by $\gamma_i=v_i-w_i+\epsilon$. This is the largest increment preserving $\epsilon$-complementary slackness for the new pair; an increment satisfying $\epsilon\le\gamma_i\le v_i-w_i+\epsilon$ also preserves that condition. If at least one feasible assignment exists, the auction terminates with a feasible assignment and prices satisfying $\epsilon$-complementary slackness. The final assignment value is within $n\epsilon$ of the optimal assignment value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epsilon-auction adds epsilon to the best-versus-second-best value gap when raising the selected object's price. Positive bids prevent zero-increment cycling; provided a feasible assignment exists, the method terminates with epsilon-complementary slackness and an assignment value within n epsilon of optimal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \gamma_i=v_i-w_i+\epsilon\ge\epsilon;\qquad\text{the process terminates with a feasible }\epsilon\text{-CS assignment, and }0\le\operatorname{OPT}_{\rm primal}-V_{\rm assignment}\le n\epsilon.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Combined forward–reverse assignment auction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Alternation of finite forward- and reverse-auction blocks with prescribed coupling updates after each iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Execute a finite number of forward-auction iterations, subject to the forward-auction termination condition. At the end of each iteration, after increasing the prices of objects receiving bids, set \(\pi_i=a_{ij_i}-p_{j_i}\) for every pair \((i,j_i)\) entering the assignment during that iteration. Next execute a finite number of reverse-auction iterations, subject to the reverse-auction termination condition. At the end of each iteration, after increasing the profits of persons receiving bids, set \(p_j=a_{i_jj}-\pi_{i_j}\) for every pair \((i_j,j)\) entering the assignment during that iteration. Then return to the forward phase.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The combined algorithm alternates finite blocks of forward and reverse auction iterations. A newly assigned forward pair determines the person's profit from the object's price, while a newly assigned reverse pair determines the object's price from the person's profit.
assumptions_latex: \text{Each executed forward or reverse block contains finitely many iterations}
\text{Each phase is subject to its corresponding termination condition}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (i,j_i)\text{ enters }S\text{ in a forward iteration}\Rightarrow\pi_i=a_{ij_i}-p_{j_i},\qquad(i_j,j)\text{ enters }S\text{ in a reverse iteration}\Rightarrow p_j=a_{i_jj}-\pi_{i_j}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epsilon-auction algorithm for assignment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The perturbed bidding, price update, and displacement rule for constructing a complete assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(S=\varnothing\) with project prices \(p\). At an iteration, each \(i\notin S\) chooses \(k_i\in\arg\max_k(p_k-c_{ik})\) and a second-best \(k_i'\) satisfying \(p_{k_i'}-c_{ik_i'}\ge p_k-c_{ik}\) for every \(k\ne k_i\). Define \(\Delta_i=(p_{k_i}-c_{ik_i})-(p_{k_i'}-c_{ik_i'})\), and bid \(b_i=p_{k_i}-\Delta_i-\epsilon\) for project \(k_i\). Every project receiving bids is assigned to a lowest bidder, its price is set to the lowest bid, and its former holder, if any, becomes unassigned.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epsilon-auction starts with no assigned persons. Each unassigned person bids for a best project by lowering its price by the best-versus-second-best profit gap plus epsilon. Each project is awarded to a lowest bidder at the lowest bid, and any former holder becomes unassigned.
assumptions_latex: S\text{ is the set of currently assigned persons}
\text{Each bidder has a well-defined best and second-best project}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: b_i=p_{k_i}-\Big[(p_{k_i}-c_{ik_i})-(p_{k_i'}-c_{ik_i'})\Big]-\epsilon,\quad\text{followed by lowest-bid reassignment}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: M-auction iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Names the restricted-auction operation for a similarity class and records its singleton reduction to an ordinary auction iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((p,S)\) satisfy \(\epsilon\)-complementary slackness, and let \(M\) be a similarity class of \(m\) persons, exactly \(q\) of whom are assigned under \(S\). The operation that applies the stated \(M\)-restricted auction update to produce a new assignment-price pair is called an \(M\)-auction iteration. If \(|M|=1\), an \(M\)-auction iteration has the same result as the ordinary auction iteration; consequently, an algorithm formed from a sequence of \(M\)-auction iterations generalizes the ordinary auction algorithm to similarity classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given an epsilon-complementary-slackness assignment-price pair and a similarity class containing m persons, q of them assigned, the corresponding restricted auction operation is called an M-auction iteration. For a singleton class it agrees with the ordinary auction iteration, so sequences of these operations generalize the ordinary auction algorithm to similarity classes.
assumptions_latex: M\text{ is a similarity class with }|M|=m
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The stated }M\text{-restricted update is an }M\text{-auction iteration, and }|M|=1\implies\text{the ordinary auction-iteration result}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Naive Auction Algorithm for Assignment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unperturbed assignment-auction iterations that preserve exact complementary slackness but carry no termination guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Starting with a partial assignment and prices satisfying complementary slackness on all assigned pairs, while the assignment is incomplete select an unassigned person $i$, choose $j_i\in\arg\max_{j\in A(i)}\{a_{ij}-p_j\}$, assign $i$ to $j_i$ and unassign any former occupant of $j_i$, and update $p_{j_i}\leftarrow p_{j_i}+\gamma_i$, where $\gamma_i=v_i-w_i$, $v_i=\max_{j\in A(i)}\{a_{ij}-p_j\}$, and $w_i=\max_{j\in A(i),\,j\ne j_i}\{a_{ij}-p_j\}$. If all persons become assigned, the algorithm terminates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The naive auction repeatedly assigns an unassigned person to a best object, displaces any incumbent, and raises the object's price by the gap between the person's best and second-best net values. The update preserves exact complementary slackness, but this extract supplies no termination guarantee.
assumptions_latex: \text{At the start of each iteration, every assigned pair satisfies complementary slackness.}
\text{The assignment is incomplete and an unassigned person }i\text{ is selected.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \gamma_i=v_i-w_i\ge 0,\qquad p_{j_i}\leftarrow p_{j_i}+\gamma_i,\qquad a_{ij_i}-p_{j_i}=\max_{j\in A(i)}\{a_{ij}-p_j\}\text{ after the update.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal and dual error bounds from epsilon-complementary slackness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximate primal-dual optimality certificate for the asymmetric assignment problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a feasible asymmetric assignment \(S\), with \(m\) persons, satisfies all three \(\epsilon\)-complementary-slackness conditions with \((\pi,p)\), then \(S\) is within \(m\epsilon\) of primal optimality. Define \(\lambda=\min_{k:\,k\text{ assigned under }S}p_k\), \(\widehat\pi_i=\pi_i+\epsilon\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and \(\widehat p_j=p_j\) for assigned objects and \(\widehat p_j=\lambda\) for unassigned objects. Then \((\widehat\pi,\widehat p,\lambda)\) is within \(m\epsilon\) of an optimal solution of the associated dual problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible asymmetric assignment satisfying epsilon-complementary slackness is within m epsilon of optimality. Raising each person potential by epsilon and replacing each unassigned-object price by the minimum assigned-object price also produces a dual solution within m epsilon of dual optimality.
assumptions_latex: S\text{ is a feasible asymmetric assignment with }m\text{ persons}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{OPT}_{P}-\operatorname{val}(S)\le m\epsilon,\qquad \operatorname{val}_{D}(\widehat\pi,\widehat p,\lambda)-\operatorname{OPT}_{D}\le m\epsilon.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose an initial value $\epsilon^0>0$ and an integer $\theta>1$. Apply the auction algorithm in successive scaling phases, using the prices produced by one phase to initialize the next, and update
\[
 \epsilon^{k+1}=\frac{\epsilon^k}{\theta},\qquad k=0,1,\ldots.
\]
Stop at a chosen final value $\bar\epsilon$ for which $n\bar\epsilon$ is deemed sufficiently small.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Epsilon-scaling repeatedly applies the auction algorithm, warm-starting each phase with prices from the preceding phase and reducing epsilon geometrically by an integer factor greater than one until the desired final error scale is reached.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \epsilon^{k+1}=\epsilon^k/\theta\quad(k=0,1,\ldots)\text{ until the selected final phase with parameter }\bar\epsilon

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Consequences of joint epsilon-complementary slackness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Derivation of the two one-sided auction conditions and the feasible-assignment approximation guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an assignment \(S\) and profit-price pair \((\pi,p)\) satisfy joint \(\epsilon\)-complementary slackness. Then, for every \((i,j)\in S\), \(a_{ij}-\pi_i\ge\max_{k\in B(j)}\{a_{kj}-\pi_k\}-\epsilon\) and \(a_{ij}-p_j\ge\max_{k\in A(i)}\{a_{ik}-p_k\}-\epsilon\). If \(S\) is feasible, then \(S\) is within \(n\epsilon\) of an optimal assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint epsilon-complementary slackness implies both one-sided epsilon-complementary-slackness conditions on assigned pairs. If the assignment is feasible, it also gives an additive optimality gap of at most n epsilon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}&\forall(i,j)\in S:\quad a_{ij}-\pi_i\ge\max_{k\in B(j)}\{a_{kj}-\pi_k\}-\epsilon,\\&\forall(i,j)\in S:\quad a_{ij}-p_j\ge\max_{k\in A(i)}\{a_{ik}-p_k\}-\epsilon,\\&S\text{ feasible}\Rightarrow \operatorname{OPT}-\operatorname{val}(S)\le n\epsilon.\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(\varepsilon_0\geq C\), initialize object prices, and set \(k=0\). In phase \(k\), starting from the preceding prices and assignment, repeatedly apply admissible price and reassignment updates until every bidder \(i\) satisfies \(a_{i,\sigma(i)}-p_{\sigma(i)}\geq\max_j(a_{ij}-p_j)-\varepsilon_k\). If \(\varepsilon_k<1/n\), stop and output \(\sigma\); otherwise set \(\varepsilon_{k+1}=\varepsilon_k/\theta\), retain the current prices as warm-start dual variables, and refine again. Every completed phase produces an assignment within \(n\varepsilon_k\) of optimum. Because assignment values are integral, the stopping phase is exactly optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve a sequence of increasingly accurate auction or primal-dual subproblems, reusing prices between phases. Integral costs make the final sufficiently accurate assignment exactly optimal.

children.title: Assignment Postoptimality
children.top_down_role: Optimal-solution behavior after modifications to a solved assignment instance.

assumptions_latex: The balanced assignment instance is represented by a finite bipartite graph \(G=(U,V;E)\) with edge-cost vector \(c\in\mathbb{R}^{E}\), and \(M\subseteq E\) is a minimum-cost perfect matching.
The costs are perturbed to \(c'=c+d\), where \(d\in\mathbb{R}^{E}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The old assignment remains optimal exactly when \(\sum_{e\in M}d_e\leq c(M')-c(M)+\sum_{e\in M'}d_e\) for every perfect matching \(M'\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact global postoptimality condition for a fixed perfect assignment under arbitrary cost perturbations.

source_refs.locator: Section 13. Duality Theory p. 53

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every perfect matching \(M'\) of \(G\), define \(c(M')=\sum_{e\in M'}c_e\) and \(d(M')=\sum_{e\in M'}d_e\). The previously optimal matching \(M\) is optimal for the perturbed costs \(c'=c+d\) if and only if \[d(M)-d(M')\leq c(M')-c(M)\qquad\text{for every perfect matching }M'.\] For a perfect matching \(M'\neq M\), equality holds precisely when \(M'\) is also optimal under the perturbed costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An old optimal assignment survives a cost change exactly when no competing assignment gains more from the perturbation than its original optimality gap permits. A distinct competitor is tied after the perturbation exactly when the corresponding inequality is tight.
knowledge_statements.title: Assignment Postoptimality

children.title: Assignment Cost Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Stability of optimal assignments under changes to edge costs.

assumptions_latex: The cost-minimizing perfect matching \(M\) has value \(z=c(M)\).
Only one edge \(e\) has its cost changed, from \(c_e\) to \(c_e+\delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(e\notin M\), stability is equivalent to \(\delta\geq-\alpha_e\); if \(e\in M\), it is equivalent to \(\delta\leq\beta_e\).

notation.meaning: minimum original penalty for forcing edge e
minimum original penalty for excluding edge e

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact one-edge allowable cost interval for a fixed optimal assignment.

source_refs.locator: Section 13. Duality Theory p. 53

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(e\notin M\), set \(\alpha_e=\min\{c(M')-z:M'\text{ is a perfect matching and }e\in M'\}\). Then \(M\) remains optimal after changing only \(c_e\) by \(\delta\) if and only if \(\delta\geq-\alpha_e\). For \(e\in M\), set \(\beta_e=\min\{c(M')-z:M'\text{ is a perfect matching and }e\notin M'\}\). Then \(M\) remains optimal if and only if \(\delta\leq\beta_e\). A minimum over an empty family is \(+\infty\). At a finite boundary, a competing perfect matching becomes co-optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The allowable change of one edge cost equals the cheapest replacement gap: decreases are bounded for unused edges, while increases are bounded for used edges.
knowledge_statements.title: Assignment Cost Sensitivity

children.title: Assignment Structural Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Effects of adding, removing, or restricting assignment edges.

assumptions_latex: The bipartite graph \(G=(U,V;E)\) admits a cost-minimizing perfect matching \(M\) of value \(z\).
A single edge is inserted into or deleted from \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Insertion preserves optimality of \(M\) exactly when the best assignment using the new edge costs at least \(z\); deletion preserves value \(z\) exactly when an old optimum avoids the deleted edge.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-edge insertion and deletion sensitivity for minimum-cost perfect assignments.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 Weighted matchings of bipartite graphs p. 111

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a new edge \(e\notin E\) with cost \(c_e\) is inserted, define \(z_e=\min\{c(M'):M'\text{ is a perfect matching in }G+e,\ e\in M'\}\). The old matching \(M\) remains optimal precisely when \(z_e\geq z\). If an edge \(f\in E\) is deleted, the optimum value remains \(z\) precisely when some original optimal perfect matching excludes \(f\); in particular, deleting \(f\notin M\) leaves \(M\) feasible and optimal. Deleting an edge belonging to every optimum either destroys perfect-matchability or raises the optimum value to the cheapest feasible assignment avoiding that edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A new edge matters only if it creates a cheaper assignment. Deleting an edge preserves the optimum exactly when some old optimal assignment did not use it.
knowledge_statements.title: Assignment Structural Sensitivity

children.title: Optimal-Basis Stability
children.top_down_role: Ranges over which a selected optimal assignment remains valid.

assumptions_latex: The assignment linear program is written as \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\).
A nonsingular basis \(B\) is primal feasible and optimal for cost vector \(c\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The basis \(B\) remains optimal under \(c'=c+d\) if and only if \(c'_N-A_N^{\mathsf T}A_B^{-\mathsf T}c'_B\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduced-cost stability cone for a fixed assignment LP basis.

source_refs.locator: Section 13. Duality Theory p. 53

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_B\) be nonsingular, let \(N\) index the nonbasic columns, and suppose \(x_B=A_B^{-1}b\geq0\). Cost perturbations do not change this primal basic solution. For \(c'=c+d\), define the associated dual vector \(y'=A_B^{-\mathsf T}c'_B\). The same basis \(B\) is optimal if and only if every perturbed nonbasic reduced cost is nonnegative: \[r'_N=c'_N-A_N^{\mathsf T}y'=c'_N-A_N^{\mathsf T}A_B^{-\mathsf T}c'_B\geq0.\] Strict positivity of all components of \(r'_N\), together with nondegeneracy, places \(c'\) in the relative interior of the basis-stability region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed assignment LP basis stays optimal precisely while every nonbasic reduced cost computed from the perturbed objective remains nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-Basis Stability

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bipartite matching and vertex-coverage terminology
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines matchings and vertex-coverage terminology in an undirected bipartite graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(S,T,A)\) be an undirected bipartite graph. A subset \(X\subseteq A\) is a matching if no two edges in \(X\) are incident to the same vertex. Relative to \(X\), a vertex \(j\in S\cup T\) is matched (or covered) if an edge in \(X\) is incident to \(j\), and unmatched (or exposed) otherwise. The matching \(X\) is complete if it leaves no vertex exposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In an undirected bipartite graph, a matching is a set of edges no two of which share a vertex. A vertex is matched or covered if it is incident to a matching edge, and unmatched or exposed otherwise. A matching is complete if every vertex is matched.
assumptions_latex: G=(S,T,A)\text{ is an undirected bipartite graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X\text{ is complete}\iff \forall j\in S\cup T,\ \exists a\in X\text{ incident to }j.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integral weighted bipartite matching–cover duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The collection of points permits repeated vertices; its size is the sum of their multiplicities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be bipartite and let $w\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}^{E}$. Then
\[
\max_{M\text{ matching}}\sum_{e\in M}w_e
=
\min\left\{\sum_{v\in V}y_v:y\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}^{V},\ y_u+y_v\ge w_{uv}\ \forall uv\in E\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a bipartite graph with nonnegative integral edge weights, maximum matching weight equals the minimum total multiplicity of a vertex multiset covering every edge to its prescribed weight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max_{M\text{ matching}}\sum_{e\in M}w_e=\min\left\{\sum_{v\in V}y_v:y\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}^{V},\ y_u+y_v\ge w_{uv}\ \forall uv\in E\right\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Duality for Minimum-Weight Perfect Bipartite Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes integral attainment of the dual when all edge weights are integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let G=(V,E) be bipartite and admit a perfect matching, and let w:E\to\mathbb{Q}. Then
\[
\min_{M\text{ perfect}}\sum_{e\in M}w_e
=
\max\left\{\sum_{v\in V}y_v:y\in\mathbb{Q}^{V},\ y_u+y_v\leq w_{uv}\ \text{for every }uv\in E\right\}.
\]
If w:E\to\mathbb{Z}, an optimal y can be chosen in \mathbb{Z}^{V}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a bipartite graph admitting a perfect matching, the minimum weight of a perfect matching equals the maximum sum of rational vertex potentials satisfying y_u+y_v≤w_uv on every edge. If the edge weights are integral, an optimal integral potential exists.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is bipartite and admits a perfect matching}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{M\text{ perfect}}w(M)=\max\left\{y(V):y_u+y_v\leq w_{uv}\ \forall uv\in E\right\},\qquad w(E)\subseteq\mathbb{Z}\Rightarrow\exists\,y^*\in\mathbb{Z}^{V}\text{ optimal.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Superstars and the Superstar Polytope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of the combinatorial objects, their incidence-vector polytope, and the associated edge-cover inequality system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph \(G=(V,E)\), an edge set \(F\subseteq E\) is a superstar if \(F\supseteq\delta_G(v)\) for some \(v\in V\). Its superstar polytope is \[P_{\mathrm{superstar}}(G):=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^F:F\subseteq E,\ \exists v\in V\text{ with }F\supseteq\delta_G(v)\}.\] The associated system is \(0\leq x_e\leq1\) for all \(e\in E\), together with \(x(C)\geq1\) for every edge cover \(C\) of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A superstar is an edge set containing every edge incident with at least one vertex. The superstar polytope is the convex hull of superstar incidence vectors. The associated system consists of unit-box constraints and an inequality requiring total value at least one on every edge cover.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_{\mathrm{superstar}}(G)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^F:F\subseteq E,\ \exists v\in V,\ F\supseteq\delta_G(v)\},\quad 0\leq x_e\leq1\ (e\in E),\quad x(C)\geq1\ \text{for every edge cover }C.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Construct a directed network with arcs \(s\to u\) for \(u\in U\), arcs \(u\to v\) for \(uv\in E\), and arcs \(v\to t\) for \(v\in V\), each having capacity \(1\). Every matching \(M\) induces an integral \(s\)-\(t\) flow of value \(|M|\) by sending one unit along \(s\to u\to v\to t\) for each \(uv\in M\). Conversely, the middle arcs carrying one unit in any integral flow form a matching. Consequently, \[\max\{|M|:M\text{ is a matching of }G\}=\max\{\operatorname{val}(f):f\text{ is a feasible }s\text{-}t\text{ flow}\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Connect a source to the left class and the right class to a sink with unit capacities. Integral flow paths correspond exactly to matched edges.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Assignment Problem as a Minimum-Cost Flow Linear Program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Flow representation of minimum-weight perfect matching in a balanced bipartite graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $G=(N_1\cup N_2,A)$ be a weighted bipartite graph with $|N_1|=|N_2|$ and costs $c_{ij}$, with every edge oriented from $N_1$ to $N_2$. The minimum-weight perfect-matching problem, called the assignment problem, is represented by
\[\min\sum_{(i,j)\in A}c_{ij}x_{ij}\]
subject to
\[\sum_{j:(i,j)\in A}x_{ij}=1\quad(i\in N_1),\qquad \sum_{j:(j,i)\in A}x_{ji}=1\quad(i\in N_2),\qquad x_{ij}\ge 0\quad((i,j)\in A).\]
This is a special minimum-cost-flow formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a balanced weighted bipartite graph, minimum-weight perfect matching—the assignment problem—has a minimum-cost-flow linear formulation in which every vertex has assignment value one and all assignment variables are nonnegative.
assumptions_latex: G=(N_1\cup N_2,A)\text{ is a weighted bipartite graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\left\{\sum_{(i,j)\in A}c_{ij}x_{ij}:\sum_{j:(i,j)\in A}x_{ij}=1\ (i\in N_1),\ \sum_{j:(j,i)\in A}x_{ji}=1\ (i\in N_2),\ x\ge0\right\}\text{ is a minimum-cost-flow formulation of the assignment problem.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a bipartite graph \(B=(V,U,E)\), introduce new vertices \(s,t\), let \(W=\{s,t\}\cup V\cup U\), give every arc unit capacity, and define \[A=\{(s,v):v\in V\}\cup\{(v,u):[v,u]\in E\}\cup\{(u,t):u\in U\}.\] The resulting network is \(N(B)=(s,t,W,A)\). Every vertex of \(V\) has indegree one and every vertex of \(U\) has outdegree one, so \(N(B)\) is a simple network.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a bipartite graph with parts V and U, add a source and sink and unit-capacity arcs from the source to V, along graph edges from V to U, and from U to the sink. This produces the associated simple network N(B).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N(B)=(s,t,\{s,t\}\cup V\cup U,A)\text{ is the specified unit-capacity simple network.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Flow reductions for bipartite matching problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bipartite-graph definition and flow formulations for maximum matching and minimum-weight perfect matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A graph \(G=(V,E)\) is bipartite if \(V=V_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}V_2\) and every edge has one endpoint in each part. The maximum-cardinality matching problem in a bipartite graph reduces to an integral maximum-flow problem, and the minimum-weight perfect-matching problem in a bipartite graph can be solved as a minimum-cost-flow problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bipartite graph has a vertex bipartition with every edge crossing between its two sides. Maximum bipartite matching reduces to integral maximum flow, while minimum-weight perfect bipartite matching can be solved by minimum-cost flow.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite bipartite graph with }V=V_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}V_2
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Maximum bipartite matching reduces to integral maximum flow, and minimum-weight perfect bipartite matching reduces to minimum-cost flow.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Criterion for Packing Edge-Disjoint Matchings of Fixed Size
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The notation \(q(X,Y)\) is retained from the surrounding source because its definition is not included in the extracted theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(A,B)\) be a bipartite graph. Then \(G\) contains \(h\) pairwise edge-disjoint matchings, each of size \(t\), if and only if, for every \(X\subseteq A\) and \(Y\subseteq B\), \[q(X,Y)\ge h\bigl(t-|A\setminus X|-|B\setminus Y|\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bipartite graph contains h pairwise edge-disjoint matchings of size t exactly when, for every X contained in A and Y contained in B, q(X,Y) is at least h times t minus the numbers of vertices outside X and outside Y. The quantity q(X,Y) is the source's previously defined set function.
assumptions_latex: q(X,Y)\text{ has the meaning defined in the surrounding source}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ has }h\text{ pairwise edge-disjoint matchings of size }t\iff\forall X\subseteq A\ \forall Y\subseteq B,\ q(X,Y)\ge h\bigl(t-|A\setminus X|-|B\setminus Y|\bigr)

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Create arcs \(s\to u\) for \(u\in U\), \(u\to v\) for \(uv\in E\), and \(v\to t\) for \(v\in V\), all with capacity \(1\). Give each middle arc \(u\to v\) cost \(c_{uv}\) and every other arc cost \(0\). Add a return arc \(t\to s\) with lower and upper bound both equal to \(n\). Flow conservation forces every integral feasible circulation to use exactly one middle arc incident with each vertex. Thus its positive middle arcs form a perfect matching, every perfect matching induces such a circulation, and circulation cost equals assignment cost. Minimum-cost feasible circulation therefore solves minimum-cost perfect assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Force n units around a source-left-right-sink-return network. Integral feasible circulations then correspond exactly, and cost-preservingly, to perfect assignments.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a bipartite matching or assignment instance be represented by a network whose node-arc incidence matrix is \(D\), with integral lower bounds, upper bounds, and balance vector. If the network system is feasible, its feasible polyhedron has integral extreme points; if a finite linear optimum exists, an integral optimum \(f^*\) exists. Under the standard reduction, define \(x^*_{uv}=f^*_{uv}\) on arcs corresponding to bipartite edges. Unit capacities and flow conservation imply \(x^*_{uv}\in\{0,1\}\) and the matching degree constraints. Hence projection preserves integrality and objective value, yielding an integral maximum matching or minimum-cost assignment solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integral network data guarantee an integral optimal flow. Projecting its assignment arcs therefore yields an integral optimal matching rather than merely a fractional solution.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each vertex \(v\), let \(\delta(v)\) denote its incident edges. The bipartite matching polyhedron is \[P_M(G)=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{E}_{\geq0}:\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e\leq1\ \text{for every }v\in U\cup V\right\}.\] For bipartite \(G\), these inequalities give the complete convex-hull description \[P_M(G)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^M:M\subseteq E\text{ is a matching}\}.\] Consequently every extreme point of \(P_M(G)\) is a zero-one matching incidence vector; no odd-set inequalities are required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegativity and one degree inequality per vertex describe exactly the convex hull of bipartite matchings, so every extreme point is integral.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cut Characterization of Bipartite Exact-Degree Factors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The notation $\widetilde z(U)$ denotes the sum of $z$ over $U$, and $d_G(X,T)$ retains the source's bipartite cut-edge notation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(S,T;E)$ be bipartite and let $z:S\cup T\to\mathbb Z_+$. There is a spanning subgraph $H$ with $d_H(v)=z(v)$ for every $v\in S\cup T$ if and only if $\widetilde z(S)=\widetilde z(T)$ and, for every $X\subseteq S\cup T$, $\widetilde z(X\cap S)\le \widetilde z(X\cap T)+d_G(X,T)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bipartite graph has a spanning subgraph realizing every prescribed nonnegative integral degree exactly if and only if the total prescribed degrees on the two shores agree and every vertex subset satisfies the stated cut inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\exists H\subseteq G\text{ spanning}:\forall v,\ d_H(v)=z(v)\bigr)\iff\bigl[\widetilde z(S)=\widetilde z(T)\ \land\ \forall X\subseteq S\cup T,\ \widetilde z(X\cap S)\le\widetilde z(X\cap T)+d_G(X,T)\bigr]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matching and Node Cover in a Bipartite Network
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational definitions for bipartite matching-cover theory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(N_1\cup N_2,A)\) be a directed bipartite network. A set \(M\subseteq A\) is a matching if no two arcs in \(M\) have a common endpoint. A set \(C\subseteq N_1\cup N_2\) is a node cover if every arc in \(A\) has at least one endpoint in \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matching in a bipartite network is a set of arcs with no shared endpoint. A node cover is a set of nodes incident to every arc of the network.
assumptions_latex: G=(N_1\cup N_2,A)\text{ is a directed bipartite network}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\subseteq A\text{ is a matching}\iff \forall e\ne f\in M,\ e\text{ and }f\text{ have no common endpoint};\quad C\subseteq N_1\cup N_2\text{ is a node cover}\iff \forall e\in A,\ e\text{ has an endpoint in }C.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polytope of Edge Sets Containing a Bipartite Perfect Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the convex hull of incidence vectors of edge sets containing a perfect matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be bipartite. Then
\[
\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^F:F\subseteq E,\ F\text{ contains a perfect matching}\}
=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^E:0\le x_e\le1\ (e\in E),\ x(E[S])\ge |S|-\tfrac12|V|\ (S\subseteq V)\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a bipartite graph, the convex hull of incidence vectors of edge sets containing a perfect matching consists exactly of the vectors in the unit cube satisfying every induced-edge lower bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{conv}\{\chi^F:F\subseteq E,\ \exists M\subseteq F\text{ a perfect matching}\}=\{x\in[0,1]^E:(\forall S\subseteq V)\ x(E[S])\ge |S|-\tfrac12|V|\}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear description of the convex hull of rank-\(r\) subpermutation matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\). A matrix \(M\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) belongs to the convex hull of the subpermutation matrices of rank \(r\) if and only if \(M\ge 0\), every row sum and column sum is at most \(1\), and \(\sum_{i,j}M_{ij}=r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix lies in the convex hull of rank-r subpermutation matrices exactly when it is nonnegative, every row and column sum is at most one, and the sum of all entries is r.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\in\operatorname{conv}\{P:P\text{ is a subpermutation matrix and }\operatorname{rank}(P)=r\}\iff\left(M\ge0,\ \sum_jM_{ij}\le1\ \forall i,\ \sum_iM_{ij}\le1\ \forall j,\ \sum_{i,j}M_{ij}=r\right).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Linear-programming duality gives \[\max\left\{\sum_{e\in E}w_ex_e:x\geq0,\ \sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e\leq1\ \text{for all }v\right\}=\min\left\{\sum_{v\in U\cup V}y_v:y\geq0,\ y_u+y_v\geq w_{uv}\ \text{for all }uv\in E\right\}.\] Because the bipartite incidence system is integral, an optimal primal solution is a matching incidence vector. If \(w\) is integral, an integral optimal dual potential may also be chosen. For \(w_e=1\) on every edge, the dual integral solutions are vertex covers, yielding equality between maximum matching cardinality and minimum vertex-cover cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum-weight bipartite matching is dual to minimum vertex potentials covering every edge weight. With unit weights this becomes the matching–vertex-cover min-max equality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Constructing a Minimum-Size w-Vertex Cover from a Maximum-Weight Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A primal–dual construction for nonnegative integral edge weights in a bipartite graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G=(U\cup W,E) be bipartite, let w:E\to\mathbb{Z}_{+}, and let M be a maximum-weight matching. Form a digraph with an arc (u,v) of length -w_{uv} for every uv\in E and, when uv\in M, an arc (v,u) of length w_{uv}. Compute a feasible integral potential p satisfying the stated zero and sign conditions on unmatched and matched vertices, and set y_u=-p(u) for u\in U and y_v=p(v) for v\in W. Then y is a w-vertex cover and y(V)=w(M); hence y is minimum-size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: From a maximum-weight matching, build the associated residual digraph, compute an integral feasible potential with the prescribed boundary and sign conditions, and convert it into vertex labels. The resulting w-vertex cover has size equal to the matching weight and is therefore minimum-size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y_u+y_v\ge w_{uv}\ \forall uv\in E,\qquad y(V)=w(M),\qquad y\text{ is a minimum-size }w\text{-vertex cover.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Edge cover and stable-set parameters
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for a graph, including the existence boundary for edge covers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph \(G=(V,E)\), an edge cover is a set \(F\subseteq E\) such that \(\forall v\in V\,\exists e\in F\) with \(v\in e\); one can exist only if \(G\) has no isolated vertices. A stable set is a set \(S\subseteq V\) containing no adjacent pair, and \(S\) is stable if and only if \(V\setminus S\) is a vertex cover. Define \(\alpha(G):=\max\{|S|:S\text{ is stable}\}\) and \(\rho(G):=\min\{|F|:F\text{ is an edge cover}\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An edge cover covers every vertex by an incident selected edge and can exist only in graphs without isolated vertices. A stable set contains no adjacent pair, equivalently its complement is a vertex cover. The stable-set number is the maximum stable-set size, and the edge-cover number is the minimum edge-cover size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ stable}\iff V\setminus S\text{ is a vertex cover},\quad \alpha(G)=\max_{S\text{ stable}}|S|,\quad \rho(G)=\min_{F\text{ edge cover}}|F|

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted edge-cover min–max theorem for bipartite graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real-weight duality with an integer optimal dual solution for integer edge weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be bipartite and let $w:E\to\mathbb{R}_+$. Then
\[
\min\{w(F):F\text{ is an edge cover of }G\}=\max\left\{\sum_{v\in V}y_v:y\in\mathbb{R}_+^V,\ y_u+y_v\le w_{uv}\ \forall uv\in E\right\}.
\]
If $w\in\mathbb{Z}_+^E$, the maximum may be restricted to $y\in\mathbb{Z}_+^V$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a bipartite graph, the minimum weight of an edge cover equals the maximum total nonnegative vertex weight subject to the sum at the endpoints of every edge being at most that edge's weight. With integer edge weights, an integer vertex-weight vector suffices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{F\text{ edge cover}}w(F)=\max_{\substack{y\in\mathbb{R}_+^V\\y_u+y_v\le w_{uv}\ \forall uv\in E}}y(V),\quad w\in\mathbb{Z}_+^E\Rightarrow y\text{ may be chosen in }\mathbb{Z}_+^V

knowledge_statements.title: Integral Extreme-Point Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extreme points of the fractional matching polytope for a finite bipartite graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(U\mathbin{\dot\cup}W,E)\) be a finite bipartite graph and define \[P(G)=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{E}:\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e\leq 1\text{ for every }v\in U\mathbin{\dot\cup}W\right\}.\] Every extreme point of \(P(G)\) is the incidence vector \(\chi^M\) of a matching \(M\subseteq E\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-Sided Feasibility Criterion for Capacitated Bipartite Matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduces integer feasibility with simultaneous lower and upper marginal bounds to feasibility of two complementary one-sided capacitated systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=(c_{ij})\in\mathbb R_+^{m\times n}\), and let \(a,b\in\mathbb Z_+^m\) and \(a',b'\in\mathbb Z_+^n\) satisfy \(a\le b\) and \(a'\le b'\). There exists an integer matrix \(X=(x_{ij})\) satisfying \(0\le x_{ij}\le c_{ij}\), \(a_i\le\sum_jx_{ij}\le b_i\), and \(a'_j\le\sum_ix_{ij}\le b'_j\) if and only if there exist matrices \(X'=(x'_{ij})\) and \(X''=(x''_{ij})\) satisfying, respectively, \(0\le x'_{ij}\le c_{ij}\), \(\sum_jx'_{ij}\le b_i\), \(a'_j\le\sum_ix'_{ij}\), and \(0\le x''_{ij}\le c_{ij}\), \(a_i\le\sum_jx''_{ij}\), \(\sum_ix''_{ij}\le b'_j\), for all applicable indices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A capacity-bounded integer matrix satisfying every lower and upper row and column bound exists exactly when both complementary one-sided marginal systems are feasible.

knowledge_statements.title: Bipartite Incidence Matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unsigned vertex-edge incidence represented as a signed directed incidence matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite bipartite graph \(G=(U\mathbin{\dot\cup}W,E)\), its unsigned vertex-edge incidence matrix is \(A\in\{0,1\}^{(U\cup W)\times E}\), where \(A_{v,e}=1\) exactly when \(v\in e\). Let \(D\) be diagonal with \(D_{vv}=1\) for \(v\in U\) and \(D_{vv}=-1\) for \(v\in W\). Then every column of \(DA\) has one entry \(1\), one entry \(-1\), and all other entries zero; thus \(DA\) is the node-arc incidence matrix obtained by orienting every edge from \(W\) to \(U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Signing one bipartition class converts the unsigned incidence matrix of a bipartite graph into a directed node-arc incidence matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(DA\) is a directed node-arc incidence matrix.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Integrality Consequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral right-hand sides yield integral bipartite degree-constraint polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be the unsigned vertex-edge incidence matrix of a finite bipartite graph and let \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^{V}\). The polyhedron \[P(b)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{E}:Ax\leq b,\ x\geq 0\}\] is integral whenever it is nonempty: every extreme point of \(P(b)\) belongs to \(\mathbb{Z}^{E}\). In particular, for \(b=\mathbf{1}\), every extreme point is a zero-one vector and therefore the incidence vector of a matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total unimodularity makes bipartite degree-constraint polyhedra integral for integral capacities; unit capacities recover matching vectors.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is a bipartite vertex-edge incidence matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ext}P(b)\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^{E}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Nonbipartite Matrix Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The triangle witnesses failure of incidence-matrix unimodularity and degree-only matching integrality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=K_3\), order its vertices and edges cyclically, and let \[A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\1&1&0\\0&1&1\end{pmatrix}.\] Then \(A\) is the unsigned vertex-edge incidence matrix of \(G\) and \(\det(A)=2\), so \(A\) is not totally unimodular. Moreover, \(x=(1/2,1/2,1/2)\) is an extreme point of \(\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq0}^{3}:Ax\leq\mathbf{1}\}\), but it is not the incidence vector of a matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A triangle has incidence determinant two and a half-integral extreme point, so bipartite matrix integrality does not extend to nonbipartite graphs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is not totally unimodular, and the degree-only matching relaxation is not integral.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Bipartite Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided convex bipartite graphs with consecutive neighborhoods in a fixed order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite bipartite graph \(G=(U\mathbin{\dot\cup}W,E)\) is convex on \(W\) if there is a linear order \(w_1<\cdots<w_q\) of \(W\) such that, for every \(u\in U\), its neighborhood is an interval in that order: either \(N(u)=\varnothing\), or there exist \(1\leq \ell(u)\leq r(u)\leq q\) with \[N(u)=\{w_j:\ell(u)\leq j\leq r(u)\}.\] It is called a convex bipartite graph if it is convex on at least one bipartition class.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) is convex on \(W\) exactly when every \(N(u)\) is an interval in one common order of \(W\).

knowledge_statements.title: Monge Assignment Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monge inequality for a minimization-form rectangular assignment cost array.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=(c_{ij})\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), with rows and columns carrying their natural linear orders. The array \(C\) is Monge if, for every \(1\leq i<k\leq m\) and \(1\leq j<\ell\leq n\), \[c_{ij}+c_{k\ell}\leq c_{i\ell}+c_{kj}.\] Equivalently, every ordered two-by-two subarray has the sum on its northwest-to-southeast diagonal no greater than the sum on its northeast-to-southwest diagonal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cost array is Monge when every ordered two-by-two subarray favors its aligned diagonal over its crossed diagonal.
assumptions_latex: Rows and columns have fixed linear orders.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c_{ij}+c_{k\ell}\leq c_{i\ell}+c_{kj}\) for all \(i<k\) and \(j<\ell\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed inequality is the standard minimization-form Monge condition and fits the condition leaf, but no source confirms the terminology and sign convention.

children.title: Ordered Assignment Structure
children.top_down_role: Assignment instances whose vertex order constrains optimal pairings.

knowledge_statements.title: Ordered Assignment Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Assignments between equally sized linearly ordered sets, classified by inversions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U=\{u_1<\cdots<u_n\}\) and \(W=\{w_1<\cdots<w_n\}\). A perfect assignment is represented by a permutation \(\pi\in S_n\), matching \(u_i\) to \(w_{\pi(i)}\). A pair \((i,k)\) with \(i<k\) is an inversion when \(\pi(i)>\pi(k)\). The assignment is order-compatible when it has no inversions, equivalently when \(i<k\) implies \(\pi(i)<\pi(k)\). For equal finite chains, the unique order-compatible perfect assignment is \(\pi(i)=i\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ordered perfect assignment is order-compatible when matched indices never cross; for two equal chains this is the identity assignment.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) and \(W\) are linearly ordered sets of the same finite cardinality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi\) is order-compatible if and only if \(\pi(i)=i\) for every \(i\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inversion-based formulation is internally correct, including uniqueness of the increasing permutation, but the locally introduced term “order-compatible” lacks a cited source.

children.title: Order-Compatible Optimal Matchings
children.top_down_role: Optimal matching patterns supported by compatible ordering.

knowledge_statements.title: Order-Compatible Optimal Matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uncrossing theorem for square Monge minimization assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=(c_{ij})\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) satisfy the Monge inequalities. For a permutation \(\pi\in S_n\), define its assignment cost by \(F(\pi)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_{i,\pi(i)}\). If \(\pi\) has an inversion, exchanging the two inverted images produces a permutation \(\pi'\) with \(F(\pi')\leq F(\pi)\). Repeated exchanges therefore yield the order-compatible permutation \(\operatorname{id}\), and \[F(\operatorname{id})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_{ii}\leq F(\pi)\qquad\text{for every }\pi\in S_n.\] Thus an order-compatible optimal perfect matching exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a square Monge cost matrix, uncrossing inversions never increases cost, so the identity matching is optimal.
assumptions_latex: The objective is to minimize total assignment cost.

notation.meaning: total cost of permutation assignment π

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The uncrossing statement is correct for square minimization-form Monge arrays and fits the theorem leaf, but neither the theorem nor its convention has an inspectable source locator.

children.title: Monge Structure Violations

knowledge_statements.title: Monge Structure Violations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A violated two-by-two Monge inequality defeats guaranteed order-compatible optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a two-by-two minimization assignment array \(C=(c_{ij})\). If \[c_{11}+c_{22}>c_{12}+c_{21},\] then the Monge inequality is violated. The order-compatible assignment has cost \(c_{11}+c_{22}\), whereas the crossed assignment has strictly smaller cost \(c_{12}+c_{21}\). Hence the order-compatible assignment is not optimal. More generally, a violated ordered two-by-two inequality reverses the local uncrossing comparison on those rows and columns, so Monge-based order-compatible optimality is no longer guaranteed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single reversed two-by-two Monge inequality can make the crossed assignment cheaper than the order-compatible assignment.
assumptions_latex: The objective is to minimize assignment cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{id}\) is not an optimal assignment for \(C\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two-by-two failure example is mathematically correct and appropriately classified as a failure boundary, but it has no source confirming the Monge sign convention or claim context.

knowledge_statements.title: Edge-Coloring Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correspondence between one-factorizations and optimal edge colorings.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bipartiteness regimes for signed graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes definitions, implications, minor closure, and forbidden-minor characterizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a signed graph $G=(V,E,\Sigma)$, let $Q(G)=\{x\in\mathbb R^E:0\le x_e\le1\ (e\in E),\ x(C)\ge1\text{ for every odd circuit }C\}$. The graph is weakly bipartite when every vertex of $Q(G)$ is integral; strongly bipartite when this system is totally dual integral; and evenly bipartite when, for every $w\in\mathbb Z_+^E$ satisfying $w(\delta(v))$ even for all $v$, the minimum of $w^Tx$ over $Q(G)$ has integral primal and dual optima. Equivalently, the latter two properties give equality between the minimum weight of an odd-circuit cover and the maximum cardinality of a family of odd circuits using each edge $e$ at most $w(e)$ times, respectively for all nonnegative integral $w$ or for those satisfying the even-degree condition. Strong bipartiteness implies even bipartiteness, which implies weak bipartiteness; all three classes are minor-closed. Moreover, strong bipartiteness is equivalent to excluding $\operatorname{odd}\text{-}K_4$ as a minor, while weak and even bipartiteness are equivalent and are characterized by excluding $\operatorname{odd}\text{-}K_5$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the signed odd-circuit-cover system, weak bipartiteness means vertex integrality, strong bipartiteness means TDI, and even bipartiteness means integral primal and dual optima for nonnegative integral weights having even incident weight at every vertex. Strong implies even implies weak, each class is minor-closed, strong graphs exclude exactly odd-K4, and weak and even graphs coincide and exclude exactly odd-K5.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{strong}\Rightarrow\text{even}\Rightarrow\text{weak},\qquad \text{strong}\iff \operatorname{odd}\text{-}K_4\not\preceq G,\qquad \text{even}\iff\text{weak}\iff \operatorname{odd}\text{-}K_5\not\preceq G.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weakly and strongly bipartite graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the defining polyhedra, equivalent complement formulation, separation consequence, forbidden odd-minor characterizations, and the strict failure example.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an undirected graph $G=(V,E)$, an edge set $B\subseteq E$ is bipartite iff it contains no odd circuit iff it is contained in a cut. Define $P_{\mathrm{bs}}(G)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^B:B\subseteq E\text{ is bipartite}\}$. Every $x\in P_{\mathrm{bs}}(G)$ satisfies $0\le x_e\le1$ and $x(C)\le |C|-1$ for every odd circuit $C$; these inequalities are not sufficient in general, as shown by $K_5$ and $x_e=2/3$. The graph is weakly bipartite when these inequalities determine $P_{\mathrm{bs}}(G)$, equivalently when $0\le y_e\le1$ and $y(C)\ge1$ determine the odd-circuit-cover polytope under $y=\mathbf1-x$. This class is closed under odd minors and consists exactly of graphs having no $K_5$ odd minor. It is strongly bipartite when the displayed system is totally dual integral; equivalently, it has no odd $K_4$-subdivision, or no $K_4$ odd minor. On weakly bipartite graphs, a maximum-capacity cut is computable in strongly polynomial time by separation over the odd-circuit inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bipartite edge set is equivalently an edge set containing no odd circuit or one contained in a cut. Its incidence-vector hull satisfies box and odd-circuit inequalities, although these fail to describe the hull for K5. Weakly bipartite graphs are exactly those for which they do describe it, equivalently those whose odd-circuit-cover polytope has the complementary description; they are precisely the graphs with no K5 odd minor. Strongly bipartite graphs are those for which the system is TDI, equivalently those with no odd K4 subdivision or K4 odd minor. Maximum-capacity cut is strongly polynomial-time solvable on weakly bipartite graphs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is weakly bipartite}\iff K_5\text{ is not an odd minor of }G,\qquad G\text{ is strongly bipartite}\iff K_4\text{ is not an odd minor of }G.

knowledge_statements.title: Hall-Deficiency Obstructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deficient vertex sets as certificates against left-saturating matchings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite bipartite graph \(G=(L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R,E)\), define \[\delta_L(G)=\max_{S\subseteq L}\bigl(|S|-|N(S)|\bigr).\] Every matching leaves at least \(\delta_L(G)\) vertices of \(L\) unmatched, and a maximum matching leaves exactly that many. Hence any \(S\subseteq L\) with \(|S|>|N(S)|\) is a directly verifiable certificate that no matching saturates \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set with fewer neighbors than vertices certifies failure of a left-saturating matching; maximum matching size is governed exactly by maximum Hall deficiency.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nu(G)=|L|-\delta_L(G)\), where matching size is measured by vertices matched in \(L\).

knowledge_statements.title: Odd-Cycle Obstructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Odd cycles mark failure of the bipartite matching relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) contain an odd cycle \(C\). Set \(x_e=1/2\) for \(e\in E(C)\) and \(x_e=0\) otherwise. Then \(x\ge0\) and \(x(\delta(v))\le1\) for every \(v\in V\), but \[x(E(C))=|C|/2>(|C|-1)/2.\] Thus the degree-only matching relaxation admits a point excluded by every convex combination of matchings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Half-weighting every edge of an odd cycle satisfies degree constraints but violates the matching bound for that odd vertex set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The degree-only fractional matching relaxation of \(G\) is not the matching polytope.

notation.meaning: The edge set of the odd cycle C.
The edges incident with vertex v.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is bipartite}\iff G\text{ contains no odd-length cycle}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Three Stable Sets Force an Odd-K4 Subdivision
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A local structural criterion for an odd-K4 subdivision through three prescribed incident edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a graph, let \(u\in V\), and let \(v_1,v_2,v_3\) be distinct neighbors of \(u\). Let \(S_1,S_2,S_3\) be pairwise disjoint stable sets with \(v_i\in S_i\) for \(i=1,2,3\). If, for every distinct \(i,j\in\{1,2,3\}\), the subgraph \(G[S_i\cup S_j]\) contains a \(v_i\)-\(v_j\) path, then \(G\) contains an odd \(K_4\)-subdivision containing \(uv_1,uv_2,uv_3\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If three pairwise disjoint stable sets contain three neighbors of a common vertex and every pair of sets induces a path between its designated neighbors, then the graph contains an odd K4 subdivision using the three incident edges.
assumptions_latex: S_1,S_2,S_3\text{ are pairwise disjoint stable sets}
\forall i\ne j,\ G[S_i\cup S_j]\text{ contains a }v_i\text{-}v_j\text{ path}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ contains an odd }K_4\text{-subdivision containing }uv_1,uv_2,uv_3

children.title: Bipartite Integrality Regime
children.top_down_role: Integral matching behavior supported by bipartiteness.

knowledge_statements.title: Bipartite Integrality Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degree description of the bipartite matching polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite bipartite graph \(G=(V,E)\), the matching polytope is \[P_M(G)=\left\{x\in\mathbb R_{}^{E}:x_e\ge0\ \text{for all }e\in E,\quad x(\delta(v))\le1\ \text{for all }v\in V\right\}.\] Every extreme point of this polytope is the incidence vector of a matching; hence every linear objective over the displayed relaxation has an integral optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In bipartite graphs, nonnegativity and vertex-degree inequalities describe exactly the convex hull of matchings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The degree relaxation equals \(\operatorname{conv}\{\mathbf 1_M:M\text{ is a matching of }G\}\) and is integral.

notation.meaning: The set of edges incident with v.

children.title: Fractional Nonbipartite Behavior
children.top_down_role: Fractional relaxation behavior arising beyond the bipartite regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Fractional Nonbipartite Behavior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Half-integral extreme point on an odd cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the cycle \(G=C_{2k+1}\) with \(k\ge1\), define \(x_e=1/2\) for every edge. This vector satisfies \(x_e\ge0\) and \(x(\delta(v))=1\) at every vertex. It is an extreme point of the degree-only relaxation, yet it is not integral and cannot be a convex combination of matching incidence vectors because \(x(E)=k+1/2>k=\nu(G)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The all-one-half vector on an odd cycle is a fractional extreme point of the degree relaxation and lies outside the matching polytope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The degree-only matching relaxation has the nonintegral extreme point \(x=\tfrac12\mathbf 1_E\).

children.top_down_role: Additional constraints used to recover integral matching geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Odd-Set Repair Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edmonds's odd-set description of the general matching polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), its matching polytope equals the set of \(x\in\mathbb R^{E}\) satisfying \[x_e\ge0,\qquad x(\delta(v))\le1\quad(v\in V),\qquad x(E(S))\le\frac{|S|-1}{2}\quad(S\subseteq V,\ |S|\text{ odd}).\] Thus adding all odd-set inequalities repairs the degree relaxation and yields precisely the convex hull of matching incidence vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For general graphs, degree constraints become exact after adding one matching-capacity inequality for every odd vertex set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed system equals \(\operatorname{conv}\{\mathbf 1_M:M\text{ is a matching of }G\}\).

notation.meaning: Edges having both endpoints in S.
The sum of x over an edge set F.

children.title: Assignment Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Degenerate primal or dual structure in assignment instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Assignment Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degeneracy understood locally as nonuniqueness of the optimal assignment face, rather than basic-solution degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 1}\), let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(C=(c_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\). Define \(B_n=\{x\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{n\times n}:\sum_{j\in[n]}x_{ij}=1\text{ for every }i\in[n],\ \sum_{i\in[n]}x_{ij}=1\text{ for every }j\in[n]\}\) and \(F^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in B_n}\langle C,x\rangle\). In the optimal-face sense used here, the assignment instance is degenerate if \(F^*\) is not a singleton. Equivalently, \(\dim F^*\ge1\), or at least two distinct permutation matrices attain the minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the local optimal-face convention, an assignment instance is degenerate when its optimal face is not a singleton, equivalently when it has at least two distinct optimal permutation matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Optimal-face degeneracy means \(|F^*|>1\), equivalently \(\dim F^*\ge1\).

notation.meaning: The Birkhoff polytope of n by n doubly stochastic matrices.
The optimal face for cost matrix C.

children.title: Multiple Optimal Assignments
children.top_down_role: Instances admitting more than one optimal assignment.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple Optimal Assignments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Alternating-cycle criterion in the zero-reduced-cost graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\), let \(C=(c_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), and consider the minimum-cost perfect-matching problem on the complete bipartite graph with vertex classes \(L=R=[n]\). Let \(M\) be an optimal perfect matching and let \((u,v)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n\) be an optimal dual solution satisfying \(u_i+v_j\le c_{ij}\) for every \((i,j)\in L\times R\). Define the equality graph \(H=(L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R,E_H)\) by \(E_H=\{ij:c_{ij}-u_i-v_j=0\}\). A distinct optimal assignment exists if and only if \(H\) contains an \(M\)-alternating cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given an optimal assignment and optimal dual potentials, a second optimal assignment exists exactly when the zero-reduced-cost equality graph contains an alternating cycle relative to the first assignment.
assumptions_latex: \((u,v)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n\) is an optimal dual solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There are multiple optimal assignments if and only if \(H\) contains an \(M\)-alternating cycle.

notation.meaning: Optimal row and column dual potentials.

children.title: Optimal-Face Structure
children.top_down_role: Geometric organization of all optimal assignment solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-Face Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal assignment face represented by the equality graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\), let \([n]=\{1,ldots,n\}\), and let \(C=(c_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\). Define \(B_n=\{x\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{n\times n}:\sum_{j\in[n]}x_{ij}=1\text{ for every }i\in[n],\ \sum_{i\in[n]}x_{ij}=1\text{ for every }j\in[n]\}\). For any optimal dual solution \((u,v)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n\), let \(H\) be the bipartite graph on two copies of \([n]\) with \(E(H)=\{ij:c_{ij}=u_i+v_j\}\). The optimal face is \[F^*=\{x\in B_n:x_{ij}=0\text{ whenever }ij\notin E(H)\}=\operatorname{conv}\{\mathbf 1_M:M\text{ is a perfect matching of }H\}.\] Consequently, \(F^*\) is the perfect-matching polytope of \(H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any optimal dual solution, the optimal assignment face consists exactly of the doubly stochastic matrices supported on zero-reduced-cost edges, and it is the convex hull of the perfect matchings in that equality graph.
assumptions_latex: \((u,v)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n\) is an optimal dual solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F^*\) is the perfect-matching polytope of the equality graph \(H\).

notation.meaning: The optimal face of the assignment polytope.

children.title: Tie-Breaking Stability
children.top_down_role: Effects of perturbations or selection rules on tied optima.

knowledge_statements.title: Tie-Breaking Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lexicographic perturbation of a finite assignment problem without changing its primary optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A\) be the finite set of feasible assignments, let \(c:\mathcal A\to\mathbb R\), and order the assignment edges as \(e_1,\ldots,e_m\). Define \(c_\varepsilon(A)=c(A)+\sum_{e_i\in A}\varepsilon^i\). There exists \(\varepsilon_0>0\) such that, for every \(0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0\), every minimizer of \(c_\varepsilon\) minimizes \(c\); moreover, the perturbed problem has the unique minimizer whose incidence vector is lexicographically smallest among the \(c\)-optimal assignments, with respect to the stated edge order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For all sufficiently small positive perturbation parameters, primary optimality is preserved and the unique selected assignment is the one with lexicographically smallest incidence vector among the original cost-optimal assignments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmin}_{A\in\mathcal A}c_\varepsilon(A)=\{A^{\mathrm{lex}}\}\subseteq\operatorname*{argmin}_{A\in\mathcal A}c(A)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonbipartite maximum-matching algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Queue-based augmenting-path search with blossom handling in a general graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a graph $G=(V,E)$, initialize $\operatorname{mate}[v]=0$ and $\operatorname{considered}[v]=0$ for every $v\in V$. At each stage, select an unconsidered exposed vertex $u$, construct the auxiliary digraph induced by the current matching, and search it from $u$ using a queue. If the search reaches another exposed vertex, augment the matching and restart; when the search detects the prescribed blossom condition, invoke the blossom procedure. Terminate when no unconsidered exposed vertex remains and output the matching encoded by $\operatorname{mate}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize the empty matching. From each unconsidered exposed vertex, search an auxiliary directed graph, augment upon reaching another exposed vertex, handle detected blossoms, and restart after augmentation. When no eligible start vertex remains, output the matching stored in mate.
assumptions_latex: \operatorname{augment}\text{ and }\operatorname{blossom}\text{ denote the algorithm's specified subroutines}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{mate}\text{ is the algorithm's output matching}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Characterization of the Perfect 2-Matching Space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A support-and-vertex-sum characterization of the linear span of perfect 2-matchings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a graph. Its perfect \(2\)-matching space consists exactly of the vectors \(x\in\mathbb{R}^E\) such that \(x_e=0\) whenever \(e\) is not in the support of any perfect \(2\)-matching and \(x(\delta(v))=x(\delta(u))\) for all \(u,v\in V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector belongs to the perfect 2-matching space exactly when it vanishes on every edge unsupported by any perfect 2-matching and has the same incident-edge sum at every vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in\mathcal{S}_{2\mathrm{M}}(G)\iff\left[\forall e\in E,\ e\text{ is in no perfect }2\text{-matching}\Rightarrow x_e=0\right]\land\left[\forall u,v\in V,\ x(\delta(u))=x(\delta(v))\right].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lifting a Perfect Matching and Dual Solution Through Odd-Circuit Expansion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Retains the source's numbered feasibility and compatibility conditions, whose definitions are not included in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \((G',c')\) is obtained from \((G,c)\) by shrinking an odd circuit \(C\) of equality edges relative to a dual-feasible solution \(y\). Let \(M'\) be a perfect matching of \(G'\), and let \((y',Y')\) be feasible for \((5.17)\) on \((G',c')\), satisfy \((5.22)\) and \((5.23)\) with \(M'\), and have \(y'_C\geq0\). Extend \(M'\) through \(C\) to a perfect matching \(M\) of \(G\). Set \(y_v=y'_v\) for \(v\notin V(C)\), retaining the already defined values on \(V(C)\), and set \(Y_D=Y'_D\) if \(Y'_D>0\), \(Y_D=y'_C\) if \(D=\delta'(C)\), and \(Y_D=0\) otherwise. Then \((y,Y)\) is feasible for \((5.17)\) on \((G,c)\), and \(M,(y,Y)\) satisfy \((5.22)\) and \((5.23)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compatible perfect matching and dual-feasible solution on a graph obtained by shrinking an odd equality circuit can be lifted using the stated matching extension and dual assignments. The lifted solution remains feasible and preserves the required compatibility conditions.
assumptions_latex: (G',c')\text{ is obtained from }(G,c)\text{ by shrinking an odd equality circuit }C\text{ relative to dual-feasible }y
M'\text{ is a perfect matching of }G'
M\text{ is obtained by extending }M'\text{ through }E(C)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (y,Y)\text{ is feasible for }(5.17)\text{ on }(G,c),\qquad M,(y,Y)\text{ satisfy }(5.22),(5.23).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Augmenting Path
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition relative to a matching, including the cardinality-increasing flip.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a matching. An augmenting path with respect to \(M\) is an odd alternating path whose first and last vertices are unmatched by \(M\). Interchanging matched and unmatched edges along such a path produces a matching of cardinality \(|M|+1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An augmenting path is an odd alternating path whose endpoints are unmatched. Flipping matched and unmatched status along it yields a matching with one additional edge.
assumptions_latex: P\text{ is an odd alternating path with respect to }M
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ is augmenting with respect to }M,\quad M\oplus E(P)\text{ is a matching, and }|M\oplus E(P)|=|M|+1.
