knowledge_statements.statement_title: Root-transfer exchange lemma for matching forests
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Redistributes the common union of two matching forests so a specified root transfers to the first forest, with controlled size and root behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $F_1,F_2$ be matching forests in a mixed graph $(V,E,A)$ and let $s\in R(F_2)\setminus R(F_1)$. Then there exist matching forests $F_1',F_2'$ such that $F_1'\cap F_2'=F_1\cap F_2$, $F_1'\cup F_2'=F_1\cup F_2$, and $s\in R(F_1')$, and one of the following holds: (i) $|F_1'|<|F_1|$; (ii) $|F_1'|=|F_1|$ and $|R(F_1')|>|R(F_1)|$; or (iii) $|F_1'|=|F_1|$, $R(F_1')=(R(F_1)\setminus\{t\})\cup\{s\}$ for some $t\in R(F_1)$, and for every strong component $K$ of $(V,A)$, $|R(F_1'\cap A)\cap K|=|R(F_1\cap A)\cap K|$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given two matching forests and a vertex that is a root only of the second, their shared union can be repartitioned into two matching forests so that the vertex becomes a root of the first. The first forest then either becomes smaller, gains roots without changing size, or exchanges one root for the specified vertex while preserving the number of branching roots in every directed strong component.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists F_1',F_2'\text{ matching forests}:\ F_1'\cap F_2'=F_1\cap F_2,\ F_1'\cup F_2'=F_1\cup F_2,\ s\in R(F_1'),\text{ and (i), (ii), or (iii) holds as stated.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equimatchable Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines equimatchability and states that it is determined componentwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A graph \(G\) is equimatchable if every matching of \(G\) extends to a maximum matching; equivalently, every maximal matching of \(G\) is maximum. Furthermore, \(G\) is equimatchable if and only if every connected component of \(G\) is equimatchable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph is equimatchable when every matching extends to a maximum matching, equivalently when every maximal matching is maximum. The graph is equimatchable exactly when each of its connected components is equimatchable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is equimatchable}\iff(\forall M\text{ maximal in }G,\ |M|=\nu(G))\iff(\forall K\text{ a connected component of }G,\ K\text{ is equimatchable}).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Augmenting-Path Flip Increases Matching Cardinality

assumptions_latex: P\text{ is an augmenting path with respect to }M
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\oplus E(P)\text{ is a matching},\quad |M\oplus E(P)|=|M|+1,\quad V(M)\subseteq V(M\oplus E(P)),\quad V(M\oplus E(P))\setminus V(M)=\{\text{endpoints of }P\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: TDI description for partitionable matching-forest polytopes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simplified polyhedral system using classwise directed-cycle inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E,A)\) be partitionable into \(R,S\), with each undirected edge regarded as oriented from \(R\) to \(S\), and let \(\delta^{\mathrm{head}}(v)\) contain the edges and arcs having head \(v\). The system
\[x_e\ge0\quad(e\in E\cup A),\qquad x(\delta^{\mathrm{head}}(v))\le1\quad(v\in V),\]
\[x(A[U])\le |U|-1\quad(\varnothing\ne U\subseteq R\text{ or }\varnothing\ne U\subseteq S)\]
is totally dual integral and determines the matching-forest polytope of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a mixed graph partitionable into R and S, nonnegativity, head-capacity constraints, and directed acyclicity inequalities within either class form a TDI system describing its matching-forest polytope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{System (59.32) is TDI and its feasible region equals }P_{MF}(G).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Expansion of a Zero-Dual Odd Pseudonode
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the matching, alternating-tree, graph, and boundary-cost updates performed during blossom expansion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M'\) be an equality-edge matching of a derived graph \(G'\), let \(T\) be an equality-edge \(M'\)-alternating tree, and let \(v\) be an odd pseudonode with \(y_v=0\). Let \(f,g\) be the tree edges incident with \(v\), let \(C\) be the circuit shrunk to form \(v\), let \(u,w\in V(C)\) be the ends of \(f,g\) within \(C\), and let \(P\) be the even-length path in \(C\) joining \(u\) and \(w\). Expand \(C\), extend \(M'\) to a matching of the expanded graph, replace the tree edge set by \(E(T)\cup E(P)\), and for every edge \(st\) with \(s\in V(C)\) and \(t\notin V(C)\), set \(c'_{st}\leftarrow c'_{st}+y_s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When an odd pseudonode in the alternating tree has zero dual value, expand its contracted odd circuit, extend the matching through it, add the appropriate even circuit path to the tree, and update the costs of edges leaving the circuit.
assumptions_latex: M'\text{ is an equality-edge matching of the derived graph }G'
v\text{ is an odd pseudonode with }y_v=0
f,g\text{ are the edges of }T\text{ incident with }v
P\text{ is the even-length path in the contracted circuit }C\text{ joining the internal ends of }f,g
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G'\leftarrow\operatorname{expand}_C(G'),\quad M'\leftarrow\operatorname{extend}_C(M'),\quad E(T)\leftarrow E(T)\cup E(P),\quad c'_{st}\leftarrow c'_{st}+y_s\ \text{for }s\in V(C),\ t\notin V(C).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Contraction gluing for the perfect matching lattice
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lifts lattice membership from contractions of both sides of an odd set under the stated cut-edge realization condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\), let \(U\subseteq V\) be odd, and suppose that for every \(e\in\delta(U)\) there is a perfect matching \(M_e\) of \(G\) such that \(M_e\cap\delta(U)=\{e\}\). Set \(G_1=G/\bar U\) and \(G_2=G/U\). If \(x\in\mathbb Z^E\) projects, for each \(i\in\{1,2\}\), to an element of the perfect matching lattice of \(G_i\), then \(x\) belongs to the perfect matching lattice of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every edge crossing an odd set can be the unique crossing edge of a perfect matching, lattice membership of an integral edge vector in both associated contractions implies its membership in the original graph's perfect matching lattice.
assumptions_latex: \forall e\in\delta(U)\;\exists M_e\text{ a perfect matching of }G:\ M_e\cap\delta(U)=\{e\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in\mathcal L_{\mathrm{PM}}(G)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tight-Edge Matching Certificates and Label Update
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States two termination certificates and the feasible label update that creates an additional tight edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G be a graph, c:E(G)\to\mathbb R, and z\in\mathbb R^{V(G)} satisfy z_v+z_w\le c(e) for every e=\{v,w\}\in E(G). Let G_z=(V(G),\{e=\{v,w\}\in E(G):z_v+z_w=c(e)\}), let M be a matching in G_z, and let F be a maximal alternating forest in G_z with respect to M, with inner vertices X and outer vertices Y. Then: (a) if M is perfect, it is a minimum-weight perfect matching in G; (b) if \Gamma_G(y)\subseteq X for every y\in Y, then M is a maximum matching in G; (c) otherwise, define \varepsilon=\min\!\left\{\min_{e=\{v,w\}\in E(G[Y])}\frac{c(e)-z_v-z_w}{2},\min_{e=\{v,w\}\in\delta_G(Y)\cap\delta_G(V(F))}\bigl(c(e)-z_v-z_w\bigr)\right\} and set z'_v=z_v-\varepsilon for v\in X, z'_v=z_v+\varepsilon for v\in Y, and z'_v=z_v for v\notin V(F). Then z'_v+z'_w\le c(e) for every e=\{v,w\}\in E(G), M\cup E(F)\subseteq E(G_{z'}), and \Gamma_{G_{z'}}(y)\setminus X\ne\varnothing for some y\in Y.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For feasible vertex labels, consider the tight-edge graph and a maximal alternating forest for a tight matching. A perfect matching is minimum-weight perfect; the stated neighborhood condition certifies maximum cardinality; otherwise, the minimum-slack label update remains feasible, preserves the matching and forest edges as tight, and creates a tight neighbor outside the inner set for some outer vertex.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is a graph and }c:E(G)\to\mathbb R
z\in\mathbb R^{V(G)}\text{ satisfies }z_v+z_w\le c(e)\text{ for every }e=\{v,w\}\in E(G)
F\text{ is a maximal alternating forest in }G_z\text{ with respect to }M
X\text{ and }Y\text{ are respectively the inner and outer vertex sets of }F
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[M\text{ perfect}\Rightarrow M\text{ is minimum-weight perfect}\bigr]\land\bigl[(\forall y\in Y,\Gamma_G(y)\subseteq X)\Rightarrow M\text{ is maximum}\bigr]\land\bigl[\text{otherwise the stated }z'\text{ is feasible, preserves }M\cup E(F)\text{ as tight, and creates the stated new tight adjacency}\bigr]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Blossom shrinking update
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The contraction step used when an alternating-tree search edge joins two outer vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M'\) be a matching of \(G'\), let \(T\) be an \(M'\)-alternating tree, and let \(vw\in E(G')\) satisfy \(v,w\in B(T)\). Let \(C\) be the circuit formed by \(vw\) and the path in \(T\) from \(v\) to \(w\). Replace \(G'\) by \(G'\times C\), replace \(M'\) by \(M'\setminus E(C)\), and replace \(T\) by the tree in the contracted graph having edge set \(E(T)\setminus E(C)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When an edge joins two B(T) vertices, combine it with their tree path to form a blossom, contract that circuit, remove its edges from the matching, and update the alternating tree by deleting its edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (G',M',T)\leftarrow\bigl(G'\times C,\,M'\setminus E(C),\,T\text{ with edge set }E(T)\setminus E(C)\bigr)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bottleneck k-Matching Min–Max Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates the largest attainable minimum edge weight in a k-edge matching to a minimum over odd-set contraction and deletion certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G=(N,A) have edge weights w_{ij}. Let X_k range over matchings containing k edges. Let H_{k-1} range over graphs obtained from G by contracting odd vertex sets of cardinality at least three and deleting singleton vertex sets, where the total capacity of the family of odd sets is k-1 and the family need not cover G. Then \[\max_{X_k}\min\{w_{ij}:(i,j)\in X_k\}=\min_{H_{k-1}}\max\{w_{ij}:(i,j)\in H_{k-1}\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum bottleneck value among k-edge matchings equals the minimum, over odd-set contractions and singleton deletions having total capacity k-1, of the largest edge weight remaining in the resulting graph.
assumptions_latex: w_{ij}\text{ is the weight of edge }(i,j)
X_k\text{ ranges over matchings containing }k\text{ edges}
H_{k-1}\text{ is obtained by contracting odd sets of size at least }3\text{ and deleting singleton sets}
\{N_i\}\text{ need not be an odd-set cover of }G
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max_{X_k}\min_{(i,j)\in X_k}w_{ij}=\min_{H_{k-1}}\max_{(i,j)\in H_{k-1}}w_{ij}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Structural invariants of the weighted matching algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous invariants holding at every stage of the specified weighted matching algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At every stage, define X(j):=\{v\in V(G):j\in\{b^1(v),\ldots,b^{k_v}(v)\}\} and \mathcal B:=\{X(j):1\le j\le K\}\cup\{\{v\}:v\in V(G)\}. Then: (a) \mathcal B is laminar; the sets V_r:=\{v:\rho^{k_v}(v)=r\} with \rho^{k_r}(r)=r are exactly its maximal elements, are each uniformly outer, inner, or out-of-forest, and carry blossoms with base r; (b) the edges \{x,\mu(x)\} form a matching M containing a near-perfect matching in every member of \mathcal B; (c) the maintained \mu- and \varphi-data associated with each X(b) describe an M-alternating ear decomposition of G[X(b)]; (d) all designated matching, \varphi-, and maximal-inner-blossom connector edges are tight; (e) the designated edges form a general blossom forest F with respect to M, consistently with the vertex marks; (f) contracting the maximal sub-blossoms of any B\in\mathcal B with |B|>1 yields a circuit; and (g) for every outer vertex v, \operatorname{TREEPATH} returns an M-alternating v-r path, where r is the root of v's tree in F.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every stage, the maintained blossom sets form a laminar family with uniformly marked maximal blossoms. The mate edges form a matching that is near-perfect within every blossom; the stored data describe alternating ear decompositions; the designated edges are tight and form a mark-consistent general blossom forest; contraction of maximal sub-blossoms yields a circuit; and TREEPATH returns an alternating path from each outer vertex to its tree root.
assumptions_latex: \text{The specified weighted matching algorithm is at an arbitrary stage.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{All structural properties (a)--(g) concerning }\mathcal B,M,\text{ ear decompositions, tightness, }F,\text{ contraction, and }\operatorname{TREEPATH}\text{ hold.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fractional Edge-Coloring Number and Multigraph Characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the fractional chromatic index and records its relation to integral edge coloring.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a graph \(G=(V,E)\), let \(\mathcal M\) be its matchings and \(\chi^M\) the incidence vector of \(M\). Define
\[
\chi'^*(G):=\min\left\{\sum_{M\in\mathcal M}\lambda_M:\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^{\mathcal M},\ \sum_{M\in\mathcal M}\lambda_M\chi^M=\mathbf 1\right\}.
\]
Then \(\chi'^*(G)\leq\chi'(G)\). If \(G_k\) replaces every edge of \(G\) by \(k\) parallel edges, then
\[
\chi'^*(G)=\min_{k\geq1}\frac{\chi'(G_k)}{k}.
\]
The value \(\chi'^*(G)\) is polynomial-time computable. For the Petersen graph, \(\chi'^*(G)=3<4=\chi'(G)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The fractional edge-coloring number is the minimum total nonnegative weight of matchings whose weighted incidence vectors equal one on every edge. It lower-bounds the ordinary edge-chromatic number, equals the minimum scaled edge-chromatic number over uniform parallel-edge expansions, and is polynomial-time computable. The Petersen graph has fractional value 3 and integral value 4.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \chi'^*(G)\leq\chi'(G),\qquad \chi'^*(G)=\min_{k\geq1}\frac{\chi'(G_k)}{k}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reduction of nonbipartite matching to bidirected flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction converting a weighted nonbipartite matching problem into a unit-capacity bidirected-flow problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a weighted nonbipartite matching problem, add a dummy node when the number of nodes is odd. Add zero-weight slack arcs to obtain a degree-constrained subgraph problem requiring degree one at every node. Replace each undirected arc by a bidirected arc with two tail ends and unit capacity, convert the arc weights to costs, and set $b_i=1$ at every node $i$. The resulting bidirected-flow problem represents the original matching problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Add a dummy node if necessary, introduce zero-weight slack arcs to form a one-factor problem, replace every undirected edge by a unit-capacity bidirected arc with two tails, convert weights to costs, and set every node balance to one. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gallai–Edmonds Characterization of Connected Equimatchable Graphs Without Perfect Matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient conditions expressed using the Gallai–Edmonds decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a connected graph with no perfect matching, and let \(V(G)=D\mathbin{\dot\cup}A\mathbin{\dot\cup}C\) be its Gallai\text{--}Edmonds decomposition. Then \(G\) is equimatchable if and only if: (1) \(C=\varnothing\) and \(A\) is independent; (2) for every \(v\in A\), \(G-v\) has no matching covering \(\Gamma(v)\); (3) whenever distinct nonadjacent vertices \(u,v\) lie in the same component of \(G[D]\), \(G-u-v\) has no matching covering \(\Gamma(u)\cup\Gamma(v)\); and (4) no component of \(G[D]\) is joined to \(A\) by two independent edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a connected graph without a perfect matching, equimatchability is equivalent to four conditions on its Gallai–Edmonds decomposition: C is empty and A is independent; deleting any vertex of A leaves no matching covering all its neighbors; deleting any two nonadjacent vertices in one D-component leaves no matching covering both neighborhoods; and no D-component has two vertex-disjoint edges to A.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is equimatchable}\iff\begin{cases}C=\varnothing\text{ and }A\text{ is independent};\\ \forall v\in A,\ G-v\text{ has no matching covering }\Gamma(v);\\ \forall u,v\text{ nonadjacent in one component of }G[D],\ G-u-v\text{ has no matching covering }\Gamma(u)\cup\Gamma(v);\\ \text{no component of }G[D]\text{ has two independent edges to }A.\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Blossom algorithm for perfect matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A general-graph procedure that either constructs a perfect matching or returns an exhausted contracted search state certifying nonexistence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a graph \(G\) and a nonperfect matching \(M\), set \(G'=G\) and \(M'=M\), choose an \(M'\)-exposed root, and grow an \(M'\)-alternating tree \(T\). For an edge \(vw\in E(G')\) with \(v\in B(T)\) and \(w\notin A(T)\), augment when \(w\) is exposed, extend \(T\) when \(w\notin V(T)\) is covered, and shrink the resulting odd circuit when \(w\in B(T)\). After augmentation, extend the contracted matching to \(G\), restore \(G'=G\), and restart from an exposed vertex; if none exists, return the perfect matching. If no eligible edge remains, return \((G',M',T)\) and conclude that \(G\) has no perfect matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a nonperfect matching, grow an alternating tree, augment when it reaches an exposed vertex, extend it through a covered vertex, and contract a blossom when an edge joins two outer vertices. The procedure returns either a perfect matching or an exhausted contracted search state certifying that none exists.
assumptions_latex: M\text{ is not perfect, so an }M\text{-exposed vertex exists}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The algorithm returns either a perfect matching of }G\text{ or a state }(G',M',T)\text{ certifying that none exists}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matching-forest polytope and defining inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the matching-forest polytope and its mixed-graph inequality description.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a mixed graph \(G=(V,E,A)\), the matching-forest polytope is \(P_{MF}(G)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^F:F\text{ is a matching forest}\}\subseteq\mathbb R^{E\cup A}\). Let \(\delta^{\mathrm{head}}(v)\) be the edges and arcs having head \(v\). For a subpartition \(\mathcal L\) of \(V\), let \(\gamma(\mathcal L)\) contain the undirected edges spanned by \(\bigcup\mathcal L\) and the directed arcs spanned by individual classes of \(\mathcal L\). Then \(P_{MF}(G)\) is described by \(x_e\ge0\) for \(e\in E\cup A\), \(x(\delta^{\mathrm{head}}(v))\le1\) for \(v\in V\), and \(x(\gamma(\mathcal L))\le\left\lfloor|\bigcup\mathcal L|-|\mathcal L|/2\right\rfloor\) for every subpartition \(\mathcal L\) having an odd number of nonempty classes. Every integral solution is the incidence vector of a matching forest.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The matching-forest polytope is the convex hull of matching-forest incidence vectors. It is described by nonnegativity, at-most-one-head constraints, and odd-subpartition inequalities; its integral feasible points are exactly matching forests.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal L\text{ ranges over subpartitions of }V\text{ with an odd number of nonempty classes}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_{MF}(G)=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^{E\cup A}:x_e\ge0,\ x(\delta^{\mathrm{head}}(v))\le1,\ x(\gamma(\mathcal L))\le\left\lfloor|\bigcup\mathcal L|-\frac12|\mathcal L|\right\rfloor\right\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Majorization of Edge-Set Families

knowledge_statements.statement_title: K-gon-free 2-matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and parity reduction for forbidden cycle lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb N\). A 2-matching \(\omega\) in a graph \(G\) is \(K\)-gon-free if there is no cycle of length \(k\in K\) all of whose edges have positive \(\omega\)-weight. Only odd members of \(K\) affect existence of a perfect \(K\)-gon-free 2-matching, since even cycles can be eliminated from any perfect 2-matching without creating new cycles.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A 2-matching is K-gon-free when it has no positively weighted cycle whose length belongs to K. For existence of a perfect such 2-matching, only the odd lengths in K matter, because even cycles can be eliminated without creating new cycles.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a derived pair \((G',c')\), a feasible solution \(y\) of \((5.17)\), an equality-edge matching \(M'\), and an equality-edge \(M'\)-alternating tree \(T\), define \(\varepsilon_1=\min\{\bar c_e:e\text{ joins a vertex in }B(T)\text{ to a vertex outside }V(T)\}\), \(\varepsilon_2=\min\{\bar c_e/2:e\text{ joins two vertices in }B(T)\}\), and \(\varepsilon_3=\min\{y_v:v\in A(T)\text{ is a pseudonode of }G'\}\). Set \(\varepsilon=\min\{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2,\varepsilon_3\}\). Replace \(y_v\) by \(y_v+\varepsilon\) for \(v\in B(T)\), by \(y_v-\varepsilon\) for \(v\in A(T)\), and leave it unchanged otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose the smallest of three event values: an edge leaving the alternating tree becomes tight, an edge joining two outer tree vertices becomes tight, or an inner pseudonode's dual value reaches zero. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matching, Matched Elements, and Cardinality Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational terminology for a finite graph matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(N,A)\) be a finite graph with \(n=|N|\). A matching is a set \(M\subseteq A\) such that no two edges of \(M\) are incident to the same node. Edges in \(M\) are matched and edges in \(A\setminus M\) are unmatched; nodes incident to edges of \(M\) are matched and all other nodes are unmatched. Consequently, every node has degree \(0\) or \(1\) in \((N,M)\), and \(|M|\leq\lfloor n/2\rfloor\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matching is a set of graph edges with pairwise disjoint endpoints. Its edges and incident vertices are matched, while the others are unmatched. The matching subgraph has degrees zero or one and contains at most floor(n/2) edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\text{ is a matching exactly when its edges have pairwise disjoint endpoints; then }\deg_{(N,M)}(v)\in\{0,1\}\text{ and }|M|\leq\lfloor n/2\rfloor.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions and basic representation properties for graphs obtained by successive odd-circuit shrinkings.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reduction of bidirected flow to maximum-weight complete matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Four-stage construction preserving optimal solutions and detecting infeasibility through complete-matching existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each node $i$ of a bidirected network $G$, construct nodes $i$ and $i'$ in an undirected graph $G^*$. Attach a tail end at $i$ to node $i$ and a head end at $i$ to node $i'$, preserving costs and capacities; add $(i,i')$ with zero cost and unbounded capacity. Choose sufficiently large nonnegative integers $b_i^*,b_{i'}^*$ with $b_i^*-b_{i'}^*=b_i$. Eliminate every finite capacity $c_{ij}$ by replacing $(i,j)$ with $(i,k),(k,k'),(k',j)$, setting $b_k^*=b_{k'}^*=c_{ij}$, assigning zero cost to the outer edges and the original cost to $(k,k')$. Replace each node $i$ by $b_i^*$ copies and reproduce every edge between all corresponding copies, thereby requiring degree one at every copy. Finally set $w_{ij}=M-a_{ij}^{**}$ for sufficiently large $M$. A maximum-weight matching is complete whenever a complete matching exists and then corresponds to a minimum-cost flow in $G$; if no complete matching exists, the original bidirected-flow problem is infeasible. When $G$ is directed, $G^*$ is bipartite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Split each node into tail and head sides, add a zero-cost unbounded edge between them, and choose nonnegative integer split balances whose difference is the original balance. Remove finite capacities with subdivision gadgets, expand each node into the prescribed number of copies, and convert costs to weights using a sufficiently large constant. A maximum-weight complete matching then corresponds to a minimum-cost bidirected flow, while absence of a complete matching certifies infeasibility. The first expansion is bipartite when the original network is directed.
assumptions_latex: b_i^*,b_{i'}^*\in\mathbb Z_+\text{ are sufficiently large and satisfy }b_i^*-b_{i'}^*=b_i
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[G^{**}\text{ has a complete matching}\bigr]\iff\bigl[\text{the original bidirected-flow problem is feasible}\bigr],\quad\text{and an optimal maximum-weight complete matching corresponds to a minimum-cost flow.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matching forests in mixed graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines matching forests and gives their equivalent matching–branching decomposition and root identities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(V,E,A)$ be a loopless mixed graph, with both endpoints of each $e\in E$ regarded as heads. A set $F\subseteq E\cup A$ is a matching forest if its underlying undirected graph contains no circuit and every $v\in V$ is the head of at most one member of $F$. Equivalently, $B:=F\cap A$ is a branching and $M:=F\cap E$ is a matching covering only roots of $B$. Its root set is $R(F):=\{v\in V:v\text{ is the head of no member of }F\}$. For every matching forest, $R(F)=R(M)\cap R(B)$ and $V=R(M)\cup R(B)$. More generally, for any matching $M\subseteq E$ and branching $B\subseteq A$, $M\cup B$ is a matching forest if and only if $R(M)\cup R(B)=V$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a loopless mixed graph, a matching forest is an acyclic set of undirected edges and directed arcs for which each vertex is a head of at most one selected element. Equivalently, its arcs form a branching and its undirected edges form a matching that covers only branching roots. The roots are precisely the common roots of these two parts, and a matching and branching have a matching-forest union exactly when their root sets together cover every vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is a matching forest}\iff B\text{ is a branching, }M\text{ is a matching, and }M\text{ covers only roots of }B;\quad R(F)=R(M)\cap R(B),\quad R(M)\cup R(B)=V.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cross-free cuts and family contractions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions of shores, cross-free cut collections, family contractions, and the associated nonbipartite-contraction count.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(U\subseteq V\) satisfying \(C=\delta(U)\) is a shore of \(C\). Cuts \(C,C'\) are cross-free if they have disjoint shores \(U,U'\); a family \(\mathcal F\) is cross-free if every two of its cuts are cross-free. For a cross-free collection \(\mathcal F\) of nontrivial cuts, an \(\mathcal F\)-contraction is obtained by choosing \(U_0\subseteq V\) with \(\delta(U_0)\in\mathcal F\), contracting \(U_0\), and contracting each maximal proper subset \(U\subset V\setminus U_0\) with \(\delta(U)\in\mathcal F\). If \(G\) is connected, it has exactly \(|\mathcal F|+1\) such contractions. The number of these contractions that are nonbipartite is denoted \(\operatorname{nonbip}_G(\mathcal F)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A shore is a vertex set defining a cut. A pair of cuts is cross-free when disjoint shores can be chosen, and a family is cross-free pairwise. Contracting one chosen shore and the maximal eligible shores on its other side defines a family contraction. A connected graph has exactly one more such contraction than the family has cuts, and nonbip counts the nonbipartite contractions.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal F\text{ is a cross-free collection of nontrivial cuts}
G\text{ is connected for the counting assertion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \#\{\mathcal F\text{-contractions of }G\}=|\mathcal F|+1,\qquad \operatorname{nonbip}_G(\mathcal F)=\#\{H:H\text{ is a nonbipartite }\mathcal F\text{-contraction}\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Measure-theoretic Hall condition for a supported uniform coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient condition for a closed relation on the unit interval to support a coupling with two Lebesgue marginals.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bounded Conformal Decomposition Lemma
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Each summand preserves both edge-coordinate signs and the signs of vertex-incidence sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(V,E)$ be a graph and $x\in\mathbb{Z}^{E}$. Then $x$ can be expressed as a finite sum $x=\sum_{k=1}^{m}y^k$ of vectors $y^k\in\mathbb{Z}^{E}$ such that, for every $k$, $y^k$ is conformal to $x$, $(y^k(\delta(v)):v\in V)$ is conformal to $(x(\delta(v)):v\in V)$, and $\lVert y^k\rVert_\infty\le 2$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every integral edge vector of a graph is a finite sum of integral edge vectors that are sign-compatible with the original vector both coordinatewise and in their vertex-incidence sums, with every summand having infinity norm at most two.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0},\ y^1,\ldots,y^m\in\mathbb{Z}^{E}:\ x=\sum_{k=1}^{m}y^k,\ \forall k,\ \bigl[(\forall e\in E,\ x_e\ge0\Rightarrow y^k_e\ge0,\ x_e\le0\Rightarrow y^k_e\le0)\land(\forall v\in V,\ x(\delta(v))\ge0\Rightarrow y^k(\delta(v))\ge0,\ x(\delta(v))\le0\Rightarrow y^k(\delta(v))\le0)\land\lVert y^k\rVert_\infty\le2\bigr].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Criterion for a Matching Covering a Prescribed Vertex Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes when a graph has a matching covering every vertex of a specified subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a graph and let \(T\subseteq V\). Then \(G\) has a matching covering \(T\) if and only if, for every \(U\subseteq V\), the number \(o_T(G-U)\) of odd components of \(G-U\) whose vertex sets are contained in \(T\) satisfies \(o_T(G-U)\le |U|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph has a matching covering T exactly when, after deleting any vertex set U, the number of odd components lying entirely in T is at most the size of U.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ has a matching covering }T\iff \forall U\subseteq V,\;o_T(G-U)\le |U|.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Couplings with prescribed marginals and constrained support
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions used to formulate a measure-theoretic bipartite matching problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let (S_i,\mathcal A_i,P_i), i=1,2, be probability spaces, and let (S_1\times S_2,\mathcal A,P) be their product probability space. A probability measure Q on (S_1\times S_2,\mathcal A) has marginals P_1 and P_2 if Q(X\times S_2)=P_1(X) for every X\in\mathcal A_1 and Q(S_1\times Y)=P_2(Y) for every Y\in\mathcal A_2. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cycle Shrinking Lemma
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of maximum-matching optimality before and after contracting a suitably matched odd cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G$ be a graph, $M$ a matching in $G$, and $Z$ a cycle of length $2k+1$ containing exactly $k$ edges of $M$ and vertex-disjoint from every edge of $M\setminus E(Z)$. Let $G'$ be obtained from $G$ by shrinking $Z$ to one vertex, and let $M'=M\setminus E(Z)$. Then $M'$ is a maximum matching in $G'$ if and only if $M$ is a maximum matching in $G$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If an odd cycle has exactly one vertex left unmatched by the matching edges within it and is vertex-disjoint from all remaining matching edges, contracting that cycle preserves maximum-matching optimality in both directions.
assumptions_latex: Z\text{ is a cycle of length }2k+1
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M'\text{ is a maximum matching in }G'\iff M\text{ is a maximum matching in }G

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gallai–Edmonds list algorithm for maximum matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the initialization, certificate test, progress alternatives, and finite descent used by the algorithm without reproducing its case analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(k=0\) and \(\mathcal L=\{\varnothing\}\). At a general iteration choose \(M_1\in\mathcal L\). If \(M_1\) has no edge from \(A(\mathcal L)\) to \(A(\mathcal L)\cup C(\mathcal L)\) and \(M_1\cap E(T)\) is near-perfect for every component \(T\) of \(G[D(\mathcal L)]\), stop with the maximum matching \(M_1\). Otherwise, alternating-path or alternating-cycle switches produce either a matching of cardinality \(k+1\), after which the algorithm advances to the larger cardinality, or a \(k\)-edge matching missing a vertex outside the current \(D(\mathcal L)\), which is added to \(\mathcal L\) and strictly enlarges \(D(\mathcal L)\). In the component subcase using a shortest path, each unresolved repetition strictly decreases the relevant within-component distance and therefore reaches one of the progress cases after at most \(|V(T)|\) repetitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start with the empty matching list. Test any listed matching against the Gallai–Edmonds certificate. If it passes, it is maximum. If it fails, alternating switches either increase the matching size or add an equal-size matching that strictly enlarges the set of vertices missed by the list. The only recursive component subcase decreases a path distance and terminates within the component.
assumptions_latex: M_1\in\mathcal L\text{ is selected at each iteration}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Each failed certificate test yields either a matching larger than }k\text{ or a strict enlargement of }D(\mathcal L);\text{ a successful test returns a maximum matching.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matching and Perfect Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for arbitrary graphs, including nonbipartite graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a graph and let \(S\subseteq E\). The set \(S\) is a matching if \(\lvert\delta_G(v)\cap S\rvert\le 1\) for every \(v\in V\). It is a perfect matching if \(\lvert\delta_G(v)\cap S\rvert=1\) for every \(v\in V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a graph G, a set S of edges is a matching when at most one edge of S is incident with each vertex. It is perfect when exactly one edge of S is incident with every vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ is a matching iff }\forall v\in V,\ |\delta_G(v)\cap S|\le 1;\quad S\text{ is perfect iff }\forall v\in V,\ |\delta_G(v)\cap S|=1.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequence-relative sets D, A, and C
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines vertex sets relative to a nonempty sequence of equal-cardinality matchings and states the condition under which they equal the Gallai–Edmonds sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph and let \(\mathcal L=(M_1,\ldots,M_t)\), where \(t\ge 1\), be a sequence of \(k\)-edge matchings. Define \(D(\mathcal L)=\{x\in V(G):\exists i\in\{1,\ldots,t\},\ x\notin V(M_i)\}\), \(A(\mathcal L)=\{x\in V(G)\setminus D(\mathcal L):x\text{ is adjacent to a vertex of }D(\mathcal L)\}\), and \(C(\mathcal L)=V(G)\setminus(D(\mathcal L)\cup A(\mathcal L))\). If \(k=\nu(G)\) and \(\mathcal L\) consists of all maximum matchings of \(G\), then \(D(\mathcal L)=D(G)\), \(A(\mathcal L)=A(G)\), and \(C(\mathcal L)=C(G)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty sequence of k-edge matchings, D contains the vertices missed by at least one listed matching, A contains the vertices outside D adjacent to D, and C contains the remaining vertices. If the sequence consists of all maximum matchings, these are the Gallai–Edmonds sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D(\mathcal L),A(\mathcal L),C(\mathcal L)\text{ are defined as above; if }k=\nu(G)\text{ and }\mathcal L\text{ consists of all maximum matchings, they equal }D(G),A(G),C(G),\text{ respectively.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Augmenting paths and maximum matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Augmenting-path terminology, matching coverage terminology, and the maximum-cardinality criterion for simple graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(V,E)$ be a simple graph and let $M\subseteq E$ be a matching. A path $P$ is $M$-augmenting if it has odd length, joins two vertices not covered by $M$, and its edges alternate between $E\setminus M$ and $M$. A vertex is covered by $M$ if it is incident with an edge of $M$, and otherwise is missed by $M$. Then $M$ has maximum cardinality if and only if no $M$-augmenting path exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a simple graph, an M-augmenting path is an odd-length path joining two vertices missed by M, with edges alternating outside and inside M. A vertex is covered when it is incident with a matching edge and missed otherwise. A matching is maximum exactly when it has no augmenting path.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\text{ has maximum cardinality}\iff\text{there is no }M\text{-augmenting path}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Blossom Algorithm for maximum-cardinality matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction of a maximum matching by repeated perfect-matching Blossom searches, together with a Tutte–Berge-type deficiency certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a graph \(G\), apply the perfect-matching Blossom Algorithm to the current derived graph. If it returns a perfect matching, that matching is maximum. If it returns a matching and a frustrated tree \(T\), delete \(V(T)\) from the derived graph, retain the matching edges not deleted, and repeat while an exposed node remains. After restoring all deleted parts and matching edges, let \(T_1,\ldots,T_k\) be the generated frustrated trees. The matching extends to a matching \(M\) of \(G\) with exactly \(k\) exposed vertices. For \(A=\bigcup_{i=1}^k A(T_i)\), \(\operatorname{oc}(G\setminus A)\ge |A|+k\), and therefore \(M\) is a maximum matching of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run the perfect-matching Blossom Algorithm repeatedly. Whenever it produces a frustrated tree, delete that tree and continue on the remaining derived graph. Restoring the deleted pieces yields a matching with one exposed vertex per frustrated tree. The union of their A-sets supplies an odd-component deficiency bound, proving that the matching is maximum.
assumptions_latex: T_1,\ldots,T_k\text{ are the frustrated trees generated by the repeated Blossom Algorithm runs.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\text{ has exactly }k\text{ exposed vertices and }\operatorname{oc}(G\setminus A)\ge |A|+k;\text{ hence }M\text{ is a maximum matching of }G.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Shrinking lemma for an odd cycle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimality equivalence before and after contracting a nearly perfectly matched odd cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be an undirected graph, \(S\) a matching of \(G\), and \(C\) a cycle of length \(2\ell+1\), where \(\ell\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\). Suppose \(|S\cap E(C)|=\ell\) and \(S\setminus E(C)\) is vertex-disjoint from \(C\). If \(G'\) is obtained by shrinking \(C\) to one vertex and \(S'=S\setminus E(C)\), then \(S'\) is maximum-cardinality in \(G'\) if and only if \(S\) is maximum-cardinality in \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If an odd cycle contains exactly one fewer matching edge than a perfect matching on its vertices and all other matching edges avoid the cycle, contracting the cycle preserves and reflects maximum-cardinality optimality.
assumptions_latex: C\text{ is a cycle with }|C|=2\ell+1,\quad \ell\in\mathbb Z_{>0}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S'\text{ is maximum-cardinality in }G'\iff S\text{ is maximum-cardinality in }G

knowledge_statements.title: Perfect General-Graph Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perfect matchings in finite undirected graphs, including nonbipartite graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph. A matching \(M\subseteq E\) is perfect if every vertex of \(G\) is incident with exactly one edge of \(M\). Equivalently, the endpoint sets of the edges in \(M\) partition \(V\), so \[|M|=|V|/2.\] Consequently, existence of a perfect matching requires \(|V|\) to be even.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A perfect matching consists of vertex-disjoint edges covering every vertex exactly once; therefore the graph must have even order.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: V=\biguplus_{e\in M}e\quad\text{and}\quad |M|=|V|/2

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Blossom Algorithm for Minimum-Weight Perfect Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-dual shrink-and-expand procedure for minimum-weight perfect matching in a general graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Start with a feasible dual solution $y$, a matching $M'$ in the current contracted graph $G'$, and an $M'$-alternating tree rooted at an exposed vertex. Repeatedly augment when an equality edge joins $B(T)$ to an exposed vertex outside $T$; extend $T$ when such an edge reaches a covered vertex; shrink when an equality edge joins two vertices of $B(T)$; expand a pseudonode $v\in A(T)$ when $y_v=0$; and otherwise change $y$. After an augmentation, extend $M'$ to a perfect matching of $G$ and stop if no exposed vertex remains. If every edge incident with $B(T)$ has its other end in $A(T)$ and $A(T)$ contains no pseudonode, stop and report that $G$ has no perfect matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Grow an equality-edge alternating tree, augment when it reaches an exposed vertex, shrink blossoms, expand zero-dual pseudonodes, and otherwise update the dual variables. Stop with a perfect matching when all vertices are covered, or report nonexistence under the stated blocked-tree condition.
assumptions_latex: y\text{ is feasible for the associated dual problem.}
M'\text{ is a matching in the current contracted graph }G'.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure stops with a perfect matching when no exposed vertex remains, or reports nonexistence under the stated blocked-tree condition.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Control-zone lower bound for Euclidean perfect matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A geometric disk-packing certificate for the total length of a perfect matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\subset\mathbb{R}^2\). For each \(v\in V\), let \(D_v\) be a disk centered at \(v\) with radius \(r_v\ge 0\). Such a disk is called a control zone. If the control zones are pairwise nonoverlapping, then every perfect matching \(M\) of \(V\) satisfies
\[
\sum_{e\in M}\operatorname{length}(e)\ge \sum_{v\in V}r_v.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A disk centered at a matching point is called a control zone. If the control zones are pairwise nonoverlapping, their radii sum to a lower bound on the Euclidean length of every perfect matching.
assumptions_latex: M\text{ is a perfect matching of }V
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{e\in M}\operatorname{length}(e)\ge \sum_{v\in V}r_v

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Odd-component characterization of perfect-matching existence in a general graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A graph \(G=(V,E)\) has a perfect matching if and only if, for every \(X\subseteq V\), the number \(o(G-X)\) of odd-order connected components of \(G-X\) satisfies \(o(G-X)\le |X|\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ has a perfect matching}\iff \forall X\subseteq V,\ o(G-X)\le |X|

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph and \(X\subseteq V(G)\) satisfy \[|V(G)|-2\nu(G)=q_G(X)-|X|.\] Then every maximum matching of \(G\) restricts to a perfect matching in each even connected component of \(G-X\), restricts to a near-perfect matching in each odd connected component of \(G-X\), and matches every vertex of \(X\) to a vertex in a distinct odd connected component of \(G-X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If X attains the Tutte–Berge deficiency, every maximum matching is perfect on each even component of G-X, near-perfect on each odd component, and matches all vertices of X into distinct odd components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}&\text{Every maximum matching is perfect on each even component of }G-X,\\&\text{near-perfect on each odd component of }G-X,\text{ and matches }X\\&\text{injectively into distinct odd components of }G-X.\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tutte determinant criterion for perfect matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An algebraic characterization of perfect matchability in a simple undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G\) be a simple undirected graph and let \(T_G(x)\) be its Tutte matrix over independent edge indeterminates. Then
\[
G\text{ has a perfect matching}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \det T_G(x)\not\equiv 0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simple undirected graph has a perfect matching if and only if the determinant polynomial of its Tutte matrix is not identically zero.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is a simple undirected graph}
T_G(x)\text{ is the Tutte matrix over independent edge indeterminates}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ has a perfect matching}\iff \det T_G(x)\not\equiv 0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Goemans–Williamson dual-growth component-merging procedure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The extracted parity-directed forest and dual-variable update procedure; no unstated optimality or approximation guarantee is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(F=\varnothing\), \(\mathcal C=\{\{v\}:v\in V\}\), and every component of \(y\) and \(Y\) to zero. Repeat the following steps. If \(\mathcal C\) has no odd-cardinality member, remove the even edges from \(F\) and stop. Otherwise choose an edge \(e=vw\), with \(v\in C_i\), \(w\in C_j\), and \(C_i\ne C_j\), minimizing
\[
\varepsilon=\frac{\bar c_e}{\operatorname{parity}(C_i)+\operatorname{parity}(C_j)},
\]
where at least one of \(C_i,C_j\) is odd. Add \(\varepsilon\) to \(y_v\) for every singleton \(\{v\}\in\mathcal C\), and add \(\varepsilon\) to \(Y_C\) for every odd \(C\in\mathcal C\) with \(|C|>1\). Add \(e\) to \(F\), replace \(C_i,C_j\) in \(\mathcal C\) by \(C_i\cup C_j\), and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start with isolated vertices, an empty forest, and zero dual variables. While an odd component exists, choose the specified minimum-ratio edge between components, raise the indicated dual variables, add the edge, and merge its endpoint components. When every component is even, remove the even edges from the forest and stop.
assumptions_latex: \bar c_e\text{ and the classification of even edges are those of the surrounding matching construction}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{When no odd member remains in }\mathcal C,\text{ remove the even edges from }F\text{ and terminate.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Covered and exposed vertices; perfect matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertex-coverage terminology and the definition of a perfect matching in a general graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a graph and let \(M\subseteq E\) be a matching. For \(v\in V\), the vertex \(v\) is covered by \(M\) if \(v\in e\) for some \(e\in M\), and is exposed by \(M\) otherwise. The matching \(M\) is perfect if every vertex of \(G\) is covered by \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Let G be a graph and M a matching in G. A vertex is covered by M if it belongs to an edge of M, and exposed otherwise. The matching M is perfect if it covers every vertex of G.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall v\in V:\quad v\text{ is covered by }M\iff \exists e\in M\text{ such that }v\in e;\qquad v\text{ is exposed by }M\iff \nexists e\in M\text{ such that }v\in e;\qquad M\text{ is perfect}\iff \forall v\in V\,\exists e\in M\text{ such that }v\in e.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometric moat definition and packing lower bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric odd-set certificates for the length of Euclidean perfect matchings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\subset\mathbb{R}^2\). A moat is a pair of compact sets \((N,I)\) satisfying
\[
I\subset N,\qquad |I\cap V|\text{ is odd},\qquad V\cap\bigl(N\setminus\operatorname{int}(I)\bigr)=\varnothing.
\]
Its width is
\[
w(N,I)=\min\{\|x-z\|:x\in I,\ z\in\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\operatorname{int}(N)\}.
\]
Every perfect matching of \(V\) contains an edge that traverses the moat by at least \(w(N,I)\). Consequently, if control zones and moats form a disjoint packing, then every perfect matching \(M\) satisfies
\[
\operatorname{length}(M)\ge \sum_v r_v+\sum_{(N,I)}w(N,I).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A moat consists of nested compact sets: its inner set contains an odd number of matching points, while the region between the inner and outer boundaries contains no matching point. Every perfect matching must traverse each moat by at least its width, so a disjoint packing of moats and control zones gives a lower bound equal to the sum of their widths and radii.
assumptions_latex: M\text{ is a perfect matching of }V
\text{for the summed bound, the control zones and moats form a disjoint packing}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{length}(M)\ge \sum_v r_v+\sum_{(N,I)}w(N,I)

knowledge_statements.title: Near-Perfect General-Graph Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Near-perfect matchings under the one-exposed-vertex convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph. A matching \(M\subseteq E\) is near-perfect if exactly one vertex is not incident with an edge of \(M\). Thus \(|V|\) is odd and \[|M|=(|V|-1)/2.\] If \(v\) is the unique exposed vertex, then \(M\) is a perfect matching of the vertex-deleted graph \(G-v\); conversely, every perfect matching of \(G-v\) is near-perfect in \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A near-perfect matching leaves exactly one vertex exposed, equivalently becoming perfect after that vertex is deleted.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\text{ is near-perfect with exposed vertex }v\iff M\text{ is perfect in }G-v

knowledge_statements.title: Parity-Controlled Coverage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parity restriction on the vertices left uncovered by a matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a matching in a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), and let \(U(M)\) be the set of vertices not covered by \(M\). Since every matching edge covers exactly two vertices, \[|U(M)|=|V|-2|M|\quad\text{and hence}\quad |U(M)|\equiv |V|\pmod 2.\] Therefore a perfect matching can occur only when \(|V|\) is even, while a matching with exactly one exposed vertex can occur only when \(|V|\) is odd.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every matching leaves a number of exposed vertices having the same parity as the graph order.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |U(M)|=|V|-2|M|\equiv |V|\pmod 2

notation.meaning: set of vertices uncovered by the matching

knowledge_statements.title: Factor-Critical Connection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Factor-criticality expressed through near-perfect matchings with prescribed exposed vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) is factor-critical if, for every vertex \(v\in V\), the vertex-deleted graph \(G-v\) has a perfect matching. Equivalently, for every \(v\in V\), the graph \(G\) has a near-perfect matching whose unique exposed vertex is \(v\). In particular, every nonempty factor-critical graph has odd order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph is factor-critical exactly when each vertex can individually be the unique exposed vertex of some near-perfect matching.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite nonempty undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is factor-critical}\iff \forall v\in V,\ G-v\text{ has a perfect matching}

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted General-Graph Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum-weight matching without a prescribed cardinality in a general graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph and let \(w:E\to\mathbb R\). The weight of a matching \(M\) is \(w(M)=\sum_{e\in M}w(e)\). A maximum-weight matching is any matching \(M^*\) satisfying \[w(M^*)=\max\left\{\sum_{e\in M}w(e):M\subseteq E\text{ is a matching}\right\}.\] Under this unconstrained convention, negative-weight edges need not be selected and the empty matching is feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximum-weight matching maximizes the sum of selected edge weights; its cardinality is not fixed.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: w(M^*)=\max\{w(M):M\text{ is a matching in }G\}

notation.meaning: sum of weights of matching edges

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted matching, completion reductions, and bipartite versus general-graph formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines maximum-weight matching under nonnegative edge weights and records objective-preserving completion, fixed-cardinality cost conversion, and the algorithmic distinction between bipartite and nonbipartite instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph \(G=(V,E)\) with weights \(w_e\ge 0\), the weighted matching problem is \(\max\{\sum_{e\in M}w_e:M\subseteq E\text{ is a matching}\}\); maximum-cardinality matching is the special case \(w_e=1\) for every \(e\in E\). Assigning weight zero to missing edges, adding a zero-weight dummy vertex when necessary, and, in the bipartite case, balancing the two parts produce complete even-order or complete balanced-bipartite instances without changing the optimal value. An optimal matching in the completed instance can be chosen perfect. For perfect matchings, replacing \(w_e\) by \(c_e=W-w_e\), where \(W>\max_e w_e\), converts weight maximization into equivalent cost minimization. The bipartite case is the assignment problem and is solvable by the Hungarian method in \(O(n^3)\) arithmetic operations for two parts of size \(n\). In general nonbipartite graphs, the elementary bipartite matching linear formulation is not exact: it has basic feasible solutions that do not represent matchings, so blossom structure must be handled. The described general-graph primal-dual algorithm has complexity \(O(|V|^4)\), while the source notes refinements to \(O(|V|^3)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted matching maximizes the total nonnegative weight of selected, vertex-disjoint edges; unit weights recover maximum-cardinality matching. Zero-weight missing edges and dummy vertices permit reduction to complete perfect-matching instances, after which subtracting weights from a sufficiently large constant converts maximization to minimum cost. The bipartite case is assignment and admits a cubic Hungarian algorithm. For nonbipartite graphs, the elementary bipartite LP is not exact because of blossom structure; the described primal-dual algorithm is quartic, with cubic refinements noted by the source.
assumptions_latex: \text{The cost transformation is applied after reduction to perfect matchings of fixed cardinality.}
\text{For the assignment specialization, the completed bipartite graph has two parts of equal size }n.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max_{M\text{ matching}}\sum_{e\in M}w_e;\qquad w_e\equiv1\Rightarrow\text{maximum-cardinality matching};\qquad \arg\max_{M\text{ perfect}}\sum_{e\in M}w_e=\arg\min_{M\text{ perfect}}\sum_{e\in M}(W-w_e);\qquad T_{\mathrm{Hungarian}}(n)=O(n^3),\quad T_{\mathrm{general}}(|V|)=O(|V|^4).

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Cost General-Graph Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-cost matching over an explicitly specified feasible matching family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph, let \(c:E\to\mathbb R\), and let \(\mathcal F\) be a nonempty family of matchings encoding the required cardinality or coverage. For \(M\in\mathcal F\), set \(c(M)=\sum_{e\in M}c(e)\). A minimum-cost matching is any \(M^*\in\mathcal F\) satisfying \[c(M^*)=\min_{M\in\mathcal F}c(M).\] Specifying \(\mathcal F\) is essential because the unconstrained empty matching may otherwise be optimal.

assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{M\in\mathcal F}\sum_{e\in M}c(e)

knowledge_statements.title: Weight–Cost Transformation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine equivalence of weight maximization and cost minimization at fixed cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be finite, let \(w:E\to\mathbb R\), fix \(k\ge 0\), and define \(c(e)=C-w(e)\) for a constant \(C\in\mathbb R\). For every matching \(M\) with \(|M|=k\), \[c(M)=\sum_{e\in M}(C-w(e))=kC-w(M).\] Hence, over the family \(\mathcal M_k\) of size-\(k\) matchings, maximizing \(w(M)\) and minimizing \(c(M)\) have exactly the same optimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For fixed-size matchings, replacing each weight by a constant minus that weight converts maximum weight into minimum cost without changing optimizers.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmax}_{M\in\mathcal M_k}w(M)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{M\in\mathcal M_k}c(M)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous oracle-polynomial solvability of minimum-weight blocker optimization and maximum fractional edge packing for a nonnegative-rational MFMC hypergraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a hypergraph with \(V=\bigcup H\) and the \(\mathbb{Q}_+\)-MFMC property. Suppose an oracle returns, for every \(c:V\to\mathbb{Q}_+\), a minimum-\(c\)-weight edge of \(H\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph, let \(w:E\to\mathbb R\), and choose an integer \(k\) with \(0\le k\le\nu(G)\). A cardinality-constrained maximum-weight matching is a matching \(M_k^*\) satisfying \[|M_k^*|=k\quad\text{and}\quad w(M_k^*)=\max\{w(M):M\text{ is a matching and }|M|=k\}.\] The constraint prevents changes in cardinality from being traded against edge weight.

assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M_k^*\in\operatorname*{argmax}\{w(M):M\text{ is a matching},\ |M|=k\}

knowledge_statements.title: Matching with Prescribed Vertex Coverage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact characterization of a prescribed set as the covered vertices of a matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph and let \(S\subseteq V\). A matching \(M\) covers exactly \(S\) when the union of the endpoint sets of its edges equals \(S\). Such a matching exists if and only if the induced subgraph \(G[S]\) has a perfect matching. Equivalently, there is a matching \(M\subseteq E(G[S])\) with \[|M|=|S|/2.\] In particular, \(|S|\) must be even.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exactly the vertices in S can be covered by a matching precisely when the induced graph on S has a perfect matching.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists M\text{ with covered vertex set }S\iff G[S]\text{ has a perfect matching}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cliques, stable sets, matchings, and covers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the principal vertex- and edge-selection structures, their cardinality parameters, matching mates, and matchable vertex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G=(V,E). A clique is C\subseteq V whose vertices are pairwise adjacent; a stable set is C\subseteq V whose vertices are pairwise nonadjacent; and a vertex cover is C\subseteq V meeting every edge. A matching is M\subseteq E whose edges are pairwise disjoint; an edge cover is M\subseteq E incident with every vertex; and a perfect matching is both, necessarily with |M|=|V|/2. Define \omega(G)=\max\{|C|:C\text{ is a clique}\},\ \alpha(G)=\max\{|C|:C\text{ is stable}\},\ \tau(G)=\min\{|C|:C\text{ is a vertex cover}\},\ \nu(G)=\max\{|M|:M\text{ is a matching}\},\ \rho(G)=\min\{|M|:M\text{ is an edge cover}\}. Under a matching M, u and v are mates when uv\in M. A set U\subseteq V is matchable iff G[U] has a perfect matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cliques, stable sets, and vertex covers are vertex subsets defined by adjacency or edge interception. Matchings and edge covers are edge subsets defined by disjointness or vertex coverage; a perfect matching has both properties and contains half as many edges as vertices. The symbols ω, α, τ, ν, and ρ denote the corresponding maximum or minimum cardinalities. A vertex set is matchable when its induced subgraph has a perfect matching.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\text{ perfect matching}\Rightarrow |M|=\tfrac12|V|;\quad U\text{ matchable}\Longleftrightarrow G[U]\text{ has a perfect matching}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence under an externally incident even alternating path to the blossom base.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph, \(M\) a matching, and \(C\) a blossom with base \(r\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Alternating and augmenting paths in matching optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions of matching-alternating and augmenting paths, their bipartite flow correspondence, and the general maximum-matching criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a matching in a graph \(G\). A path is \(M\)-alternating if its edges alternate between membership and nonmembership in \(M\), with no prescribed membership status for its first or last edge. It is \(M\)-augmenting if its endpoints are distinct and both are \(M\)-exposed. For the integral-flow formulation of bipartite matching, flow-augmenting paths correspond to \(M\)-augmenting paths. In every graph, \(M\) is maximum if and only if no \(M\)-augmenting path exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An M-alternating path alternates between matched and unmatched edges, without prescribing the status of its first or last edge. It is augmenting when its distinct endpoints are exposed. These paths correspond to flow-augmenting paths in the bipartite flow formulation, and a matching in any graph is maximum exactly when no augmenting path exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\text{ is maximum}\iff\nexists\text{ an }M\text{-augmenting path};\qquad G\text{ bipartite}\Rightarrow\text{flow-augmenting paths correspond to }M\text{-augmenting paths}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Edmonds maximum-cardinality matching algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Grow–augment–shrink procedure and its stopping condition; no complexity claim is included here.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Starting with a matching \(S_k\), seed an alternating forest at all exposed vertices. Repeatedly grow through an edge from an even forest vertex to a vertex outside the forest and then through that vertex's matching edge; augment when an edge joins even vertices in distinct forest components; or switch along a root path and shrink the resulting odd cycle when an edge joins even vertices in the same component. After augmentation, unshrink contracted cycles to obtain a matching \(S_{k+1}\) of \(G\). If no grow, augment, or shrink operation applies, \(S_k\) is maximum-cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The algorithm maintains an alternating forest, grows it through unmatched–matched edge pairs, augments between different components, and contracts an odd cycle when two even vertices in one component are joined. An augmentation increases the matching size by one after contracted cycles are expanded. If no operation applies, the current matching is maximum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{An augmentation yields }S_{k+1}\text{ with }|S_{k+1}|=k+1;\quad\text{if no step applies, }S_k\text{ is maximum-cardinality.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lifting a matching from a shrunk odd circuit
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A matching-level lifting result; it does not assert equality of the graph deficiencies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be an odd circuit of \(G\), let \(G'=G\times C\), and let \(M'\) be a matching of \(G'\). Then there exists a matching \(M\) of \(G\) such that \(M\subseteq M'\cup E(C)\) and the number of \(M\)-exposed nodes of \(G\) equals the number of \(M'\)-exposed nodes of \(G'\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any matching in the graph formed by shrinking an odd circuit can be lifted to the original graph using only its matching edges and circuit edges, with the same number of exposed vertices.
assumptions_latex: C\text{ is an odd circuit of }G
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists M\subseteq M'\cup E(C):\ M\text{ is a matching of }G\ \land\ |\operatorname{Exp}_G(M)|=|\operatorname{Exp}_{G'}(M')|

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Shortest Alternating-Walk Dichotomy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes a shortest alternating walk between vertices missed by a matching as augmenting or as containing an initial flower.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a matching, let \(X\) be the set of vertices missed by \(M\), and let \(P=(v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_t)\) be a shortest \(M\)-alternating \(X\)-\(X\) walk. knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A shortest M-alternating walk between vertices missed by M is either an augmenting path or has an initial segment that is an M-flower.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ is an }M\text{-augmenting path}\ \lor\ \exists j\le t:\ (v_0,\ldots,v_j)\text{ is an }M\text{-flower}

knowledge_statements.title: Berge Augmenting-Path Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Berge’s optimality criterion for matchings in finite general graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph and let \(M\subseteq E\) be a matching. An \(M\)-augmenting path is a simple path whose endpoints are uncovered by \(M\) and whose edges alternate between \(E\setminus M\) and \(M\), beginning and ending outside \(M\). Then \(M\) is a maximum-cardinality matching if and only if no \(M\)-augmenting path exists in \(G\). If such a path \(P\) exists, \(M\triangle E(P)\) is a matching of cardinality \(|M|+1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matching is maximum exactly when it admits no alternating path joining two exposed vertices; flipping such a path increases cardinality by one.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\text{ is maximum-cardinality}\iff G\text{ has no }M\text{-augmenting path}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Auxiliary-digraph representation of alternating walks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of matching-alternating walks and a directed-path encoding for positive-length walks between a vertex set and itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $G=(V,E)$, let $M$ be a matching, and let $X\subseteq V$. A walk $P=(v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_t)$ is $M$-alternating if, for every $i=1,\ldots,t-1$, exactly one of $v_{i-1}v_i$ and $v_iv_{i+1}$ belongs to $M$. Define the auxiliary digraph $D=(V,A)$ by
\[
A:=\{(u,v)\in V\times V:\exists x\in V,\ ux\in E\text{ and }xv\in M\}.
\]
Then positive-length $M$-alternating $X$-$X$ walks correspond to directed $X$-$N(X)$ paths in $D$. Consequently, a shortest such alternating walk can be found by a directed-path search in $D$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An M-alternating walk has successive edges alternating between membership and nonmembership in M. In the auxiliary digraph containing an arc from u to v whenever u can traverse a graph edge to some x and then the matching edge xv, positive-length alternating walks from X back to X correspond to directed paths from X to the neighbor set of X. Thus a shortest such walk can be found by directed-path search.
assumptions_latex: N(X):=\{v\in V:\exists x\in X,\ xv\in E\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{\text{positive-length }M\text{-alternating }X\text{-}X\text{ walks}\}\longleftrightarrow\{\text{directed }X\text{-}N(X)\text{ paths in }D\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Alternating Paths and Alternating Cycles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parity and cycle terminology for paths alternating relative to a matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a matching \(M\), a path \(P=i_1-i_2-\cdots-i_k\) is alternating with respect to \(M\) if every consecutive pair of edges on \(P\) contains one edge in \(M\) and one edge outside \(M\). It is even or odd according as it contains an even or odd number of edges. An alternating cycle is a closed alternating path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative to a matching, a path is alternating when matched and unmatched edges alternate. Its parity is the parity of its number of edges, and a closed alternating path is an alternating cycle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ is alternating iff consecutive edges alternate between }M\text{ and }A\setminus M;\quad P\text{ is even or odd according to }|E(P)|,\text{ and a closed alternating }P\text{ is an alternating cycle}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Alternating, Exposed, Covered, and Augmenting Structures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions relative to a fixed matching in a graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $S$ be a matching of a graph $G$. A path or cycle $P$ is $S$-alternating if its edges alternate between $S$ and $E(G)\setminus S$. A vertex $v\in V(G)$ is $S$-exposed if $\delta_G(v)\cap S=\varnothing$, and it is covered otherwise. An $S$-alternating path is augmenting if both endpoints are exposed with respect to $S$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative to a matching S, an alternating path or cycle alternates between matching and nonmatching edges. A vertex is exposed if no matching edge is incident to it and covered otherwise. An alternating path is augmenting when both endpoints are exposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ is }S\text{-alternating}\iff E(P)\text{ alternates between }S\text{ and }E(G)\setminus S;\quad v\text{ is }S\text{-exposed}\iff\delta_G(v)\cap S=\varnothing;\quad P\text{ is }S\text{-augmenting}\iff P\text{ is }S\text{-alternating and both endpoints are }S\text{-exposed}.

knowledge_statements.title: Alternating Paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Alternation is defined relative to a fixed matching in a finite undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph and \(M\subseteq E\) a matching. A simple path \(P=(v_0,e_1,v_1,\ldots,e_k,v_k)\) with \(k\ge 1\) is \(M\)-alternating if consecutive edges alternate between \(M\) and \(E\setminus M\); equivalently, for every \(1\le i<k\), exactly one of \(e_i,e_{i+1}\) belongs to \(M\). It is \(M\)-augmenting if both endpoints are unmatched by \(M\) and \(e_1,e_k\notin M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-length alternating path switches between matching and nonmatching edges. It is augmenting when both endpoints are unmatched and its first and last edges are outside the matching.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a simple path of length \(k\ge 1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\text{ is }M\text{-alternating}\iff |\{e_i,e_{i+1}\}\cap M|=1\text{ for every }1\le i<k.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Alternating and Augmenting Paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions relative to a matching in an arbitrary graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph and let \(M\) be a matching in \(G\). A path \(P\) is \(M\)-alternating if \(E(P)\setminus M\) is a matching. An \(M\)-alternating path is \(M\)-augmenting if it has positive length and its endpoints are exposed by \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative to a matching M in any graph, a path is M-alternating when its non-M edges form a matching. It is M-augmenting when it has positive length and both endpoints are exposed by M.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ is }M\text{-alternating}\iff E(P)\setminus M\text{ is a matching};\quad P\text{ is }M\text{-augmenting}\iff P\text{ is }M\text{-alternating, }|E(P)|>0,\text{ and both endpoints are exposed by }M

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Alternating, Exposed, and Augmenting Paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions and the elementary augmentation consequence for matchings in arbitrary graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph and \(M\) a matching in \(G\). A path \(P=v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_m\) is \(M\)-alternating if every two consecutive edges of \(P\) have opposite membership in \(M\). A vertex is \(M\)-exposed if no edge of \(M\) is incident with it. An \(M\)-alternating path joining two exposed vertices is an \(M\)-augmenting path. If \(P\) is augmenting, then \(M'=(M\setminus E(P))\cup(E(P)\setminus M)\) is a matching with \(|M'|=|M|+1\), so \(M\) is not maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An alternating path relative to a matching has consecutive edges alternately in and outside the matching. A vertex is exposed when it is incident with no matching edge. An alternating path joining two exposed vertices is augmenting, and exchanging matching and nonmatching edges along it increases the matching size by one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ is }M\text{-augmenting}\implies M'=(M\setminus E(P))\cup(E(P)\setminus M)\text{ is a matching with }|M'|=|M|+1.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Alternating and augmenting paths relative to a matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Alternating-search terminology relative to a fixed matching; broad matching variants and the illustrated examples are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $M$ be a matching in a graph $G$. Edges in $M$ are matched, edges outside $M$ are free, and a vertex incident to no edge of $M$ is exposed. A path $p=[u_1,\ldots,u_k]$ is alternating with respect to $M$ if its successive edges alternate between free and matched, beginning with a free edge. On such a path beginning at an exposed vertex, vertices in odd positions are outer and vertices in even positions are inner. An alternating path is augmenting if both endpoints are exposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative to a fixed matching, an alternating path begins with a free edge and alternates between free and matched edges. On one starting at an exposed vertex, odd-position vertices are outer and even-position vertices are inner. It is augmenting when both endpoints are exposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p\text{ is augmenting with respect to }M\iff p\text{ is alternating with respect to }M\text{ and both endpoints of }p\text{ are exposed}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: BLOSSOMPATH alternating-path reconstruction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Assumes a valid weighted-blossom search state with matching map \(\mu\), blossom family \(\mathcal B\), and maps \(b^j,\rho^k,\varphi^i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_0\), initialize \(h:=0\) and \(B:=\{b^j(x_0):1\le j\le k_{x_0}\}\). While \(x_{2h}\ne\rho^{k_{x_0}}(x_0)\), set \(x_{2h+1}:=\mu(x_{2h})\), choose \(i:=\min\{j\in\{1,\ldots,k_{x_{2h+1}}\}:b^j(x_{2h+1})\in B\}\), and set \(x_{2h+2}:=\varphi^i(x_{2h+1})\). Add to \(B\) every blossom containing \(x_{2h+2}\) but not \(x_{2h+1}\), delete every blossom in \(B\) whose base is \(x_{2h+2}\), and increment \(h\). Return the path \(Q(x_0)=(x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_{2h})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting at x0, follow matched edges and the appropriate nested-blossom links, updating the active blossom set after every step. Stop at the highest recorded blossom representative and return the resulting vertex sequence.
assumptions_latex: (M,\mathcal B,\mu,b^j,\rho^k,\varphi^i)\text{ form a valid blossom-search state}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q(x_0)\text{ is an }M\text{-alternating path from }x_0\text{ to }\rho^{k_{x_0}}(x_0).

knowledge_statements.title: Alternating Cycles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The cycle is simple and alternates relative to a fixed matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph and \(M\subseteq E\) a matching. A simple cycle \(C=(v_0,e_1,v_1,\ldots,e_k,v_0)\) is \(M\)-alternating if, cyclically, exactly one edge of every consecutive pair belongs to \(M\). Consequently \(k\) is even and \(|E(C)\cap M|=|E(C)\setminus M|=k/2\). Replacing \(M\cap E(C)\) by \(E(C)\setminus M\) yields another matching of the same cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An alternating cycle has matching and nonmatching edges in cyclic alternation. It is even, and flipping all its edges preserves matching feasibility and cardinality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M' = M\mathbin{\triangle}E(C)\text{ is a matching and }|M'|=|M|.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric-Difference Decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Component decomposition for two matchings in a finite graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M,N\) be matchings in a finite undirected graph \(G\). Every nontrivial connected component of the spanning subgraph \((V,M\mathbin{\triangle}N)\) is either a path or an even cycle, and its edges alternate between \(M\setminus N\) and \(N\setminus M\). Cycle components contain equally many edges of both matchings. A path component has equal counts or has one more edge from exactly one of \(M\) and \(N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The symmetric difference of two matchings decomposes into edge-alternating paths and even cycles, with each path having matching-edge counts differing by at most one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\mathbin{\triangle}N\text{ is a vertex-disjoint union of alternating paths and even alternating cycles.}\)

notation.meaning: edges belonging to exactly one of the two matchings
