knowledge_statements.title: Matching-Exchange Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible exchanges are obtained by flipping alternating components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M,N\) be matchings of a finite graph \(G\), and let \(K\) be a connected component of \(M\mathbin{\triangle}N\). Then \(M_K=M\mathbin{\triangle}E(K)\) is a matching. Moreover, \(|M_K|-|M|=|E(K)\cap N|-|E(K)\cap M|\), which belongs to \(\{-1,0,1\}\). In particular, a component beginning and ending with edges of \(N\setminus M\) is an \(M\)-augmenting path and its flip increases cardinality by one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Flipping any component of the symmetric difference of two matchings remains feasible; its cardinality change is minus one, zero, or one according to the component endpoints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\mathbin{\triangle}E(K)\text{ is a matching and }|M\mathbin{\triangle}E(K)|-|M|\in\{-1,0,1\}.\)

notation.meaning: matching obtained by flipping the edges of the component

knowledge_statements.title: Odd-Cycle Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Odd alternating cycles are expressed as blossoms with a distinguished base.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a matching in a finite graph \(G\). An \(M\)-blossom cycle is a simple odd cycle \(C\) with a distinguished vertex \(b\), called its base, such that \(M\cap E(C)\) matches every vertex of \(V(C)\setminus\{b\}\) within \(C\). Thus the two cycle edges incident with \(b\) lie outside \(M\), while all remaining cycle edges alternate between outside and inside \(M\). The cycle minus \(b\) has a perfect matching supplied by \(M\cap E(C)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A blossom cycle is odd and has one base vertex; all other cycle vertices are paired by alternating matching edges within the cycle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\cap E(C)\text{ is a perfect matching of }C-b.\)

notation.meaning: base vertex of the blossom cycle

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Graph obtained by shrinking an odd circuit
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of odd-circuit contraction in a general graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be an odd circuit of \(G=(V,E)\). The graph \(G\times C\) obtained by shrinking \(C\) has node set \((V\setminus V(C))\cup\{C\}\) and edge set \(E\setminus\gamma(V(C))\). For every remaining edge, each endpoint outside \(V(C)\) is unchanged, while each endpoint in \(V(C)\) is replaced by the new node \(C\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: V(G\times C)=(V\setminus V(C))\cup\{C\},\qquad E(G\times C)=E\setminus\gamma(V(C))

knowledge_statements.title: Blossom Obstructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The obstruction concerns uncontracted alternating-tree search in nonbipartite graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be an \(M\)-alternating search forest rooted at vertices exposed by \(M\). If an edge joins two even-level vertices in the same tree, their tree paths to the least common ancestor together with that edge form an odd \(M\)-blossom cycle. Unlike the bipartite case, this edge need not yield an augmenting path: the two paths can meet at the blossom base. Treating the cycle as an ordinary alternating path therefore makes the uncontracted search criterion invalid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An edge between even-level vertices of one alternating tree can close an odd blossom rather than produce an augmenting path, invalidating the bipartite search rule.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is an alternating forest rooted at exposed vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{An even--even search edge within one tree may certify an odd blossom, not an }M\text{-augmenting path.}\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Flower, Stem, Blossom, and Base
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The composite flower structure relative to a matching and designated root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With respect to a matching \(M\) and root vertex \(p\), a flower consists of a stem and a blossom. The stem is an even-length \(M\)-alternating path from \(p\) to a vertex \(w\), possibly empty when \(p=w\). The blossom is an odd-length \(M\)-alternating cycle based at \(w\) and has no other vertex in common with the stem. The vertex \(w\) is the blossom base.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A flower consists of an even-length alternating stem from root p to w and an odd-length alternating cycle based at w that is otherwise disjoint from the stem. The stem may be empty when p equals w, and w is the blossom base.
assumptions_latex: p\text{ is a designated root vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F=S\cup B,\quad S:p\leadsto w\text{ is an even-length }M\text{-alternating path},\quad B\text{ is an odd-length }M\text{-alternating cycle based at }w,\quad V(S)\cap V(B)=\{w\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matching Flowers and Associated Blossoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines an odd alternating flower and its associated terminal blossom circuit relative to a matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a matching, let \(X\) be the set of vertices missed by \(M\), and let \(P=(v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_t)\) be an \(M\)-alternating walk. The walk \(P\) is an \(M\)-flower if and only if \(t\) is odd, \(v_0,\ldots,v_{t-1}\) are distinct, \(v_0\in X\), and \(v_t=v_i\) for some even \(i<t\). For such an index \(i\), the circuit \((v_i,v_{i+1},\ldots,v_t)\) is the associated \(M\)-blossom.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An M-alternating walk is an M-flower exactly when it starts at a vertex missed by M, has odd length, has distinct vertices before its endpoint, and ends by repeating a vertex in an even position. The resulting terminal circuit is its associated M-blossom.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ is an }M\text{-flower}\iff\bigl[t\text{ is odd},\ v_0,\ldots,v_{t-1}\text{ are distinct},\ v_0\in X,\ \exists\text{ even }i<t:\ v_t=v_i\bigr],\quad (v_i,\ldots,v_t)\text{ is the associated }M\text{-blossom}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Blossom with Base and Stem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of a blossom relative to a matching, including its base, stem, and internal alternating paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a matching in \(G=(N,A)\). For \(N_B\subseteq N\) with \(|N_B|=2r+1\), \(r\geq 1\), let \(B\) be the set of edges whose endpoints both lie in \(N_B\). Then \(B\) is a blossom with respect to \(X\) if: (i) \(|X\cap B|=r\), leaving a unique vertex \(b\in N_B\) exposed by \(X\cap B\), called the base; (ii) there is an even-length \(X\)-alternating path \(S\), with \(S\cap B=\varnothing\), from \(b\) to a vertex exposed by \(X\), called the root of the stem; and (iii) for every \(i\in N_B\), there is an even-length \(X\)-alternating path \(S_{b,i}\subseteq B\) between \(b\) and \(i\). Consequently, concatenating \(S\) and \(S_{b,i}\) gives an alternating path from the root to \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative to a matching X, a blossom consists of an odd vertex set with exactly r internal matching edges and hence one internally exposed base. An even alternating stem, edge-disjoint from the blossom, connects the base to an X-exposed root, and every blossom vertex has an even alternating path to the base using blossom edges.
assumptions_latex: B=\{e\in A:\text{both endpoints of }e\text{ lie in }N_B\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B\text{ is a blossom with respect to }X\iff \text{conditions (i)--(iii) hold}.

knowledge_statements.title: Nested Blossom Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Laminarity applies to blossoms maintained by recursive contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a recursive blossom-contraction regime, regard each contracted blossom as the union of its represented original vertices. If a new blossom is formed in the current contracted graph, then every previously contracted blossom is either wholly contained in the new blossom or disjoint from it. Hence the represented blossom sets form a laminar family \(\mathcal B\): for all \(B_1,B_2\in\mathcal B\), either \(B_1\cap B_2=\varnothing\), \(B_1\subseteq B_2\), or \(B_2\subseteq B_1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recursive contraction maintains blossoms as a laminar family: any two represented blossom sets are disjoint or one contains the other.
assumptions_latex: Blossoms are created after contracting all currently active blossoms.
Each contracted vertex represents its full set of original vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal B\text{ is laminar.}\)

notation.meaning: family of represented blossom vertex sets

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matching, coverage, maximum cardinality, and deficiency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational terminology for finite general graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph \(G=(V,E)\), a matching is a set \(M\subseteq E\) such that each vertex is incident with at most one edge of \(M\). A vertex is \(M\)-covered if it is incident with an edge of \(M\), and otherwise is \(M\)-exposed. Thus \(M\) covers \(2|M|\) vertices and exposes \(|V|-2|M|\) vertices. A maximum matching maximizes \(|M|\), equivalently minimizes the number of exposed vertices. Writing \(\nu(G)\) for its cardinality and \(\operatorname{def}(G)\) for the minimum number of exposed vertices, \(\operatorname{def}(G)=|V|-2\nu(G)\). A matching is perfect if it covers every vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matching consists of pairwise vertex-disjoint edges. It covers exactly twice as many vertices as it has edges; all other vertices are exposed. Maximum matchings maximize cardinality, equivalently minimize exposed vertices. The deficiency equals the number of vertices minus twice the maximum matching size. A perfect matching covers every vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |V_{\mathrm{covered}}(M)|=2|M|,\quad |V_{\mathrm{exposed}}(M)|=|V|-2|M|,\quad \operatorname{def}(G)=|V|-2\nu(G).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matching Defect and Graph Deficiency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for a general graph, not assumed bipartite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph \(G\) and a matching \(M\) in \(G\), the defect of \(M\) is the number of vertices not covered by \(M\), namely \(|V(G)|-2|M|\). The deficiency of \(G\) is \[\operatorname{def}(G)=|V(G)|-2\nu(G),\] equivalently the number of vertices left uncovered by a maximum matching and the minimum defect over all matchings of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The defect of a matching is the number of vertices it leaves unmatched. The deficiency of a graph is the minimum matching defect, equal to the number of vertices minus twice the maximum-matching size.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{def}(G)=|V(G)|-2\nu(G)=\min_{M'\text{ matching in }G}\bigl(|V(G)|-2|M'|\bigr)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gallai–Edmonds Realization Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes exactly the graphs having prescribed Gallai–Edmonds parts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_0=(U,W)\) be bipartite with positive surplus from \(U\). For every \(w\in W\), let \(G_w\) be factor-critical, and let \(H\) be factorizable. Form \(G\) on \(U\cup V(H)\cup\bigcup_{w\in W}V(G_w)\) by retaining all edges of \(H\) and the \(G_w\), replacing each edge \(uw\in E(G_0)\) by an edge from \(u\) to an arbitrary vertex of \(G_w\), and adding arbitrary edges inside \(U\) and between \(U\) and \(V(H)\). Then \(A(G)=U\), \(C(G)=V(H)\), and \(D(G)=\bigcup_{w\in W}V(G_w)\). Conversely, every graph has a unique representation of this form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-surplus bipartite skeleton whose W-vertices are expanded into factor-critical graphs, together with a factorizable graph and arbitrary permitted edges incident with U, realizes exactly the Gallai–Edmonds classes U, V(H), and the expanded components. Every graph has a unique such representation.
assumptions_latex: G_0=(U,W)\text{ is bipartite and has positive surplus from }U
G\text{ is constructed with the specified retained and added edges}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A(G)=U,\quad C(G)=V(H),\quad D(G)=\bigcup_{w\in W}V(G_w),\quad\text{and every graph admits this representation uniquely}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gallai–Edmonds Structure Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes the factor-critical, factorizable, surplus, and maximum-matching properties of the Gallai–Edmonds decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph and let \(D=D(G)\), \(A=A(G)\), and \(C=C(G)\). Then: (i) every component of \(G[D]\) is factor-critical; (ii) \(G[C]\) has a perfect matching; (iii) the bipartite graph obtained by deleting \(C\), deleting the edges with both ends in \(A\), and contracting each component of \(G[D]\) has positive surplus from \(A\); (iv) every maximum matching contains a near-perfect matching in every component of \(G[D]\), a perfect matching in every component of \(G[C]\), and matches every vertex of \(A\) to a vertex in a distinct component of \(G[D]\); and (v) \(\nu(G)=\tfrac12\bigl(|V(G)|-c(G[D])+|A|\bigr)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The D-components are factor-critical, the C-subgraph has a perfect matching, the contracted graph from A to the D-components has positive surplus, and every maximum matching has the prescribed componentwise structure. Its size is half the number of vertices minus the number of D-components plus the size of A.
assumptions_latex: D=D(G),\ A=A(G),\ C=C(G)\text{ are the Gallai\text{–}Edmonds sets}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{comp}(G[D])\text{ are factor-critical},\quad G[C]\text{ has a perfect matching},\quad \nu(G)=\frac{|V(G)|-c(G[D])+|A|}{2},\text{ with every maximum matching having the stated decomposition.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gallai–Edmonds Structure in Bipartite Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specializes the decomposition to a bipartite graph and characterizes its maximum matchings and minimum vertex covers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(U_1,U_2)\) be bipartite, and for \(i=1,2\) put \(A_i=A\cap U_i\), \(C_i=C\cap U_i\), and \(D_i=D\cap U_i\), where \(A,C,D\) are the Gallai\text{–}Edmonds sets of \(G\). Then \(D=D_1\cup D_2\) is independent; \(G[C_1\cup C_2]\) has a perfect matching and \(|C_1|=|C_2|\); \(\Gamma(D_1)=A_2\) and \(\Gamma(D_2)=A_1\); every maximum matching consists of a perfect matching on \(C_1\cup C_2\), a matching of \(A_1\) into \(D_2\), and a matching of \(A_2\) into \(D_1\). Every minimum vertex cover \(T\) satisfies \(A_1\cup A_2\subseteq T\subseteq A_1\cup A_2\cup C_1\cup C_2\); both \(C_1\cup A_1\cup A_2\) and \(C_2\cup A_1\cup A_2\) are minimum vertex covers, so \(A_1\cup A_2\) is the intersection of all minimum vertex covers. Finally, \(G[A_1\cup D_2]\) and \(G[A_2\cup D_1]\) have positive surplus from \(A_1\) and \(A_2\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a bipartite graph, D is independent, C has a balanced perfect matching, the two sides of A are the neighborhoods of the opposite D-parts, and every maximum matching decomposes into the stated C and A-to-D matchings. All minimum vertex covers contain A and avoid D, two canonical minimum covers exist, their intersection is A, and the two A-to-D subgraphs have positive surplus.
assumptions_latex: A,C,D\text{ are the Gallai\text{–}Edmonds sets of }G
A_i=A\cap U_i,\ C_i=C\cap U_i,\ D_i=D\cap U_i\quad(i=1,2)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D\text{ is independent},\quad G[C_1\cup C_2]\text{ has a perfect matching},\quad \Gamma(D_1)=A_2,\ \Gamma(D_2)=A_1,\quad \bigcap_{T\in\mathcal C_{\min}(G)}T=A_1\cup A_2,\text{ together with the stated matching and surplus properties.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Deficiency of a Set and of a Bipartite Graph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines neighborhood deficiency relative to one side of a bipartition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(A,B;E)\) be a bipartite graph. For \(X\subseteq A\), define \(\operatorname{def}_G(X)=|X|-|\Gamma_G(X)|\). The \(A\)-deficiency of \(G\) is \(\operatorname{def}_A(G)=\max_{X\subseteq A}\operatorname{def}_G(X)\); when \(A\) is understood, write \(\operatorname{def}(G)\). Since \(\operatorname{def}_G(\varnothing)=0\), one has \(\operatorname{def}(G)\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a bipartite graph with sides A and B, the deficiency of a subset X of A is the number of vertices in X minus the number of its neighbors. The graph deficiency is the maximum of this quantity over all subsets of A and is nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{def}_G(X)=|X|-|\Gamma_G(X)|,\qquad \operatorname{def}(G)=\max_{X\subseteq A}\operatorname{def}_G(X)\ge 0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gallai–Edmonds Sets and Near-Perfect Matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the canonical vertex decomposition used in maximum-matching structure theory and the accompanying near-perfect matching notion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph \(G\), let \(D(G)=\{v\in V(G):v\text{ is uncovered by at least one maximum matching of }G\}\), let \(A(G)=\{v\in V(G)\setminus D(G):v\text{ has a neighbor in }D(G)\}\), and let \(C(G)=V(G)\setminus(A(G)\cup D(G))\). A near-perfect matching of \(G\) covers all but exactly one vertex of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any graph, D consists of vertices missed by some maximum matching; A consists of vertices outside D adjacent to D; and C is the set of all remaining vertices. A near-perfect matching leaves exactly one vertex uncovered.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gallai–Edmonds Stability Lemma
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes how the three decomposition sets change when a vertex from each class is deleted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph with Gallai\text{–}Edmonds sets \(A(G),C(G),D(G)\). If \(u\in A(G)\), then \(A(G-u)=A(G)\setminus\{u\}\), \(C(G-u)=C(G)\), and \(D(G-u)=D(G)\). If \(u\in C(G)\), then \(A(G-u)\supseteq A(G)\), \(C(G-u)\subseteq C(G)\setminus\{u\}\), and \(D(G-u)\supseteq D(G)\). If \(u\in D(G)\), then \(A(G-u)\subseteq A(G)\), \(C(G-u)\supseteq C(G)\), and \(D(G-u)\subseteq D(G)\setminus\{u\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deleting an A-vertex leaves D and C unchanged and removes only that vertex from A. Deleting a C-vertex can enlarge A and D and shrink C. Deleting a D-vertex can shrink A and D and enlarge C.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: u\in A(G)\Rightarrow(A(G-u),C(G-u),D(G-u))=(A(G)\setminus\{u\},C(G),D(G));\quad u\in C(G)\Rightarrow A(G-u)\supseteq A(G),\ C(G-u)\subseteq C(G)\setminus\{u\},\ D(G-u)\supseteq D(G);\quad u\in D(G)\Rightarrow A(G-u)\subseteq A(G),\ C(G-u)\supseteq C(G),\ D(G-u)\subseteq D(G)\setminus\{u\}.

knowledge_statements.title: Tutte One-Factor Theory
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tutte's criterion for perfect matchings in finite undirected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph, and for \(S\subseteq V\) let \(q(G-S)\) denote the number of connected components of \(G-S\) having odd order. Then \(G\) has a one-factor, equivalently a perfect matching, if and only if \(q(G-S)\le |S|\) for every \(S\subseteq V\). In particular, taking \(S=\varnothing\) shows that every connected component of a graph having a perfect matching has even order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite graph has a perfect matching exactly when deleting any vertex set leaves no more odd components than the number of deleted vertices. In particular, each connected component of such a graph has even order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\text{ has a perfect matching}\iff q(G-S)\le |S|\text{ for every }S\subseteq V.\)

notation.meaning: number of odd-order components of the vertex-deleted graph

knowledge_statements.title: Tutte–Berge Maximum-Matching Min–Max Theory
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cardinality and deficiency forms of the finite-graph Tutte–Berge formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph, let \(\nu(G)\) be its maximum matching cardinality, and let \(q(G-S)\) count the odd-order components of \(G-S\). Then
\[|V|-2\nu(G)=\max_{S\subseteq V}\bigl(q(G-S)-|S|\bigr).\]
Equivalently,
\[\nu(G)=\frac12\min_{S\subseteq V}\bigl(|V|+|S|-q(G-S)\bigr).\]
Thus a maximizing set \(S\) certifies the number of vertices necessarily exposed by every matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum matching size equals half the minimum of vertex count plus deleted-set size minus the number of resulting odd components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|V|-2\nu(G)=\max_{S\subseteq V}\{q(G-S)-|S|\}.\)

notation.meaning: maximum cardinality of a matching in the graph
number of odd-order components after deleting the vertex set

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Odd Set Cover and Its Weight
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A matching-theoretic edge-cover certificate formed from odd vertex subsets and individual vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An odd set cover of a graph \(G\) is a collection \(\mathcal H=\{S_1,\ldots,S_k,v_1,\ldots,v_r\}\), where each \(S_i\subseteq V(G)\) has odd cardinality and each \(v_j\in V(G)\), such that every edge of \(G\) is incident with at least one \(v_j\) or has both endpoints in at least one \(S_i\). Its weight is the number of selected vertices plus one half of each odd subset's size minus one.
assumptions_latex: S_i\subseteq V(G)\text{ and }|S_i|\text{ is odd for }i=1,\ldots,k
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: w(\mathcal H)=r+\sum_{i=1}^k\frac{|S_i|-1}{2}

knowledge_statements.title: Matching Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Barriers are maximizers in the Tutte–Berge deficiency formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite graph \(G=(V,E)\), define \(\operatorname{def}(G)=|V|-2\nu(G)\). A set \(S\subseteq V\) is a matching barrier if
\[q(G-S)-|S|=\operatorname{def}(G),\]
where \(q(G-S)\) is the number of odd-order components of \(G-S\). Thus a barrier attains the Tutte–Berge maximum. When \(G\) has a perfect matching, this reduces to \(q(G-S)=|S|\); conventions that require nonempty \(S\) should be stated separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matching barrier is a vertex set attaining the maximum odd-component excess in the Tutte–Berge formula, and therefore witnessing the graph's matching deficiency.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\text{ is a barrier}\iff q(G-S)-|S|=|V|-2\nu(G).\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes disjointness, stability, cardinality balance, and closure for simple barriers associated with opposite endpoints of the deleted edge.

knowledge_statements.title: Odd-Component Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Odd components after vertex deletion provide a verifiable deficiency lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be finite, let \(S\subseteq V\), and let \(Q_1,\ldots,Q_q\) be the odd-order components of \(G-S\). For every matching \(M\), at most \(|S|\) of these components can send an \(M\)-edge to \(S\). Each remaining odd component has at least one vertex unmatched by \(M\). Consequently every matching exposes at least \(q-|S|\) vertices, and
\[|M|\le \frac{|V|-q+|S|}{2}.\]
The listed components and set \(S\) therefore form a directly checkable deficiency certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deleting a set that creates many odd components certifies unmatched vertices: every matching exposes at least the number of odd components minus the deleted-set size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|V|-2|M|\ge q(G-S)-|S|\text{ for every matching }M.\)

notation.meaning: odd-order components of the vertex-deleted graph

\nu(G)=\min_{S\subseteq V}\frac{|V|+|S|-\operatorname{odd}(G-S)}{2},
\]
where \(\nu(G)\) is the maximum cardinality of a matching in \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any undirected graph, the maximum matching size equals the minimum, over all vertex sets S, of one half of the number of vertices plus the size of S minus the number of odd components left after deleting S.
assumptions_latex: \operatorname{odd}(G-S)=\#\{C:C\text{ is a component of }G-S,\ |V(C)|\text{ is odd}\}

knowledge_statements.title: General-Graph Deficiency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tutte–Berge representation of cardinality-matching deficiency in a finite undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), let \(\nu(G)\) be the maximum cardinality of a matching and let \(o(G-U)\) count the odd-order connected components of the vertex-deleted graph \(G-U\). The matching deficiency, equal to the minimum number of vertices left uncovered by a matching, satisfies
\[
\operatorname{def}(G):=|V|-2\nu(G)=\max_{U\subseteq V}\bigl(o(G-U)-|U|\bigr).
\]
Thus every set \(U\subseteq V\) gives the lower bound \(\operatorname{def}(G)\ge o(G-U)-|U|\), and at least one set attains equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimum number of unmatched vertices equals the maximum, over deleted vertex sets, of the number of resulting odd components minus the number deleted.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph; parallel edges are allowed and loops are irrelevant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{def}(G)=|V|-2\nu(G)=\max_{U\subseteq V}(o(G-U)-|U|)\).

notation.meaning: number of odd-order components of the vertex-deleted graph
minimum number of vertices uncovered by a matching

knowledge_statements.title: Maximum-Deficiency Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal–dual certificate for the Tutte–Berge deficiency value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A certificate that a matching \(M\) of a finite graph \(G=(V,E)\) is maximum consists of a set \(U\subseteq V\) such that
\[
|V|-2|M|=o(G-U)-|U|.
\]
The matching verifies \(\operatorname{def}(G)\le |V|-2|M|\), while the odd components verify \(\operatorname{def}(G)\ge o(G-U)-|U|\): after matching vertices of \(U\), at least \(o(G-U)-|U|\) odd components must retain an uncovered vertex. Equality certifies both that \(M\) is maximum and that \(U\) maximizes the deficiency expression.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matching and a deleted vertex set certify optimality when their numbers of uncovered vertices and excess odd components are equal.
assumptions_latex: \(M\subseteq E\) is a matching and \(U\subseteq V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(|V|-2|M|=o(G-U)-|U|\), then \(M\) is maximum and \(U\) is a maximum-deficiency set.

notation.meaning: vertex set furnishing the odd-component bound
number of odd-order components after deleting U

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gallai–Edmonds decomposition theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical vertex decomposition and the resulting structure and cardinality of maximum matchings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph. Let \(Y\) be the set of vertices exposed by at least one maximum matching, let \(X\) be the set of neighbors of \(Y\) in \(V(G)\setminus Y\), and let \(W=V(G)\setminus(X\cup Y)\). Every maximum matching in \(G\) contains a perfect matching of \(G[W]\), near-perfect matchings of the connected components of \(G[Y]\), and edges matching all vertices of \(X\) to distinct connected components of \(G[Y]\). Every connected component of \(G[Y]\) is factor-critical, and \(2\nu(G)=|V(G)|-q_G(X)+|X|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Gallai–Edmonds partition consists of vertices exposed by some maximum matching, their outside neighbors, and the remaining vertices. Every maximum matching is perfect on the remaining part, near-perfect on each exposed-part component, and matches each neighboring vertex into a distinct such component. Those components are factor-critical, and the stated formula gives twice the maximum-matching cardinality.
assumptions_latex: Y=\{v\in V(G):v\text{ is exposed by at least one maximum matching}\}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}&\text{Every maximum matching contains a perfect matching of }G[W]\text{ and near-perfect matchings of every component of }G[Y],\\&\text{and matches all vertices of }X\text{ to distinct components of }G[Y];\\&\text{every component of }G[Y]\text{ is factor-critical};\\&2\nu(G)=|V(G)|-q_G(X)+|X|.\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalence Relation on Vertices Exposable by Maximum Matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A structural relation on the set of vertices missed by at least one maximum matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph and let \(D=\{u\in V(G):u\text{ is missed by some maximum matching of }G\}\). For \(u,v\in D\), define \(u\sim v\) if and only if \(u=v\) or no maximum matching of \(G\) misses both \(u\) and \(v\). Then \(\sim\) is an equivalence relation on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Among vertices that can be missed by a maximum matching, two vertices are related when they are equal or no maximum matching misses them both. This is an equivalence relation.
assumptions_latex: D=\{u\in V(G):u\text{ is missed by some maximum matching of }G\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sim\text{ is an equivalence relation on }D

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matching Coverage and Avoidance Exchange Lemma
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives parallel exchange assertions for covered sets and sets avoided by maximum matchings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph and let \(A,B\subseteq V(G)\) satisfy \(|A|<|B|\). (a) If a matching covering \(A\) exists and a matching covering \(B\) exists, then some matching covers all of \(A\) and at least one vertex of \(B\setminus A\). (b) If a maximum matching avoiding \(A\) exists and a maximum matching avoiding \(B\) exists, then some maximum matching avoids all of \(A\) and at least one vertex of \(B\setminus A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If |A|<|B| and A and B can each be covered by matchings, one matching covers A and some vertex of B outside A. Likewise, if maximum matchings can separately avoid A and B, one maximum matching avoids A and some vertex of B outside A.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}&[(\exists M_A\text{ covering }A)\land(\exists M_B\text{ covering }B)]\Rightarrow \exists M\text{ covering }A\text{ and some }v\in B\setminus A,\\&[(\exists M_A^*\text{ maximum and avoiding }A)\land(\exists M_B^*\text{ maximum and avoiding }B)]\Rightarrow \exists M^*\text{ maximum, avoiding }A\text{ and some }v\in B\setminus A.\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.title: Canonical Vertex Partition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical Gallai–Edmonds partition determined by all maximum matchings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph. Define \(D\) to be the set of vertices that are uncovered by at least one maximum matching of \(G\). Define
\[
A:=N_G(D)\setminus D,
\qquad
C:=V\setminus(A\cup D).
\]
The ordered triple \((D,A,C)\) is the Gallai–Edmonds partition. It is canonical because its definition depends only on \(G\), not on a selected maximum matching. Here \(N_G(D)\) comprises all vertices outside or inside \(D\) adjacent to a vertex of \(D\), with subtraction ensuring \(A\cap D=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vertices exposable by maximum matchings form D; their external neighbors form A; all remaining vertices form C.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((D,A,C)\) is a uniquely determined partition of \(V\).

notation.meaning: vertices missed by at least one maximum matching
neighbors of D lying outside D
vertices in neither D nor A

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gallai–Edmonds Canonical Vertex Partition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the three canonical vertex classes through exposure by maximum matchings and adjacency to exposed vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph \(G=(V,E)\), let \(N(W)=\{v\in V\setminus W:\exists w\in W,\;vw\in E\}\). Define \(D(G)=\{v\in V:\text{there exists a maximum-size matching of }G\text{ that misses }v\}\), \(A(G)=N(D(G))\), and \(C(G)=V\setminus(D(G)\cup A(G))\). The partition \((D(G),A(G),C(G))\) is the Gallai\text{--}Edmonds decomposition of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Gallai–Edmonds decomposition partitions the vertices into D, the vertices missed by some maximum matching; A, the neighbors of D outside D; and C, all remaining vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: V=D(G)\mathbin{\dot\cup}A(G)\mathbin{\dot\cup}C(G)\text{ with the three classes defined above.}

knowledge_statements.title: Factor-Critical Components
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Factor-critical portion of the Gallai–Edmonds structure theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((D,A,C)\) be the Gallai–Edmonds partition of a finite graph \(G\). Every connected component \(H\) of the induced subgraph \(G[D]\) is factor-critical: for every vertex \(v\in V(H)\), the graph \(H-v\) has a perfect matching. Consequently, every maximum matching of \(G\) restricts to a near-perfect matching in each component of \(G[D]\), except that components receiving a matching edge from \(A\) can expose the endpoint incident with that edge before the edge is added.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every component induced by D remains perfectly matchable after deletion of any one of its vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every component \(H\) of \(G[D]\) and every \(v\in V(H)\), the graph \(H-v\) has a perfect matching.

notation.meaning: subgraph induced by the Gallai–Edmonds set D

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition-Based Matching Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction of a maximum matching from the Gallai–Edmonds decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input \(G\) and its Gallai–Edmonds partition \((D,A,C)\). Find a perfect matching of \(G[C]\). In the bipartite incidence graph between \(A\) and the components of \(G[D]\), find a matching saturating \(A\). For each assigned pair \((a,H)\), choose an edge \(av\) with \(v\in V(H)\) and a perfect matching of \(H-v\). In every unassigned component \(H\), choose any vertex \(w\) and a perfect matching of \(H-w\). Output the union of these edges and matchings. The output is a maximum matching of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Match C perfectly, assign each A vertex to a distinct D-component, and use near-perfect matchings inside the factor-critical components.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite undirected graph with Gallai–Edmonds partition \((D,A,C)\).
The component-incidence matching records an actual edge from each assigned \(a\in A\) to its assigned component.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The constructed union is a matching of cardinality \(\nu(G)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recursive Blossom-Contraction Augmenting-Path Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes the recursive augmenting-path procedure for cardinality matching in general graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a graph \(G\) and a matching \(M\), let \(X\) be the vertices missed by \(M\). If no positive-length \(M\)-alternating \(X\)-to-\(X\) walk exists, report that no \(M\)-augmenting path exists. Otherwise choose a shortest such walk \(P\). If \(P\) is a path, output \(P\). If it is not a path, select an initial \(M\)-flower with blossom \(B\), recursively find an \(M/B\)-augmenting path in \(G/B\), and expand it to an \(M\)-augmenting path in \(G\). Repeated augmentation yields a maximum-cardinality matching in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Search for a shortest alternating walk between exposed vertices. If none exists, there is no augmenting path. If the walk is a path, return it; otherwise contract a blossom, recurse, and expand the resulting augmenting path. Repeating this procedure finds a maximum-size matching in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure returns an }M\text{-augmenting path when one exists, otherwise certifies none exists; repeated augmentation finds a maximum-cardinality matching in polynomial time.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Alternating-Forest Blossom Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Alternating-forest search for augmenting a matching or certifying maximum cardinality in a general graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain an \(M\)-alternating forest \(F\), initially \(F:=M\), and the classes \(\operatorname{even}(F)\), \(\operatorname{odd}(F)\), and \(\operatorname{free}(F)\). Repeatedly choose an edge \(uv\) with \(u\in\operatorname{even}(F)\) and \(v\in\operatorname{even}(F)\cup\operatorname{free}(F)\). If \(v\in\operatorname{free}(F)\), extend the forest using \(uv\) and the edge of \(M\) incident with \(v\). If \(v\in\operatorname{even}(F)\), the forest paths from \(X\) to \(u\) and \(v\), together with \(uv\), either form an \(M\)-augmenting path when the paths are disjoint or contain an \(M\)-blossom, which is contracted, when they intersect. There are at most \(|V|\) iterations. The search terminates with an augmentation or, if no edge joins \(\operatorname{even}(F)\) to \(\operatorname{even}(F)\cup\operatorname{free}(F)\), with the conclusion that \(M\) has maximum size; the overall search work is \(O(n^2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The algorithm grows an alternating forest from even vertices. An edge to a free vertex extends the forest, while an edge between even vertices produces either an augmenting path or a blossom to contract. It performs at most n iterations and in quadratic time either augments the matching or concludes that it is maximum.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite graph with }n=|V|
F\text{ is maintained as an }M\text{-alternating forest rooted at }X
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The search finds an }M\text{-augmentation or concludes that }M\text{ is maximum in }O(n^2)\text{ time.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonbipartite Cardinality Matching Algorithm with Blossoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded summary of a blossom-based maximum-cardinality matching algorithm for general graphs; blossom membership and base determination rely on procedures defined elsewhere in the source.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a graph $G=(N,A)$ and an initial matching $X$ (possibly empty), initialize $b(i)=i$ for every $i\in N$ and label every exposed vertex $S:\varnothing$. Repeatedly scan an unmatched edge $(i,j)\notin X$ incident to an $S$-labeled vertex, or the unique matched edge $(i,j)\in X$ incident to a $T$-labeled vertex, ignoring the edge when $b(i)=b(j)$. An unlabeled encountered vertex receives the corresponding alternating-tree label. If the relevant backtraces reach distinct exposed roots, augment $X$, remove all labels, reset $b(i)=i$ for all $i$, and restart. If they reach the same root, form the blossom, determine its membership and base, complete its labels, update its blossom numbers, and continue. If no label remains unscanned, then no augmenting path exists, $X$ has maximum cardinality, and the final labels and blossom numbers can be used to construct an optimal dual solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start with any matching in a general graph, label all exposed vertices as roots, and grow labeled alternating trees while treating each current blossom as a unit. An encounter whose backtraces reach different exposed roots produces an augmenting path; augment the matching, clear the labels, restore singleton blossom numbers, and restart. An encounter whose backtraces reach the same root produces a blossom, which is formed and labeled before scanning continues. If all labels have been scanned without finding an augmentation, no augmenting path exists, the matching is maximum-cardinality, and the labels and blossom numbers provide an optimal-dual certificate.
assumptions_latex: G=(N,A)\text{ is a general, not necessarily bipartite, graph}
X\subseteq A\text{ is an initial matching, possibly }X=\varnothing
b(i)=i\quad\forall i\in N\text{ initially and after every augmentation}
\text{Blossom membership, base selection, labeling, and backtracing are performed as specified by the surrounding method}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{If the labeling process terminates with no unscanned labels, then no augmenting path exists, }X\text{ is maximum-cardinality, and the labels and blossom numbers construct an optimal dual solution.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonbipartite cardinality matching by blossom contraction and expansion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rooted alternating-search procedure underlying the Edmonds blossom method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a matching \(M\) and an unmatched root \(p\), perform an even-odd labeled alternating search. When the search first reveals both an even and an odd alternating path to a labeled vertex, trace predecessors to their first common vertex, identify the resulting blossom, contract it to an even pseudonode, and continue; contractions may contain earlier pseudonodes. If the search reaches an unmatched vertex \(q\), trace an augmenting path in the contracted graph, expand its pseudonodes until obtaining an augmenting path \(P\) in the original graph, and set \(M\leftarrow M\oplus P\). If the search exhausts its list, no augmenting path from \(p\) exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from an unmatched root, run an even-odd alternating search. Whenever conflicting parity paths reveal a blossom, contract it to an even pseudonode and continue, allowing nested contractions. If an unmatched endpoint is found, trace the contracted augmenting path, expand every pseudonode, and augment the original matching by symmetric difference. Exhausting the search means that no augmenting path starts at the root.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is a nonbipartite graph with current matching }M
p\text{ is an unmatched root vertex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The search either produces }M\oplus P\text{ for an augmenting path }P\text{ from }p\text{, or concludes that no such path exists.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: General and Special Blossom Forests
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition relative to a matching using maximal factor-critical blocks and their contracted alternating forest.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph and \(M\) a matching in \(G\). A subgraph \(F\subseteq G\) is a general blossom forest with respect to \(M\) if \(V(F)=V_1\dot\cup\cdots\dot\cup V_k\), each induced subgraph \(F_i:=F[V_i]\) is a maximal factor-critical subgraph of \(F\) satisfying \(\lvert M\cap E(F_i)\rvert=(\lvert V_i\rvert-1)/2\), and contracting every \(V_i\) produces an alternating forest \(F'\). Each \(F_i\), and all its vertices, is outer or inner according as its contracted vertex is outer or inner in \(F'\). A general blossom forest is special if every inner blossom consists of one vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A general blossom forest partitions its vertices into maximal factor-critical blocks that are internally matched except for one vertex, with simultaneous contraction producing an alternating forest. Blocks inherit outer or inner status from the contracted forest, and the blossom forest is special when every inner block is a singleton.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Edmonds Blossom Matching Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Alternating-forest procedure using scanning, augmentation, blossom contraction, and forest growth to obtain a maximum matching in a general graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize $\mu=\phi=\rho=\operatorname{id}$ and $\sigma=\mathrm{UNSCANNED}$. Repeatedly select an UNSCANNED blossom point $x$. Mark $x$ SCANNED when every neighbor is inner or has the same $\rho$-representative. For a blossom-point neighbor $y$ with $\rho(y)\ne\rho(x)$, augment and reinitialize when $S(x)\cap S(y)=\varnothing$; otherwise shrink the blossom determined by the first common base point by updating $\phi$ and $\rho$. For an out-of-forest neighbor $y$, grow the forest by setting $\phi(y)=x$. Stop when every blossom is SCANNED; then the edges represented by $\{x\mu(x)\}$ form a maximum matching in $G$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize the matching, forest, and blossom-representative maps and mark all blossoms unscanned. Scanning either closes a search point, augments along disjoint alternating paths, contracts a blossom when the paths meet, or grows the forest through a new neighbor. When every blossom is scanned, the matching encoded by the matching map is maximum.
assumptions_latex: S(\cdot),\rho,\phi,\mu,\sigma\text{ have the meanings fixed by the preceding algorithmic setup}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Upon termination, the edges represented by }\{x\mu(x)\}\text{ form a maximum matching in }G

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal-Dual Blossom Algorithm for Maximum-Weight Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded algorithm statement; apparent OCR corruptions in several dual-update formulas are not reproduced.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite general graph $G=(N,A)$ with edge weights $w_{ij}$, initialize $X=\varnothing$ and vertex dual variables by $u_i=\tfrac12\max\{w_{ij}:(i,j)\in A\}$. Repeatedly search the zero-reduced-weight edges using $S$- and $T$-labels; augment $X$ when distinct search roots are joined, contract a newly detected odd blossom when a search closes at one root, and, when no unscanned label remains, choose $\delta=\min\{\delta_1,\delta_2,\Delta\}$, where $\delta_1=\min_i u_i$ over the applicable labeled vertices, $\delta_2=\tfrac12\min\{z_k:k\in K_T\}$, and $\Delta$ is the smallest reduced-cost event value accumulated during scanning. Revise the vertex and blossom dual variables by $\delta$, expanding any $T$-blossom whose dual variable becomes zero. If $\delta=\delta_1$, halt: $X$ is a maximum-weight matching and $(u,z)$ is an optimal dual solution. The implementation runs in $O(n^4)$ time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite edge-weighted general graph, the algorithm maintains a matching, vertex and blossom dual variables, labeled alternating-search forests, and contracted blossoms. It scans tight edges, augments when two search trees meet, contracts odd blossoms when a search closes within one tree, expands T-blossoms whose dual value reaches zero, and otherwise changes the dual solution by the smallest vertex, blossom, or reduced-cost event. When the vertex event is reached, it returns a maximum-weight matching together with an optimal dual solution. Its running time is O(n^4).
assumptions_latex: G=(N,A)\text{ is a finite general graph with }n=|N|.
w_{ij}\text{ is specified for every }(i,j)\in A.
\text{The matching, reduced weights, blossom bases, labels, and blossom dual variables are maintained according to the stated primal-dual invariants.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Upon the event }\delta=\delta_1,\ X\text{ is a maximum-weight matching and }(u,z)\text{ is an optimal dual solution; the algorithm runs in }O(n^4)\text{ time.}

knowledge_statements.title: Alternating Forests
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Search forest used by the cardinality version of Edmonds' blossom algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a matching \(M\) in a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), an alternating forest \(F\) is a rooted forest in which every root is uncovered by \(M\), and every root-to-vertex path alternates between edges outside \(M\) and edges in \(M\), beginning with an edge outside \(M\). Vertices at even depth are outer and vertices at odd depth are inner. Every inner vertex is covered by \(M\), and its unique incident edge in \(M\) joins it to its outer child; equivalently, every nonroot outer vertex is joined to its inner parent by an edge in \(M\). During search growth from an outer vertex, an unmatched edge to an unreached matched vertex adds that vertex as inner and its mate as outer. An unmatched edge to an exposed vertex instead yields an augmenting path and does not add that exposed vertex as an inner vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An alternating forest grows from exposed roots through unmatched-then-matched edge pairs; even-depth vertices are outer, odd-depth vertices are inner, and reaching another exposed vertex produces an augmenting path.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every root-to-outer path has even length, every root-to-inner path has odd length, and every inner vertex has a unique matched outer child.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Alternating Forest
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Alternating-search forest relative to a fixed matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph and \(M\) a matching in \(G\). An alternating forest with respect to \(M\) is a forest \(F\subseteq G\) such that: (i) \(V(F)\) contains every vertex exposed by \(M\), and every component contains exactly one exposed vertex, called its root; (ii) a vertex is outer or inner according as its distance from its component root is even or odd, respectively, and every inner vertex has degree \(2\) in \(F\); and (iii) for every \(v\in V(F)\), the unique path from \(v\) to its component root is \(M\)-alternating.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An alternating forest contains all exposed vertices and exactly one exposed root per component. Vertices are outer or inner according to even or odd root distance, every inner vertex has degree two, and every vertex-to-root path alternates with respect to the matching.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is an alternating forest with respect to }M\text{ exactly when conditions (i)--(iii) hold.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matching-Alternating Forest and Its Vertex Classes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines an alternating-search forest and its even, odd, and free vertex classes relative to a designated root set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\), let \(M\subseteq E\) be a matching, and let \(X\subseteq V\). An \(M\)-alternating forest is a set \(F\subseteq E\) such that \(F\) is a forest, \(M\subseteq F\), every component of \((V,F)\) either contains exactly one vertex of \(X\) or consists of one edge of \(M\), and every path in \(F\) starting in \(X\) is \(M\)-alternating. Define \(\operatorname{even}(F)=\{v\in V: F\text{ contains an even-length }X\!\text{-}v\text{ path}\}\), \(\operatorname{odd}(F)=\{v\in V: F\text{ contains an odd-length }X\!\text{-}v\text{ path}\}\), and \(\operatorname{free}(F)=\{v\in V: F\text{ contains no }X\!\text{-}v\text{ path}\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An M-alternating forest contains M, has each component rooted at exactly one vertex of X or consisting of a single matching edge, and has alternating paths from X. Vertices are classified as even, odd, or free according to the parity or absence of a path from X.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is an }M\text{-alternating forest, with }\operatorname{even}(F),\operatorname{odd}(F),\operatorname{free}(F)\text{ defined as above.}

knowledge_statements.title: Blossom Detection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Same-tree outer–outer collision criterion for detecting a blossom.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be an alternating forest for matching \(M\). Suppose a searched edge \(xy\notin M\) joins distinct outer vertices in the same tree, and let \(b\) be their lowest common ancestor in \(F\). The union of \(xy\), the tree path from \(b\) to \(x\), and the tree path from \(b\) to \(y\) is an odd cycle \(B\). Its edges alternate with respect to \(M\), except that the two cycle edges incident with the base \(b\) are outside \(M\). This cycle, together with base \(b\), is the detected blossom.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An edge joining two outer vertices in one search tree creates an odd alternating cycle based at their lowest common ancestor.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is an alternating forest for a matching \(M\).
\(x\) and \(y\) are distinct outer vertices in the same tree and \(xy\notin M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The two tree paths to their lowest common ancestor together with \(xy\) form an \(M\)-blossom.

knowledge_statements.title: Forest Label Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parity and mate invariants maintained by an Edmonds alternating search forest.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In an alternating forest \(F\) for matching \(M\), each root is exposed and outer. Every nonroot outer vertex has an inner parent joined to it by an edge of \(M\); every inner vertex has an outer parent joined to it by an edge outside \(M\), and its unique \(M\)-mate is its outer child. Hence an outer vertex has an even-length alternating path from its root, while an inner vertex has an odd-length alternating path. These labels are relative to the current contracted search graph and must be recomputed or inherited consistently after contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outer and inner labels encode path parity, with matched edges linking each inner vertex to its unique outer child.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is an alternating forest generated from exposed roots for matching \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Outer vertices have even alternating root paths; inner vertices have odd alternating root paths and a unique matched outer child.

knowledge_statements.title: Search-Collision Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Case distinction for an unmatched edge scanned from an outer search vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: When an edge \(xy\notin M\) is scanned from an outer vertex \(x\), apply the following cases. If \(y\) is unreached and matched, add \(y\) as inner and its mate as outer; if \(y\) is unreached and exposed, the root-to-\(x\) path followed by \(xy\) is augmenting. If \(y\) is outer in a different tree, concatenate the two root paths with \(xy\) to obtain an augmenting path. If \(y\) is outer in the same tree, detect and contract the resulting blossom. Edges to inner vertices require no growth under this scan rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An outer-edge scan either grows the forest, finds an augmenting path, detects a blossom, or produces no search change.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is an alternating forest for matching \(M\).
\(x\) is outer and \(xy\notin M\) is being scanned.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The status of \(y\) determines growth, augmentation, blossom contraction, or no action.

knowledge_statements.title: Blossom Contraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shrinking a detected alternating blossom during augmenting-path search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a graph \(G\), matching \(M\), and a detected blossom \(B\) with base \(b\). Replace all vertices of \(B\) by one pseudovertex \(\beta\); delete loops and retain each edge between \(B\) and \(V(G)\setminus B\) as an edge incident with \(\beta\), preserving its original endpoint in \(B\) as metadata. Replace the internal matched edges of \(B\) by nothing and map any matching edge leaving the base to its corresponding edge at \(\beta\). In the contracted search, treat \(\beta\) as having the outer status formerly held by \(b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shrink the odd alternating cycle to an outer pseudovertex while retaining boundary-edge endpoints for later expansion.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is an odd alternating blossom detected relative to matching \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure produces the contracted graph \(G/B\) and induced matching \(M/B\) used for continued search.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shrinking a blossom replaces its vertices by one new vertex, removes its internal edges, and redirects its boundary edges to the new vertex.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: V/b=(V\setminus V(b))\cup\{v_b\},\quad E/b\text{ is obtained by omitting the internal edges of }b\text{ and redirecting its boundary edges to }v_b

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Blossom contraction operation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction of a contracted graph and an even pseudonode during cardinality-matching search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a blossom \(B=(i_1,i_2,\ldots,i_k,i_1)\) relative to the current matching and rooted search, introduce a pseudonode \(b\), set \(A^c(b)=\bigcup_{i\in B}A(i)\), add \(b\) to the adjacency list of every vertex adjacent to \(B\), retain the cyclic order of the blossom vertices in a circular doubly linked list, and delete the blossom vertices and their incident edges. The pseudonode is even, and scanning its adjacency list exposes the external adjacencies of the blossom.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Contract a blossom by replacing its vertices with an even pseudonode whose adjacency list combines their adjacencies, updating neighboring lists, recording the blossom cycle for recovery, and deleting the original vertices and incident edges.
assumptions_latex: B=(i_1,i_2,\ldots,i_k,i_1)\text{ is a blossom relative to the current matching and rooted search}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G^c\text{ represents }B\text{ by an even pseudonode }b\text{ with }A^c(b)=\bigcup_{i\in B}A(i).

children.title: Blossom Expansion
children.top_down_role: Recovery of original-graph matching structure from a contracted blossom.

knowledge_statements.title: Blossom Expansion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lifting a contracted augmenting path through an odd alternating blossom.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input an augmenting path \(P'\) for \(M/B\) in \(G/B\), together with the stored boundary endpoints of blossom \(B\). If \(P'\) avoids the pseudovertex \(\beta\), return the same path in \(G\). Otherwise replace the segment through \(\beta\) by the parity-compatible alternating arc of \(B\) joining the recorded boundary endpoint to the base or to the other recorded boundary endpoint. Choose the one of the two cycle arcs that preserves alternation with the entering and leaving edges. The resulting path \(P\) is augmenting for \(M\); output \(M\triangle E(P)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace a contracted pseudovertex on an augmenting path by the blossom arc whose parity preserves alternation, then augment.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is a contracted odd alternating blossom for \(M\).
\(P'\) is an augmenting path for \(M/B\), with original boundary endpoints retained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Expansion yields an \(M\)-augmenting path \(P\) in \(G\), and \(M\triangle E(P)\) has cardinality \(|M|+1\).

notation.meaning: augmenting path in the contracted graph

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cubic-Time Primal-Dual Algorithm for Maximum-Weight General-Graph Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete weighted blossom method and its running-time guarantee; transcription-level formula defects in the extract are not promoted as mathematical claims.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an $n$-vertex general graph $G=(N,A)$ with edge weights $w_{ij}$, maintain a matching $X$, contracted blossoms, search labels, reduced weights, and feasible vertex and blossom dual variables. Repeatedly grow alternating searches along tight edges, augment when an augmenting path is found, contract an odd blossom when one is found, expand zero-dual blossoms, and otherwise revise the dual solution by the minimum eligible slack. The procedure terminates with a maximum-weight matching and an optimal dual solution, and its running time is $O(n^3)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an n-vertex weighted general graph, the primal-dual blossom algorithm alternates tight-edge labeling searches, matching augmentation, odd-blossom contraction or expansion, and minimum-slack dual revisions. It terminates with a maximum-weight matching and a corresponding optimal dual solution in cubic time.
assumptions_latex: G=(N,A)\text{ is a finite general graph with }|N|=n.
w_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}\text{ is specified for every edge }(i,j)\in A.
\text{The matching, blossom, labeling, reduced-weight, and dual invariants of the stated algorithm are maintained.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X\text{ is a maximum-weight matching, the final vertex and blossom dual variables are optimal, and the total running time is }O(n^3).

knowledge_statements.title: Contraction Invariants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Augmenting-path invariance under valid Edmonds blossom shrinking.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\) be a blossom detected in an alternating search for matching \(M\), and let \(G/B\) and \(M/B\) be obtained by valid blossom contraction. Then \(G\) contains an \(M\)-augmenting path if and only if \(G/B\) contains an \(M/B\)-augmenting path. Any contracted augmenting path can be expanded through \(B\) to an augmenting path in \(G\), while contraction maps an augmenting path in \(G\), after the standard simplification of repeated blossom crossings, to one in \(G/B\). Therefore contraction preserves the test that \(M\) is maximum and preserves the possibility of increasing its cardinality by one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Valid blossom contraction preserves the existence of an augmenting path and hence preserves whether the current matching is maximum.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite undirected graph and \(M\) is a matching.
\(B\) is a valid alternating blossom produced by an Edmonds search.
\(G/B\) and \(M/B\) use the standard base-preserving contraction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) has an \(M\)-augmenting path if and only if \(G/B\) has an \(M/B\)-augmenting path.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Augmenting-Path Preservation under Blossom Contraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the bidirectional augmenting-path existence invariant validating blossom contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a matching in a graph \(G\), and suppose that an augmenting-path search from a vertex \(u\) discovers a blossom \(b\). Then an augmenting path from \(u\) exists in \(G\) with respect to \(M\) if and only if an augmenting path exists in \(G/b\) with respect to \(M/b\), starting from \(u\), except that the starting vertex is \(v_b\) when \(u\) is the basis of \(b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Contracting a discovered blossom preserves the existence of an augmenting path from the search vertex; when that vertex is the blossom basis, the contracted vertex is used instead.
assumptions_latex: b\text{ is a blossom discovered during an augmenting-path search from }u

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a contracted alternating walk use \(\beta\). Expanding \(\beta\) requires an alternating path inside \(B\) joining the prescribed external incidence or incidences to the blossom base with parity compatible with \(M\). If the contraction record omits the base, cyclic child order, or the attachment vertices of contracted edges, two distinct internal alternating lifts may agree after contraction, and an arbitrary lift may repeat a vertex or place two consecutive matched or unmatched edges. Thus contraction alone does not define expansion; expansion is valid only relative to retained blossom state sufficient to select a simple alternating lift.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A contracted blossom cannot always be expanded from the pseudovertex alone. Its base, internal order, and external attachment vertices must be retained to select a valid alternating lift.

source_refs.locator: Section 5. Cardinality Matching Algorithm p. 193

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nested-blossom representation consists of a laminar family \(\mathcal B\) of odd vertex sets. Each nontrivial \(B\in\mathcal B\) stores a base \(b(B)\), an odd cyclic sequence of maximal proper child blossoms and singleton vertices, and the cycle edges joining consecutive children. Laminarity means that for \(B,C\in\mathcal B\), either \(B\cap C=\varnothing\), \(B\subseteq C\), or \(C\subseteq B\). Inclusion therefore forms a rooted forest. Recursively replacing every child by its stored cycle reconstructs \(B\), while the stored base and matching parity determine the alternating route used when an augmenting path is expanded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nested blossoms form a laminar inclusion forest. Each blossom stores a base and an odd cycle of children, enabling recursive reconstruction and parity-correct expansion.
knowledge_statements.title: Nested-Blossom Representations

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical unweighted general-graph Micali–Vazirani bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A phase begins by determining \(\ell(M)\), the minimum number of edges in an \(M\)-augmenting path, using alternating levels together with blossom formation. It then finds and augments along a maximal collection of vertex-disjoint augmenting paths of length \(\ell(M)\), represented and expanded through the phase's blossom structure. The phase ends when no augmenting path at that level remains. After augmentation, the next existing shortest augmenting path is longer. With linear-time search work \(O(m)\) per phase and \(O(\sqrt n)\) phases, the total running time is \(O(m\sqrt n)\), and termination with no augmenting path certifies maximum cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Micali–Vazirani organizes general-graph matching into shortest-augmenting-path phases. Linear work per phase over at most square-root-many phases yields the classical O(m sqrt n) bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Micali–Vazirani Phase-Based Methods

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic Gabow-style cardinality framework; no specific implementation bound is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(M=\varnothing\). For each augmentation search, grow an alternating forest \(F\) from all \(M\)-exposed vertices. When an eligible edge reaches a new vertex, add the corresponding unmatched and matched forest edges. When it joins two appropriate outer vertices in one tree, contract the resulting odd alternating cycle and record it in \(\mathcal B\). When it joins outer vertices rooted at distinct exposed vertices, trace the forest paths and blossom records to obtain an augmenting path \(P\), replace \(M\) by \(M\triangle E(P)\), expand affected blossoms, and restart. If a complete search finds no augmenting path, output \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gabow-style cardinality algorithms maintain an alternating forest and nested blossoms, repeatedly contract odd cycles and augment, and stop when a complete search finds no augmenting path.
knowledge_statements.title: Gabow Cardinality-Matching Methods

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Method-specific maintained conditions for the Edmonds weighted primal–dual construction. The final clause is read as applying to two generic sets in the maintained family because the extract inconsistently uses the subscripts i and t.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The maintained state satisfies: (a) \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\), and the selected edges form a matching of \((V,J_e)\); (b) if \(S_k\in\bar J_b\), equivalently \(\gamma_k<0\), then the restriction to \(S_k\) contains \(s_k\) matched edges and hence \(\sum_{i,j\in S_k}x_{ij}=s_k\); and (c) the sets in \(\widetilde J_b\) are laminar: for \(S_t,S_k\in\widetilde J_b\), if \(S_t\cap S_k\ne\varnothing\), then \(S_t\subseteq S_k\) or \(S_k\subseteq S_t\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual-adjustment iteration of Edmonds' weighted perfect-matching algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes one primal–dual iteration on the contracted tight-edge graph, including optimality, infeasibility, and bounded-update outcomes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $z$ be a feasible dual solution and let $G_z$ be the current contracted tight-edge graph. Compute a maximum-cardinality matching $M$ in $G_z$. If $M$ is perfect, expand it to a perfect matching of $G$ using only tight edges; under the maintained optimality conditions, this matching is optimal. Otherwise, form the Gallai--Edmonds decomposition $W,X,Y$ of $G_z$. If $B(v)\in\mathcal B$ is the vertex set contracted to $v$, decrease $z_{B(v)}$ by $\varepsilon$ for every $v\in X$, and for every connected component $C$ of $G_z[Y]$ increase $z_A$ by $\varepsilon$, where $A=\bigcup_{v\in C}B(v)$. Choose the largest $\varepsilon>0$ preserving dual feasibility. Tight matching edges remain tight, and
\[
\#\operatorname{cc}(G_z[Y])>|X|,
\]
so the dual objective increases by
\[
\varepsilon\bigl(\#\operatorname{cc}(G_z[Y])-|X|\bigr)\geq\varepsilon.
\]
If arbitrarily large $\varepsilon$ remains feasible, the dual LP is unbounded, the primal perfect-matching LP is infeasible, and $G$ has no perfect matching. Otherwise, update $G_z$ to reflect newly tight edges, contractions, and unpackings, and continue. The stated finiteness argument uses the fact that between augmentations every grow, shrink, or unpack step increases the number of outer vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Find a maximum matching in the current contracted tight-edge graph. If it is perfect, expand it through tight edges to obtain an optimal perfect matching. Otherwise, use the Gallai–Edmonds decomposition to decrease dual variables associated with X and increase variables associated with components of Y, taking the largest positive step that preserves dual feasibility. This preserves tight matching edges and raises the dual objective. If the step is unbounded, no perfect matching exists; otherwise new tight edges, contractions, or unpackings produce the next iteration. Finiteness is tied to growth in the number of outer vertices between augmentations.
assumptions_latex: z\text{ is feasible for the weighted perfect-matching dual}
G_z\text{ is the current contracted graph formed from tight edges}
B(v)\in\mathcal B\text{ denotes the vertex set contracted to }v
\text{The algorithm maintains the cited primal--dual optimality conditions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The iteration returns an optimal perfect matching, certifies that no perfect matching exists when the dual step is unbounded, or performs a maximal dual-feasible update with strictly increased dual objective.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Laminar primal–dual blossom procedure for minimum-weight perfect matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted perfect matching in a simple general graph known to admit a perfect matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be simple and admit a perfect matching. Maintain a laminar collection \(\Omega\) of odd subsets of \(V\), dual values \(\pi:\Omega\to\mathbb Q\) satisfying the stated dual-feasibility invariant, a matching \(M\) in the contracted tight-edge graph \(G'=G_\pi/\Omega\), and a stored circuit \(C_U\) for every nonsingleton \(U\in\Omega\). Iteratively augment along an alternating augmenting path, shrink the circuit of an alternating flower, or make a maximal feasible dual adjustment and deshrink a nonsingleton set whose dual value reaches zero. If \(M\) becomes perfect in \(G'\), it expands to a perfect matching \(N\) of \(G\) satisfying \(w_\pi(N)=0\) and \(|N\cap\delta(U)|=1\) for every \(U\in\Omega\); hence \(N\) is minimum-weight. If \(V\ne\varnothing\), laminarity also gives \(|\Omega|\le 2|V|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The weighted primal–dual blossom procedure maintains feasible dual values, a laminar family of odd sets, and a matching in a contracted tight-edge graph. Its steps augment the matching, shrink a blossom, adjust the dual values, or expand a zero-valued blossom. A perfect contracted matching expands to a minimum-weight perfect matching, and the maintained laminar family has at most twice as many sets as vertices when the graph is nonempty.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) has at least one perfect matching.
\(\Omega\) is a laminar collection of odd-cardinality subsets of \(V\).
\(\pi:\Omega\to\mathbb Q\) satisfies the stated dual-feasibility invariant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ perfect in }G'\Rightarrow N\text{ is a minimum-weight perfect matching of }G,\ w_\pi(N)=0,\ |N\cap\delta(U)|=1\ \forall U\in\Omega;\quad V\ne\varnothing\Rightarrow |\Omega|\le2|V|.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cubic-time implementation of the weighted blossom algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Amortized implementation of weighted primal–dual perfect matching in general graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain the laminar blossom family \(\Omega\), dual values \(\pi\), matching \(M\), stored blossom circuits, and an \(M\)-alternating forest \(F\) in the contracted tight-edge graph. Represent the contracted graph implicitly by minimum reduced-weight edges \(e_{YZ}\), forest-facing minima \(e_Y\), and potentials \(p(v)=\sum_{U\in\Omega:\,v\in U}\pi(U)\). Each maximal feasible dual adjustment is followed by forest augmentation, matching augmentation, blossom shrinking, or deshrinking. There are at most \(|V|\) iterations between consecutive matching augmentations, and the total work between them is \(O(n^2)\). With at most \(n/2\) matching augmentations, the total running time is \(O(n^3)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cubic implementation reuses an alternating forest and stores the contracted tight-edge graph implicitly through minimum reduced-weight connecting edges and vertex potentials. Each dual update triggers forest growth, matching augmentation, blossom contraction, or blossom expansion. There are at most n iterations and O(n squared) work between matching augmentations, giving O(n cubed) total time.
assumptions_latex: The input is the weighted general-graph perfect-matching instance of the preceding algorithm with \(n=|V|\).
The graph admits a perfect matching.
The stated dual-feasibility invariant is maintained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\#\operatorname{iterations\ between\ consecutive\ matching\ augmentations}\le |V|,\qquad T(n)=O(n^3).\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal–Dual Blossom Algorithm for Minimum-Cost Complete Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded algorithm specification for an even-order complete graph. The extract contains minor notation and OCR inconsistencies, so the tight-edge test and pseudonode sets are referenced through their method-defined meanings rather than silently reconstructed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an even integer \(n\) and a symmetric matrix \([c_{ij}]\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{n\times n}\), initialize the vertex labels \(\alpha_i=\tfrac12\min_j c_{ij}\), all blossom labels \(\gamma_k=0\), and \(M=\varnothing\). While \(|M|<n/2\), construct the admissible tight-edge graph \(G_J\), shrink the maintained blossom sets, extend the current matching to a maximum matching in \(G_J\), classify the outer and inner vertices and pseudonodes, choose \(\theta_1=\min\{\delta_1,\delta_2,\delta_3\}\), update the vertex and blossom labels with the stated outer/inner signs, recover the corresponding maximum proper matching in \((V,J_e)\), and retain the blossom sets whose labels remain negative. On termination, output the resulting complete matching \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method repeatedly forms the tight-edge graph, contracts blossoms, finds a maximum matching, performs the minimum permitted primal–dual label adjustment, and recovers the associated proper matching until the matching is complete.
assumptions_latex: \(\delta_1,\delta_2,\delta_3\text{ and the admissible graph, blossom, and pseudonode sets have their surrounding method definitions}.\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|M|=n/2\text{ on termination, and }M\text{ is returned as the minimum-total-cost complete matching specified by the algorithm's output contract}.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each vertex \(v\in V\), the equality constraint \(x(\delta(v))=1\) has a free dual variable \(y_v\in\mathbb R\). Together with odd-set variables, dual feasibility requires, for every edge \(uv\in E\), \[y_u+y_v+\sum_{\substack{S\subseteq V:\ |S|\text{ odd},\ uv\in E(S)}}z_S\ge w_{uv}.\] The vertex contribution to the reduced slack of \(uv\) is therefore \(y_u+y_v\). Translating one vertex coordinate changes all incident edge slacks uniformly, while feasibility is preserved exactly when every affected edge inequality remains nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each degree equality produces a free vertex dual variable. An edge receives the sum of its endpoint variables, so changing one coordinate uniformly changes all incident edge slacks.
knowledge_statements.title: Vertex Dual Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The primal odd-set inequality is \[x(E(S))\le \frac{|S|-1}{2}.\] Its dual coordinate satisfies \(z_S\ge0\), contributes \(z_S\) to the covering inequality of every edge in \(E(S)\), contributes nothing to edges crossing \(\delta(S)\), and has objective coefficient \((|S|-1)/2\). Hence increasing \(z_S\) translates the dual load of all internal edges together. Complementary slackness implies that \(z_S>0\) can occur in an optimal complementary pair only when the matching uses exactly \((|S|-1)/2\) edges of \(E(S)\), equivalently exactly one matching edge crosses \(\delta(S)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An odd-set dual variable is nonnegative, prices every edge internal to that odd set, and can be positive complementarily only when the matching leaves exactly one vertex matched outward.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(L_{uv}=y_u+y_v+\sum_{S:uv\in E(S)}z_S\). Dual feasibility gives \(L_e\ge w_e\) for every \(e\in E\). If \(L_e=w_e\) for every \(e\in M\), and \(z_S>0\) implies \(x(E(S))=(|S|-1)/2\), then all complementary-slackness products vanish. Consequently the primal weight \(\sum_{e\in M}w_e\) equals the dual objective \(\sum_{v\in V}y_v+\sum_S((|S|-1)/2)z_S\). Weak duality then certifies that \(M\) is a maximum-weight perfect matching and \((y,z)\) is dual-optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible perfect matching is optimal when all its edges are dual-tight and every positively priced odd set is saturated; equality of primal and dual objectives then certifies optimality.
