children.title: Matroid Parity Boundary
children.top_down_role: Tractability limits associated with matroid parity formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Matroid Parity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independence-oracle versus linear-representation boundary for matroid parity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let a matroid \(\mathcal M\) have ground set partitioned into pairs \(P_1,\ldots,P_m\). Matroid parity maximizes \(|I|\) over index sets \(I\subseteq\{1,
ldots,m\}\) satisfying \(\bigcup_{i\in I}P_i\in\mathcal I(\mathcal M)\). In the independence-oracle model, no polynomial-query algorithm solves all instances: some families require exponentially many oracle queries. When \(\mathcal M\) is supplied by an explicit linear representation over a field, randomized algebraic polynomial-time algorithms are available in the field-operation model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matroid parity is exponentially hard in the independence-oracle model but admits randomized polynomial algebraic algorithms from an explicit linear representation.
assumptions_latex: Oracle complexity counts independence queries; linear complexity counts field operations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Oracle access alone has an exponential worst-case query barrier, whereas explicit linear representation yields a randomized polynomial-time regime.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: established oracle-versus-linear distinction for matroid parity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The oracle-versus-linear boundary needs exact lower-bound and algorithm locators, including deterministic or randomized qualifications and field assumptions. The index-set formula also contains a malformed ellipsis near the lower endpoint.

children.title: Linear-Representation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Complexity regimes governed by explicit linear matroid representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Representation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Randomized algebraic regime for linearly represented matroid parity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a matrix \(A\) over a field \(\mathbb F\), whose columns represent a matroid, together with a partition of the columns into pairs. Introduce independent random field values into the standard skew-symmetric parity matrix derived from \(A\) and the pairs, compute its generic rank by Gaussian elimination, and recover the maximum feasible number of pairs from that rank; self-reduction may recover an optimal pair set. Over a sufficiently large sampling field, polynomially many field operations give one-sided polynomially bounded error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear representation converts matroid parity into randomized rank computations, yielding polynomial field-operation complexity and optional recovery by self-reduction.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) explicitly represents the input matroid over \(\mathbb F\).
The sampling field is sufficiently large, or a suitable extension field is used.
Complexity is measured in field operations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Maximum linear matroid parity is computable by a randomized polynomial number of field operations with one-sided bounded error.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical Lovász-style algebraic treatment of linear matroid parity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claimed randomized algebraic regime is plausible, but the parity matrix, rank-to-optimum relation, field restrictions, recovery procedure, and meaning of the error guarantee are too underspecified to validate without a precise source.

children.title: Oracle-Model Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity boundaries arising under oracle access to matroid structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle-Model Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Query lower bound for parity and matching under independence-oracle access.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the independence-oracle model, an algorithm learns a matroid only through queries asking whether a supplied subset is independent. There exists a family of matroid parity instances on ground sets of size \(n\) for which every algorithm guaranteed to return an optimum requires \(2^{\Omega(n)}\) independence queries in the worst case. Since matroid parity embeds into matroid matching by using the prescribed pairs as the graph edges, the same absence of a polynomial-query algorithm applies to general matroid matching in this oracle model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact matroid parity needs exponentially many independence queries in the worst case, and the reduction by disjoint pair edges transfers this barrier to matroid matching.
assumptions_latex: Only independence-oracle access to the matroid is available.
The algorithm must return an exact optimum on every instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The worst-case exact query complexity is \(2^{\Omega(n)}\) for matroid parity and, by reduction, for matroid matching.

notation.meaning: an exponential asymptotic query lower bound

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: known oracle lower-bound phenomenon for matroid parity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A precise source is required to verify the stated 2^{Omega(n)} bound, the applicable deterministic or randomized oracle model, and the transfer to the particular matroid-matching model.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimization–Counting Complexity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum matching versus exact perfect-matching counting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an explicitly represented finite graph, a maximum-cardinality matching can be found in polynomial time. In contrast, exactly counting perfect matchings is \(\#\mathrm P\)-complete, already for bipartite graphs: if \(A\) is the bipartite adjacency matrix, then the number of perfect matchings equals \[\operatorname{perm}(A)=\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^n A_{i,\pi(i)}.\] Thus polynomial-time optimization does not imply polynomial-time exact counting for the same matching family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum matching is polynomial-time solvable, but exact perfect-matching counting is #P-complete even in bipartite graphs, where it equals a zero-one permanent.
assumptions_latex: Graphs and matrices are represented explicitly.
Counting requires the exact integer answer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Maximum matching belongs to polynomial time, whereas exact bipartite perfect-matching counting is \(\#\mathrm P\)-complete.

notation.meaning: permanent of the bipartite adjacency matrix

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical matching algorithms and Valiant permanent complexity theorem

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The optimization–counting contrast and permanent identity are standard and correctly scoped, but both the polynomial-time optimization claim and #P-completeness claim lack inspectable citations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence criterion for triangle-free perfect 2-matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary-and-sufficient vertex-deletion condition stated through triangle-cluster components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A graph \(G=(V,E)\) has a triangle-free perfect 2-matching if and only if, for every \(U\subseteq V\), the graph \(G-U\) has at most \(|U|\) components that are triangle clusters.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph has a triangle-free perfect 2-matching exactly when deleting any vertex subset U leaves at most |U| components that are triangle clusters.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ has a triangle-free perfect 2-matching}\iff \forall U\subseteq V,\ \beta(G-U)\leq|U|

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Min-max formula for maximum triangle-free 2-matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum-cardinality characterization by vertex deletion and the number of triangle-cluster components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph \(G=(V,E)\), let \(\beta(H)\) denote the number of components of \(H\) that are triangle clusters. The maximum size of a triangle-free 2-matching in \(G\) is \[\min_{U\subseteq V}\bigl(|V|+|U|-\beta(G-U)\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum size of a triangle-free 2-matching equals the minimum, over all vertex subsets U, of |V| plus |U| minus the number of triangle-cluster components of G minus U.
assumptions_latex: \beta(H)\text{ denotes the number of components of }H\text{ that are triangle clusters}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nu_{\mathrm{TF2M}}(G)=\min_{U\subseteq V}\bigl\{|V|+|U|-\beta(G-U)\bigr\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Min–Max Formula for a Simple 2-Edge Cover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the minimum simple 2-edge-cover size using disjoint vertex sets and components remaining after their deletion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have minimum degree at least \(2\). The minimum size of a simple 2-edge cover equals \[\max_{\substack{U,S\subseteq V,\ U\cap S=\varnothing\\ S\text{ stable}}}\left\{|V|-|U|+|S|-\sum_{K\in\operatorname{comp}(G-U-S)}\left\lfloor\frac{|E[K,S]|}{2}\right\rfloor\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a graph of minimum degree at least two, the minimum size of a simple 2-edge cover is the maximum, over disjoint vertex sets U and S with S stable, of |V|-|U|+|S| minus the sum over components K of G-U-S of floor(|E[K,S]|/2).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho_2^{\mathrm{s}}(G)=\max_{U\cap S=\varnothing,\ S\text{ stable}}\left(|V|-|U|+|S|-\sum_{K\in\operatorname{comp}(G-U-S)}\left\lfloor\frac{|E[K,S]|}{2}\right\rfloor\right)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Capacitated Perfect b-Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines integral perfect b-matchings with edge capacities and records the uncapacitated, unit-capacity, and bipartite transportation specializations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\), \(b\in\mathbf Z^V\), and \(u\in(\mathbf Z\cup\{\infty\})^E\). A \(u\)-capacitated perfect \(b\)-matching, or \((b,u)\)-matching, is a vector \(x\in\mathbf Z^E\) satisfying \(x(\delta(v))=b_v\) for every \(v\in V\) and \(0\le x_e\le u_e\) for every \(e\in E\). If \(u_e=1\) for all \(e\), then \(x\) is the characteristic vector of a \(b\)-factor. If \(u_e=\infty\) for all \(e\), it is called a perfect \(b\)-matching. For bipartite \(G\), minimum-weight perfect \(b\)-matching is the transportation problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A capacitated perfect b-matching is an integral nonnegative edge-multiplicity vector that realizes each vertex demand exactly while respecting every edge capacity. Unit capacities recover b-factors, infinite capacities give perfect b-matchings, and the bipartite minimum-weight uncapacitated case is a transportation problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in\mathbf Z^E,\quad x(\delta(v))=b_v\ \forall v\in V,\quad 0\le x_e\le u_e\ \forall e\in E

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines integral b-matchings with vertex-capacity inequalities and their maximum-weight optimization problem.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\ge0,\quad x(\delta(v))\le b_v\ \forall v\in V,\qquad \max\{w^Tx:x\text{ is a }b\text{-matching}\}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounds the coordinatewise distance to a suitably chosen optimal b'-matching after changing the vertex-bound vector.

knowledge_statements.title: Bipartite b-Matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uncapacitated vertex-capacitated matching in a bipartite graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R,E)\) be a finite bipartite graph and let \(b:V(G)\to\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\). A bipartite \(b\)-matching is an edge set \(F\subseteq E\) satisfying \[|F\cap\delta(v)|\le b(v)\qquad(v\in V(G)).\] Equivalently, its incidence vector lies in \(\{x\in\{0,1\}^{E}:x(\delta(v))\le b(v)\text{ for every }v\}\). The equality variant \(|F\cap\delta(v)|=b(v)\) for every vertex is a bipartite \(b\)-factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bipartite b-matching selects edges so that each vertex is incident with at most its prescribed integer capacity; equality at every vertex defines a b-factor.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\subseteq E\) is a \(b\)-matching exactly when \(|F\cap\delta(v)|\le b(v)\) for all \(v\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vertex-Cover Criterion for b-Transportation Existence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility characterization for b-transportations on bipartite graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be bipartite and let \(b\in\mathbb R_+^V\). A \(b\)-transportation exists if and only if \[b(C)\ge \tfrac12 b(V)\] for every vertex cover \(C\subseteq V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bipartite graph admits a b-transportation exactly when every vertex cover has total b-weight at least one half of the total vertex b-weight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\text{ a }b\text{-transportation}\iff \forall C\subseteq V\text{ that are vertex covers},\ b(C)\ge\tfrac12 b(V)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasibility criterion for bounded bipartite b-matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient subset inequalities for integral feasibility of system (21.39).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be bipartite with colour classes \(S,T\), and let \(a,b\in\mathbb Z^V\) and \(d,c\in\mathbb Z^E\) satisfy \(a\le b\) and \(d\le c\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-witness criterion for capacitated b-matchings and edge covers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between simultaneous lower-and-upper degree feasibility and two colour-class-oriented capacitated witnesses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be bipartite with colour classes \(S,T\), let \(a,b\in\mathbb Z_+^V\) satisfy \(a\le b\), and let \(c\in\mathbb Z_+^E\). There exists \(x\in\mathbb Z_+^E\) with \(x\le c\) that is both a \(b\)-matching and an \(a\)-edge cover if and only if there exist \(y,z\in\mathbb Z_+^E\) with \(y\le c\) and \(z\le c\) such that \[y(\delta(v))\le b_v,\ z(\delta(v))\ge a_v\quad(v\in S),\qquad y(\delta(v))\ge a_v,\ z(\delta(v))\le b_v\quad(v\in T).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A capacitated bipartite edge vector satisfying all lower and upper vertex-degree bounds exists exactly when two capacitated witnesses satisfy the complementary one-sided bounds on the two colour classes.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists x\in\mathbb Z_+^E:\ x\le c,\ a_v\le x(\delta(v))\le b_v\ (v\in V)\iff\exists y,z\in\mathbb Z_+^E\text{ satisfying the stated complementary colour-class bounds.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gale–Ryser Criterion for Bounded Bipartite Degrees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes binary matrices, equivalently simple bipartite graphs, whose row and column sums satisfy prescribed lower and upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a,b\in\mathbb Z_+^m\) and \(a',b'\in\mathbb Z_+^n\), with \(a\le b\), \(a'\le b'\), \(a_1\ge\cdots\ge a_m\), and \(a'_1\ge\cdots\ge a'_n\). There exists \(X\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\) satisfying \(a_i\le\sum_{j=1}^nX_{ij}\le b_i\) for every \(i\) and \(a'_j\le\sum_{i=1}^mX_{ij}\le b'_j\) for every \(j\) if and only if \(\sum_{i=1}^ka_i\le\sum_{j=1}^n\min\{k,b'_j\}\) for every \(k=1,\ldots,m\), and \(\sum_{j=1}^ka'_j\le\sum_{i=1}^m\min\{k,b_i\}\) for every \(k=1,\ldots,n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary matrix satisfying all lower and upper row- and column-sum bounds exists exactly when both stated families of Gale–Ryser inequalities hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists X\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\text{ satisfying the stated row and column bounds}\iff\left[\forall k\in\{1,\ldots,m\},\ \sum_{i=1}^ka_i\le\sum_{j=1}^n\min\{k,b'_j\}\right]\land\left[\forall k\in\{1,\ldots,n\},\ \sum_{j=1}^ka'_j\le\sum_{i=1}^m\min\{k,b_i\}\right]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimum Cardinality of a Simple Bipartite b-Edge Cover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Min–max cardinality formula under explicit per-vertex feasibility bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a bipartite graph and let \(b\in\mathbb Z_+^V\) satisfy \(b_v\leq\deg(v)\) for every \(v\in V\). Then
\[
\min\{ |F|:F\subseteq E\text{ is a simple }b\text{-edge cover of }G\}
=
\max_{X\subseteq V}\bigl(b(X)-|E[X]|\bigr).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a bipartite graph, if each nonnegative integral vertex demand is at most the vertex degree, the minimum size of a simple b-edge cover equals the maximum of b(X) minus the number of edges induced by X over all vertex subsets X.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\{|F|:F\subseteq E\text{ is a simple }b\text{-edge cover of }G\}=\max_{X\subseteq V}\{b(X)-|E[X]|\}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Min–max formula for the union of k pairwise edge-disjoint edge covers.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extremal sizes and interval property for bounded bipartite b-matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Min-max formulas and realization of every intermediate integral size for feasible solutions of system (21.39).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be bipartite and let \(a,b\in\mathbb Z^V\) and \(d,c\in\mathbb Z^E\). Assume that some \(x\in\mathbb Z^E\) satisfies \((21.39)\). Then \[\min x(E)=\max_{Z\subseteq V}\bigl(a(Z)-c(E[Z])+d(E[V\setminus Z])\bigr),\] \[\max x(E)=\min_{Z\subseteq V}\bigl(c(E[V\setminus Z])-d(E[Z])+b(Z)\bigr),\] where the extrema on the left range over integer vectors satisfying \((21.39)\). For every integer \(\tau\) between these two values, there is such a vector \(x\) with \(x(E)=\tau\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a feasible bounded bipartite b-matching system, the minimum and maximum total edge multiplicities have the stated subset formulas, and every integer size between the extrema is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\in(21.39)\cap\mathbb Z^E}x(E)=\max_{Z\subseteq V}\bigl(a(Z)-c(E[Z])+d(E[V\setminus Z])\bigr),\quad \max_{x\in(21.39)\cap\mathbb Z^E}x(E)=\min_{Z\subseteq V}\bigl(c(E[V\setminus Z])-d(E[Z])+b(Z)\bigr),\quad \forall\tau\in\mathbb Z\cap[\min x(E),\max x(E)]\ \exists x\in(21.39)\cap\mathbb Z^E:\ x(E)=\tau.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted Simple b-Edge-Cover Integral Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral min–max formulation for weighted simple b-edge covers in bipartite graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be bipartite, \(b\in\mathbb Z_+^V\), and \(w\in\mathbb Z_+^E\). The minimum \(w^\top x\) over simple \(b\)-edge covers \(x\) equals
\[
\max\left\{\sum_{v\in V}b_vy_v-\sum_{e\in E}z_e:
 y\in\mathbb Z_+^V,\ z\in\mathbb Z_+^E,\ y_u+y_v-z_e\leq w_e\ \forall e=uv\in E\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonnegative integral vertex demands and edge weights on a bipartite graph, the minimum weight of a simple b-edge cover equals the maximum integral dual objective sum b_v y_v minus sum z_e, subject to y_u+y_v-z_e being at most w_e for every edge e=uv.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\{w^\top x:x\text{ is a simple }b\text{-edge cover}\}=\max\left\{\sum_{v\in V}b_vy_v-\sum_{e\in E}z_e:y\in\mathbb Z_+^V,z\in\mathbb Z_+^E,\ y_u+y_v-z_e\leq w_e\ \forall e=uv\in E\right\}

knowledge_statements.title: General-Graph b-Matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uncapacitated vertex-capacitated matching in an arbitrary graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph, not necessarily bipartite, and let \(b:V\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\). A general-graph \(b\)-matching is an edge set \(F\subseteq E\) such that \[|F\cap\delta(v)|\le b(v)\qquad(v\in V).\] Its incidence vector belongs to \(\{x\in\{0,1\}^{E}:x(\delta(v))\le b(v)\text{ for all }v\}\). When \(b(v)=1\) for every \(v\), this definition reduces to an ordinary matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A general-graph b-matching is an edge set respecting an integer incidence capacity at every vertex; ordinary matching is the all-ones special case.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is a \(b\)-matching exactly when \(|F\cap\delta(v)|\le b(v)\) for every \(v\in V\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scoped edge-set definition is mathematically standard and the definition kind fits, but no inspectable source is supplied for the general-graph convention.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Perfect b-Matching Component Criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient component-parity condition for a perfect b-matching in an unrestricted graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(V,E)$ be a graph and $b\in\mathbb Z_+^V$. For $U\subseteq V$, let $I_U$ denote the isolated vertices of $G-U$. A perfect $b$-matching exists if and only if, for every $U\subseteq V$, the graph $G-U-I_U$ has at most $b(U)-b(I_U)$ components $K$ for which $b(K)$ is odd.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph has a perfect b-matching exactly when, for every vertex subset U, after deleting U and the isolated vertices of G minus U, the number of remaining components having odd total b-value is at most b(U) minus the b-value of those isolated vertices.
assumptions_latex: I_U\text{ is the set of isolated vertices of }G-U
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ has a perfect }b\text{-matching}\iff (\forall U\subseteq V)\ \#\{K\in\operatorname{comp}(G-U-I_U):b(K)\text{ odd}\}\le b(U)-b(I_U).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Min-max theorem for maximum-size 2b-matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A general-graph min-max characterization using 2-vertex covers and, equivalently, stable sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a graph and let \(b\in\mathbb Z_+^V\). The maximum size of a \(2b\)-matching equals \(\min\{y^\top b:y\text{ is a 2-vertex cover}\}\), and equivalently equals \(\min\{b(V)+b(N(S))-b(S):S\text{ is a stable set of }G\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximum-Size k-Matching Min-Max Formula
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Component-deletion formula for the maximum size of a constant-bound general-graph b-matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a graph and \(k\in\mathbb Z_+\). The maximum size of a \(k\)-matching equals \[\min_{U\subseteq V}\left(k|U|+\sum_K\left\lfloor\frac{k|K|}{2}\right\rfloor\right),\] where the sum ranges over the components \(K\) of \(G-U\) that span at least one edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum size of a k-matching is the minimum over vertex sets U of k|U| plus floor(k|K|/2) summed over the components K of G−U that contain an edge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nu_k(G)=\min_{U\subseteq V}\left\{k|U|+\sum_{\substack{K\in\operatorname{comp}(G-U)\\E(K)\neq\varnothing}}\left\lfloor\frac{k|K|}{2}\right\rfloor\right\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Perfect Capacitated b-Matching Existence Criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient component-parity condition for a perfect b-matching in an unrestricted graph with integral edge capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph, \(u:E(G)\to\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}\), and \(b:V(G)\to\mathbb N\). Then \((G,u)\) has a perfect \(b\)-matching if and only if, for every pair of disjoint sets \(X,Y\subseteq V(G)\), the number of connected components \(C\) of \(G-X-Y\) for which \[\sum_{c\in V(C)}b(c)+\sum_{e\in E_G(V(C),Y)}u(e)\] is odd is at most \[\sum_{v\in X}b(v)+\sum_{y\in Y}\left(\sum_{e\in\delta(y)}u(e)-b(y)\right)-\sum_{e\in E_G(X,Y)}u(e).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A capacitated graph has a perfect b-matching exactly when, for every pair of disjoint vertex sets X and Y, the number of residual components having the specified odd parity is bounded by the stated combination of the b-values and capacities incident with X and Y.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (G,u)\text{ has a perfect }b\text{-matching}\iff \forall X\cap Y=\varnothing,\quad q_b^u(G-X-Y;Y)\le b(X)+\sum_{y\in Y}\bigl(u(\delta(y))-b(y)\bigr)-u(E_G(X,Y))

knowledge_statements.statement_title: b-Matchings and Their Principal Specializations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines capacitated b-matchings in arbitrary undirected graphs and identifies their simple, perfect, matching, factor, and degree-two specializations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be an undirected graph, \(u:E(G)\to\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}\), and \(b:V(G)\to\mathbb N\). A \(b\)-matching in \((G,u)\) is a function \(f:E(G)\to\mathbb Z_+\) satisfying \(f(e)\le u(e)\) for every \(e\in E(G)\) and \(\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}f(e)\le b(v)\) for every \(v\in V(G)\). It is simple if \(u\equiv1\), and perfect if \(\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}f(e)=b(v)\) for every vertex. When \(b\equiv1\), this is ordinary matching; a simple perfect \(b\)-matching is also called a \(b\)-factor. A perfect simple \(2\)-matching is an edge set incident with every vertex exactly twice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A b-matching assigns nonnegative integer multiplicities to edges, subject to edge capacities and vertex degree bounds. Unit capacities give simple b-matchings, equality at every vertex gives perfect b-matchings, b=1 gives ordinary matchings, and simple perfect b-matchings are b-factors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is a }b\text{-matching in }(G,u)\iff f:E(G)\to\mathbb Z_+,\ f(e)\le u(e)\ \forall e,\ \sum_{e\in\delta(v)}f(e)\le b(v)\ \forall v

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unit-demand perturbation exchange for b-matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An exchange property for b-matchings when two nonnegative integral demand vectors differ by one unit in ℓ1 norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a graph, let \(b,b'\in\mathbb Z_+^V\) satisfy \(\lVert b-b'\rVert_1=1\), let \(x\) be a \(b\)-matching, and let \(x'\) be a \(b'\)-matching. Then there exists \(y\in\mathbb Z^E\) such that \(\lVert y\rVert_\infty\le 2\), \(x+y\) is a \(b'\)-matching, and \(x'-y\) is a \(b\)-matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If two nonnegative integral demand vectors differ by one unit, any corresponding b-matching and b'-matching admit an integral exchange vector bounded by two in maximum norm that swaps their demand regimes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists y\in\mathbb Z^E:\ \lVert y\rVert_\infty\le 2,\ x+y\text{ is a }b'\text{-matching},\ x'-y\text{ is a }b\text{-matching}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stable-set criterion for perfect even-demand b-matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A necessary-and-sufficient feasibility condition for perfect b-matchings when every vertex demand is even.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a graph and let \(b\in\mathbb Z_+^V\) satisfy \(b(v)\in2\mathbb Z\) for every \(v\in V\). Then there exists a perfect \(b\)-matching if and only if \(b(N(S))\ge b(S)\) for every stable set \(S\) of \(G\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: b-Matchings and the Vertex-Splitting Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines integral b-matchings in general graphs, including loop multiplicities, and the associated split graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(V,E)$ and $b\in\mathbb Z_+^V$. A $b$-matching is a vector $x\in\mathbb Z_+^E$ satisfying $x(\delta(v))\le b(v)$ for every $v\in V$, equivalently $Mx\le b$, where $M$ is the vertex-edge incidence matrix and a loop at $v$ contributes twice. The split graph $G_b=(V_b,E_b)$ has $V_b=\{q_{v,i}:v\in V,\ 1\le i\le b(v)\}$ and $E_b=\{q_{u,j}q_{v,i}:uv\in E,\ 1\le j\le b(u),\ 1\le i\le b(v),\ q_{u,j}\ne q_{v,i}\}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A b-matching is a nonnegative integral edge-multiplicity vector satisfying each vertex bound, with loops counted twice. The split graph replaces each vertex by b(v) copies and each edge by the permissible edges between the corresponding copies.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ is a }b\text{-matching}\iff x\in\mathbb Z_+^E\text{ and }Mx\le b;\quad G_b\text{ is defined as above.}

knowledge_statements.title: Bipartite-to-General Transition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of degree-relaxation integrality outside bipartite graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For bipartite \(G\), every extreme point of \[P_b(G)=\{x\in[0,1]^E:x(\delta(v))\le b(v)\text{ for all }v\}\] is integral when \(b\) is integral. This fails for general graphs: on a triangle with \(b(v)=1\) at every vertex, the vector \(x_e=\tfrac12\) for all three edges is an extreme feasible point. It is excluded by the blossom inequality \(x(E(V))\le1\), illustrating why general-graph formulations require odd-set inequalities beyond degree constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bipartite degree relaxations are integral, but a half-valued triangle is fractional in general graphs; odd-set inequalities repair the missing structure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Bipartiteness ensures integrality of \(P_b(G)\); without it, degree constraints alone need not describe the \(b\)-matching polytope.

knowledge_statements.title: Simple b-Matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edge-simple, degree-upper-bounded b-matchings in a finite loopless graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite loopless graph and let \(b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^{V}\). A simple \(b\)-matching is a set \(M\subseteq E\) satisfying \[|M\cap\delta(v)|\le b_v\qquad(v\in V).\] Equivalently, its incidence vector \(x\in\{0,1\}^{E}\) satisfies \(x(\delta(v))\le b_v\) for every \(v\in V\). Thus each edge may be selected at most once, while a vertex may be incident with as many as \(b_v\) selected edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simple b-matching selects each edge at most once and selects at most b_v edges incident with every vertex v.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\subseteq E\) is feasible exactly when \(|M\cap\delta(v)|\le b_v\) for all \(v\in V\).

notation.meaning: set of edges incident with vertex v

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Min–max formula for maximum simple k-matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum-cardinality simple matchings with vertex degrees bounded by a constant k in a general graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a graph and \(k\in\mathbb Z_+\). The maximum size of a simple \(k\)-matching equals \[\min_{\substack{U,W\subseteq V\\U\cap W=\varnothing}}\left(k|U|+|E[W]|+\sum_{K\in\operatorname{comp}(G-U-W)}\left\lfloor\frac{k|K|+|E[K,W]|}{2}\right\rfloor\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a graph G and positive integer k, the maximum size of a simple k-matching equals the minimum, over disjoint vertex sets U and W, of k|U| plus the number of edges within W plus, for every component K of G−U−W, the floor of half of k|K| plus the number of edges between K and W.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max\{|F|:F\text{ is a simple }k\text{-matching of }G\}=\min_{\substack{U,W\subseteq V\\U\cap W=\varnothing}}\left(k|U|+|E[W]|+\sum_{K\in\operatorname{comp}(G-U-W)}\left\lfloor\frac{k|K|+|E[K,W]|}{2}\right\rfloor\right)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Component-parity characterization of k-factors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient condition for a graph to possess a spanning k-regular subgraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a graph and \(k\in\mathbb Z_+\). Then \(G\) has a \(k\)-factor if and only if, for every partition \(V=T\mathbin{\dot\cup}U\mathbin{\dot\cup}W\), the number of components \(K\) of \(G[T]\) for which \(k|K|+|E[K,W]|\) is odd is at most \[k(|U|-|W|)+2|E[W]|+|E[T,W]|.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph has a k-factor exactly when, for every partition of its vertices into T, U, and W, the number of components K of G[T] for which k|K| plus the number of edges from K to W is odd does not exceed k(|U|−|W|), twice the number of edges within W, plus the number of edges between T and W.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ has a }k\text{-factor}\iff \forall(T,U,W),\ \#\{K\in\operatorname{comp}(G[T]):k|K|+|E[K,W]|\text{ is odd}\}\le k(|U|-|W|)+2|E[W]|+|E[T,W]|

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Simple b-Matchings and b-Factors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions of simple b-matchings and their perfect members.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\), \(b\in\mathbb Z_+^V\), and let \(x\) be a \(b\)-matching. The \(b\)-matching \(x\) is simple if \(x\in\{0,1\}^E\). Equivalently, it is the incidence vector \(\chi^F\) of an edge set \(F\subseteq E\) satisfying \(\deg_F(v)\le b(v)\) for every \(v\in V\). Simple \(b\)-matchings are precisely capacitated \(b\)-matchings with capacity function \(c=\mathbf 1\). A simple perfect \(b\)-matching is called a \(b\)-factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simple b-matching is a 0–1 b-matching, equivalently an edge set whose degree at each vertex is at most b(v). It is the unit-capacity case of capacitated b-matching. A simple perfect b-matching is a b-factor.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ is simple}\iff x\in\{0,1\}^E\iff x=\chi^F\text{ for some }F\subseteq E\text{ with }\deg_F(v)\le b(v)\ \forall v;\quad x\text{ is a }b\text{-factor if it is also perfect}.

knowledge_statements.title: Capacitated b-Matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer edge-multiplicity model with vertex and edge capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite loopless graph, \(b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^{V}\), and \(u\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^{E}\). A capacitated \(b\)-matching is a vector \(x\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^{E}\) such that \[x(\delta(v))\le b_v\quad(v\in V),\qquad x_e\le u_e\quad(e\in E).\] The integer \(x_e\) is the multiplicity with which edge \(e\) is used. The model permits repeated use precisely when \(u_e>1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A capacitated b-matching assigns each edge an integer multiplicity bounded by its edge capacity while respecting every vertex capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is feasible exactly when \(x\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^{E}\), \(x(\delta(v))\le b_v\), and \(x_e\le u_e\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximum-Size Capacitated b-Matching Min–Max Formula
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Min–max characterization of the maximum size of a capacitated b-matching in a general graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\), \(b\in\mathbb Z_+^V\), and \(c\in\mathbb Z_+^E\) with \(c>\mathbf0\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Perfect Capacitated b-Matching Criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary-and-sufficient component-parity condition for a perfect capacitated b-matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\), \(b\in\mathbb Z_+^V\), and \(c\in\mathbb Z_+^E\) with \(c>\mathbf0\). Then \(G\) has a perfect \(b\)-matching \(x\le c\) if and only if, for every partition \((T,U,W)\) of \(V\), the number of components \(K\) of \(G[T]\) such that \(b(K)+c(E[K,W])\) is odd is at most \[b(U)-b(W)+2c(E[W])+c(E[T,W]).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A perfect capacity-bounded b-matching exists exactly when every partition of the vertices into T, U, and W satisfies the stated bound on the parity-odd components of G[T].
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\text{ a perfect }b\text{-matching }x\le c\iff\forall(T,U,W)\text{ partitioning }V,\ \left|\{K\in\operatorname{comp}(G[T]):b(K)+c(E[K,W])\text{ is odd}\}\right|\le b(U)-b(W)+2c(E[W])+c(E[T,W])

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity-Model Transition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence through unit capacities and parallel-edge expansion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite loopless graph \(G=(V,E)\), the simple \(b\)-matchings are exactly the capacitated \(b\)-matchings with \(u_e=1\) for every \(e\in E\). More generally, replace each edge \(e\) by \(u_e\) parallel labeled copies of the same weight. Projection by \[x_e=\sum_{i=1}^{u_e}y_{e,i}\] maps simple \(b\)-matchings of the expanded multigraph onto capacitated \(b\)-matchings of \(G\), preserves all vertex degrees, and preserves linear objective values when every copy inherits the weight of \(e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unit edge capacities recover simple b-matchings; replacing an edge by capacity-many parallel copies converts the capacitated model into a simple multigraph model.
assumptions_latex: Parallel labeled edges are allowed in the expanded graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_e=\sum_{i=1}^{u_e}y_{e,i}\) gives a degree- and weight-preserving surjection between the two feasible families.

notation.meaning: indicator of the i-th parallel copy of e
projected multiplicity of original edge e

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The unit-capacity specialization and parallel-copy projection are mathematically plausible and fit the representation leaf, but no citation supports the stated surjection and preservation claims.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted b-Matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear optimization over a specified b-matching feasibility regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) carry weights \(w\in\mathbb R^{E}\), and let \(\mathcal B\subseteq\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{E}\) be the feasible family of simple or capacitated \(b\)-matchings under the chosen convention. A maximum-weight \(b\)-matching is any \(x^\star\in\mathcal B\) satisfying \[w^\top x^\star=\max\{w^\top x:x\in\mathcal B\}.\] For the minimum-weight version, replace the maximum by a minimum. Negative weights are permitted unless an additional cardinality or degree-equality requirement changes whether unused edges are admissible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted b-matching optimizes the sum of selected edge weights over the chosen simple or capacitated b-matching family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in\mathcal B} w^\top x\).

knowledge_statements.title: Bipartite b-Matching Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uncapacitated integer-multiplicity b-matching polytope for bipartite graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(L\cup R,E)\) be a finite bipartite graph, let \(V=L\cup R\), and let \(b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^{V}\). The convex hull of its integer-multiplicity \(b\)-matchings is \[P_b(G)=\{x\in\mathbb R_{\ge 0}^{E}:x(\delta(v))\le b_v\ \text{for every }v\in V\}.\] In particular, the vertex-edge incidence matrix of a bipartite graph is totally unimodular, so every vertex of this polyhedron is integral for integral \(b\); no odd-set inequalities are required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For bipartite graphs, nonnegativity and vertex-degree bounds completely describe the integer b-matching polytope.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(L\cup R,E)\) is finite and bipartite, with \(V=L\cup R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_b(G)=\operatorname{conv}\{x\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^{E}:x(\delta(v))\le b_v\text{ for all }v\in V\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: General-Graph b-Matching Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uncapacitated integer-multiplicity formulation with odd-set inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be finite and loopless and let \(b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^{V}\). knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed system equals \(\operatorname{conv}\{x\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^{E}:x(\delta(v))\le b_v\text{ for all }v\in V\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Capacitated General-Graph b-Matching Polytope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extracted inequality characterization for b-matchings with integral edge capacities in an unrestricted undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be an undirected graph, \(u:E(G)\to\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}\), and \(b:V(G)\to\mathbb N\). The \(b\)-matching polytope of \((G,u)\) is the set of \(x\in\mathbb R_+^{E(G)}\) satisfying \[\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e\le b(v)\qquad(v\in V(G))\] and, for every \(X\subseteq V(G)\) and \(F\subseteq\delta(X)\), \[\sum_{e\in E(G[X])}x_e+\sum_{e\in F}x_e\le\left\lfloor\frac12\left(\sum_{v\in X}b(v)+\sum_{e\in F}u(e)\right)\right\rfloor.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The extracted capacitated characterization describes the general-graph b-matching polytope by nonnegativity, vertex degree bounds, and inequalities indexed by a vertex subset together with a selected subset of its cut edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_b(G,u)=\left\{x\in\mathbb R_+^{E(G)}:\ x(\delta(v))\le b(v)\ \forall v,\quad x(E(G[X]))+x(F)\le\left\lfloor\frac{b(X)+u(F)}2\right\rfloor\ \forall X\subseteq V(G),\ F\subseteq\delta(X)\right\}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of the b-factor polytope and its face property.

knowledge_statements.title: Total Dual Integrality for b-Matching Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: TDI criterion for a chosen rational b-matching inequality system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A rational inequality system \(Ax\le d\) describing a \(b\)-matching polyhedron is totally dual integral if, for every integral objective vector \(c\in\mathbb Z^{E}\) for which the primal optimum is finite, the dual program \[\min\{d^\top y:A^\top y=c,\ y\ge0\}\] has an integral optimal solution \(y\). When additionally \(d\) is integral, total dual integrality implies that the polyhedron \(\{x:Ax\le d\}\) is integral. TDI is a property of the displayed system, not merely of the polyhedron it represents.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A b-matching inequality system is TDI when every finite dual with an integral objective admits an integral optimal multiplier vector.
assumptions_latex: \(c\in\mathbb Z^{E}\) and the corresponding primal optimum is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax\le d\) is TDI exactly when the displayed dual has an integral optimum for every such \(c\).

knowledge_statements.title: Expansion Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parallel-copy expansion of integral edge capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite capacitated instance \((G,b,u,w)\). For each edge \(e\in E\), create \(u_e\) labeled parallel copies, each having the endpoints and weight of \(e\); retain every vertex bound \(b_v\). Solve the resulting simple \(b\)-matching instance and output \(x_e=\sum_{i=1}^{u_e}y_{e,i}\). Conversely, represent any feasible \(x\) by choosing \(x_e\) copies of each edge. The reduction preserves feasibility and objective value, but its expanded size is \(\sum_{e\in E}u_e\), so it is generally pseudopolynomial when capacities are binary encoded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expand each capacity-u edge into u parallel copies, solve a simple b-matching instance, and project selected copies back to edge multiplicities.
assumptions_latex: The target matching model permits parallel labeled edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w^\top x=\sum_{e\in E}\sum_{i=1}^{u_e}w_e y_{e,i}\), with expanded edge count \(\sum_{e\in E}u_e\).

notation.meaning: selection indicator for copy i of edge e

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The expansion algorithm and pseudopolynomial binary-encoding boundary are plausible and well stated, but no source supports either the exact reduction or its complexity qualification.

children.title: Vertex-Splitting Reductions
children.top_down_role: Vertex-splitting transformations for degree-capacity structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Vertex-Splitting Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of uncapacitated multiplicity b-matchings to ordinary matchings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite loopless graph \(G=(V,E)\) and \(b\in\mathbb Z_{ge0}^{V}\), replace each vertex \(v\) by labeled slots \(v^1,\ldots,v^{b_v}\). For every edge \(e=uv\), join every pair \(u^i v^j\) and give the new edge weight \(w_e\). Any ordinary matching \(M'\) projects to \(x_e\), the number of selected slot edges originating from \(e\); then \(x(\delta(v))\le b_v\). Conversely, every integer-multiplicity \(b\)-matching admits such a slot assignment. The projection preserves weight, although the construction may have \(\sum_{uv\in E}b_u b_v\) edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Split each vertex into b_v unit slots and connect compatible slot pairs; ordinary matchings then project exactly to uncapacitated integer-multiplicity b-matchings.
assumptions_latex: \(b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{V}\); repeated use of an original edge is allowed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_e=|M'\cap\{u^iv^j:1\le i\le b_u,\ 1\le j\le b_v\}|\) preserves feasibility and total weight.

notation.meaning: ordinary matching in the split graph
number of matched slot edges representing e

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The slot construction is coherent for the explicitly stated integer-multiplicity model and the representation kind fits the reduction leaf, but the exact bidirectional correspondence and size bound have no citation.

children.title: Ordinary-Matching Reductions
children.top_down_role: Reductions from b-matching instances to ordinary matching instances.

assumptions_latex: \(b:V\to\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) satisfies \(b(v)\le d_G(v)\) for every \(v\in V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) has a \(b\)-factor if and only if \(H_b\) has a perfect matching.

notation.meaning: Incidence-slack expansion of the input graph
Degree of vertex v in G

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incidence-slack reduction of exact \(b\)-factors to perfect matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every incidence \((v,e)\), create a vertex \(v_e\). For each edge \(e=uv\), add the edge \(u_ev_e\). For every \(v\), create \(d_G(v)-b(v)\) slack vertices and join each of them to every incidence vertex \(v_e\). Call the resulting graph \(H_b\). Then \(G\) contains a spanning subgraph \(F\) with \(d_F(v)=b(v)\) for all \(v\) if and only if \(H_b\) has a perfect matching. Under this correspondence, \(e=uv\) belongs to \(F\) exactly when \(u_ev_e\) belongs to the perfect matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact b-factor is encoded as a perfect matching by pairing selected edge incidences together and unmatched incidences with vertex-specific slack vertices.
knowledge_statements.title: Ordinary-Matching Reductions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The construction and equivalence are mathematically coherent, and representation is appropriate for this reduction leaf. However, the nontrivial reduction has no cited source or standard-field rationale, so its exact construction and attribution require an inspectable reference.

children.title: Reduction Fidelity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions under which transformation-based representations preserve the relevant instance structure.

assumptions_latex: The original graph is finite and simple, and each edge has unit multiplicity.
A proposed expansion represents an original edge only by edges between endpoint clones.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Clone expansion alone need not preserve the constraints \(x_e\le 1\), so its matchings need not project to feasible simple \(b\)-matchings.

notation.meaning: Multiplicity assigned to original edge e by projection

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of naive clone-only reductions for unit-capacity edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) consist of one edge \(e=uv\), with \(b(u)=b(v)=2\). Replacing each endpoint by two clones and replacing \(e\) by all four clone-to-clone edges produces \(K_{2,2}\), which has a matching of size \(2\). Projecting both matched clone edges back to \(e\) gives \(x_e=2\), although a simple \(b\)-matching requires \(x_e\in\{0,1\}\). Thus clone expansion is faithful only when additional gadgets or multiplicity conventions enforce one use per original edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Naively cloning endpoints can select one original unit-capacity edge multiple times; an edge gadget or an explicit multiplicity model is required.
knowledge_statements.title: Reduction Fidelity Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample correctly shows that a complete clone expansion can project two matching edges onto one unit-capacity original edge, and failure_boundary is the correct content kind. The record nevertheless supplies no evidence for the stated general fidelity boundary or its reduction context.

assumptions_latex: Every edge is represented as a bidirected link entering both of its endpoints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The integral solutions of \(Ax\le b\), \(0\le x\le 1\), are precisely the incidence vectors of simple \(b\)-matchings of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: All-inward bidirected representation of simple capacitated \(b\)-matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Orient every end of every edge of \(G\) inward, producing a bidirected graph whose incidence matrix \(A\) has \(A_{ve}=1\) when \(v\) is incident with \(e\), and \(A_{ve}=0\) otherwise. For \(b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^{V}\), an integral vector \(x\) is the incidence vector of a simple \(b\)-matching exactly when \(0\le x_e\le 1\) for every \(e\in E\) and \(Ax\le b\). Replacing the last inequality by \(Ax=b\) represents exact \(b\)-factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Viewing each ordinary edge as entering both endpoints makes the bidirected degree constraints exactly the usual b-matching or b-factor constraints.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: b-Factors and Bipartite Flow Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines b-factors, identifies the uniform degree-one and degree-two cases, and records the stated bipartite flow reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) and \(b\in\mathbf Z^V\). A \(b\)-factor is a set \(M\subseteq E\) such that \(|M\cap\delta(v)|=b_v\) for every \(v\in V\). A \(1\)-factor is a perfect matching, while a \(2\)-factor is a collection of circuits covering every vertex exactly once. The minimum-weight \(2\)-factor problem is a relaxation of the traveling-salesman problem. If \(G\) is bipartite, existence of a \(b\)-factor can be decided by network-flow methods, and a minimum-weight \(b\)-factor can be found as a minimum-cost-flow problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A b-factor selects edges so that each vertex has exactly its prescribed incident degree. Degree one gives a perfect matching and degree two gives a vertex-covering collection of circuits. Minimum-weight 2-factor relaxes TSP; for bipartite graphs, feasibility and minimum weight reduce to flow and minimum-cost flow, respectively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\subseteq E,\qquad |M\cap\delta(v)|=b_v\quad\forall v\in V

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Perfect f-Matching and Its Relation to f-Factors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines perfect f-matchings, characterizes f-factors by the additional unit-capacity restriction, and records the parallel-edge representation and unit-demand equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph and let \(f:V(G)\to\mathbb Z\). A perfect \(f\)-matching is an assignment \(x:E(G)\to\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) such that \(\sum_{e\ni v}x(e)=f(v)\) for every \(v\in V(G)\). The \(f\)-factors are exactly the perfect \(f\)-matchings satisfying \(x(e)\le 1\) for every \(e\in E(G)\). Equivalently, such an \(x\) represents a graph \(G'\) with vertex set \(V(G)\), whose edges are parallel copies of edges of \(G\), and with \(\deg_{G'}(v)=f(v)\) for every vertex. If \(f(v)=1\) for every vertex, the perfect \(f\)-matching and \(f\)-factor problems are equivalent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A perfect f-matching assigns a nonnegative integer multiplicity to each edge so that the incident multiplicities at every vertex sum to its prescribed value. It is an f-factor exactly when every multiplicity is at most one. It may equivalently be viewed as a graph made from parallel copies of the original edges and having the prescribed degrees. Under unit demands, it is equivalent to a perfect matching or one-factor.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ is a perfect }f\text{-matching}\iff \forall v\in V(G),\ \sum_{e\ni v}x(e)=f(v);\qquad x\text{ corresponds to an }f\text{-factor}\iff \forall e\in E(G),\ x(e)\le 1.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: 2-Factors and the Hamiltonian-Tour Lower Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of a 2-factor and its immediate lower-bound relationship to minimum-weight Hamiltonian tours.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an edge-weighted undirected graph. A set \(S\subseteq E\) is a 2-factor of \(G\) if \(|S\cap\delta_G(v)|=2\) for every \(v\in V\). Every Hamiltonian tour of \(G\) is a 2-factor; hence, if \(G\) has a Hamiltonian tour, \[\min\{w(S):S\text{ is a 2-factor of }G\}\leq \min\{w(H):H\text{ is a Hamiltonian tour of }G\}.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Critical lower–upper degree factor graph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines criticality through the canonical decomposition and records the stated complementary-bound consequence and deficiency characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph and let \(f,g:V(G)\to\mathbb Z\). The graph \(G\) is \((f,g)\)-critical if it is connected and \(A=B=C=\varnothing\). For such a graph, \(f=\widehat g\). Moreover, \(G\) is \((f,g)\)-critical if and only if it is connected and, for every \(v\in V(G)\), \[\delta(f^v,g)<\delta(f,g)\quad\text{and}\quad\delta(f,g^v)<\delta(f,g).\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: H-factor definition and tractability boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-family factors, the perfect-matching specialization, and the stated fixed-family complexity classifications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a family of connected graphs. An \(\mathcal H\)-factor of \(G\) is a spanning subgraph of \(G\) whose components are isomorphic to members of \(\mathcal H\). Every graph has a \(\{K_1\}\)-factor, and a \(\{K_2\}\)-factor is a perfect matching. For a fixed connected graph \(F\not\cong K_1,K_2\), deciding whether \(G\) has a \(\{F\}\)-factor is NP-complete. If \(\mathcal H=\{K_2\}\cup\mathcal H'\), where \(\mathcal H'\) is any finite family of factor-critical graphs, the \(\mathcal H\)-factor problem is polynomial-time solvable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An H-factor is a spanning subgraph whose components have types from H. The K2 case is perfect matching. Every other nontrivial fixed singleton component type gives an NP-complete problem, while K2 together with finitely many factor-critical component types gives a polynomial-time problem.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal H\text{ is a family of connected graphs}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{F\}\text{-Factor is NP-complete for fixed connected }F\not\cong K_1,K_2;\qquad \left(\{K_2\}\cup\mathcal H'\right)\text{-Factor is polynomial-time solvable when }\mathcal H'\text{ is finite and every member is factor-critical}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The maximum-weight \(f\)-factor problem is
\[\max\left\{\sum_{e\in E}w(e)x_e:\ x\in\{0,1\}^{E},\ \sum_{e\in\delta_G(v)}x_e=f(v)\ \text{for every }v\in V\right\}.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower–Upper Degree-Constrained Subgraph Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines degree-constrained subgraph optimization with vertexwise lower and upper degree bounds, including its matching reduction and exact-degree specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a graph $G=(V,E)$, an objective on its subgraphs, and permissible degree bounds $\ell_v\le u_v$ for each $v\in V$, the lower–upper degree-constrained subgraph problem seeks an optimal subgraph $H\subseteq G$ such that $\ell_v\le d_H(v)\le u_v$ for every $v\in V$. When no restrictions other than these degree bounds are imposed, the problem is reducible to ordinary matching. If $\ell_v=u_v$ for every $v$, the resulting exact-degree problem is called a factor problem. Nonbipartite matching is a special case of this problem family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower–upper degree-constrained subgraph problem seeks an optimal subgraph whose degree at each vertex lies between prescribed bounds. When these are the only restrictions, the problem reduces to ordinary matching. Equal lower and upper bounds give a factor problem, and nonbipartite matching is a special case of the broader family.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A compatibility principle for lower–upper degree factors in a bipartite graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(S,T;E)$ have lower and upper degree bounds $f\le g$. Every finite \(2k\)-regular multigraph \(G\) admits a decomposition

where each \(F_i\) is a spanning \(2\)-regular subgraph of \(G\). Equivalently, every even-regular multigraph has a two-factor, and repeatedly deleting such a factor yields a partition into two-factors. The statement uses the multigraph version of the Petersen factor theorem family.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Disjoint-set parity criterion for exact \(f\)-factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For disjoint \(S,T\subseteq V\), let \(q_f(S,T)\) be the number of components \(C\) of \(G-(S\cup T)\) for which \(f(C)+e_G(C,T)\) is odd, and define
\[\Delta_f(S,T)=f(S)+\sum_{v\in T}d_{G-S}(v)-f(T)-q_f(S,T).\]
Then \(G\) has an \(f\)-factor if and only if \(\Delta_f(S,T)\ge 0\) for every disjoint pair \(S,T\). Moreover, each \(\Delta_f(S,T)\) has the same parity as \(f(V)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An f-factor exists exactly when every disjoint vertex-set pair satisfies Tutte's degree-and-parity deficiency inequality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tutte f-Factor Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient component-parity inequalities for the existence of a prescribed-degree factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G\) be a graph and let \(f:V(G)\to\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) satisfy \(f(v)\le \deg_G(v)\) for every \(v\in V(G)\), with \(\widehat f(v)=\deg_G(v)-f(v)\). Then \(G\) has an \(f\)-factor if and only if, for every pair of disjoint sets \(X,Y\subseteq V(G)\),
\[
\left|\left\{K\in\operatorname{comp}(G-X-Y): f(V(K))+|\nabla(V(K),Y)|\equiv 1\pmod 2\right\}\right|
\le f(X)+\widehat f(Y)-|\nabla(X,Y)|.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Let f assign each vertex a nonnegative prescribed degree not exceeding its degree in G, and define f-hat(v)=deg_G(v)−f(v). The graph G has an f-factor exactly when, for every two disjoint vertex sets X and Y, the number of components K of G−X−Y for which f(V(K))+|∇(V(K),Y)| is odd is at most f(X)+f-hat(Y)−|∇(X,Y)|.

knowledge_statements.title: Factor Deficiency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tutte deficiency for prescribed-degree factors in finite undirected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be finite, let \(f:V\to\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) satisfy \(f(v)\le d_G(v)\), and assume \(f(V)\) is even. For disjoint \(S,T\subseteq V\), let \(q_f(S,T)\) count the components \(C\) of \(G-(S\cup T)\) for which \(f(C)+|E(C,T)|\) is odd, and set \[\delta_f(S,T)=f(S)-f(T)+\sum_{v\in T}d_{G-S}(v)-q_f(S,T).\] The Tutte \(f\)-factor deficiency is \[\operatorname{def}_f(G)=\max\bigl\{0,\max_{S\cap T=\varnothing}(-\delta_f(S,T))\bigr\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Factor deficiency is the greatest violation, over disjoint vertex sets, of the Tutte inequalities governing existence of a spanning subgraph with degrees exactly f.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{def}_f(G)\) is a nonnegative integer measuring the maximum violated Tutte \(f\)-factor inequality.

notation.meaning: The sum of f(v) over vertices v in X.
Number of parity-obstructing components outside S union T.
Degree of v after deleting S.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula is a plausible maximum-violation convention for the Tutte f-factor inequalities, but no inspectable source establishes that this normalization is called the f-factor deficiency.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence of an upper-bound-normalized optimal (f,g)-subgraph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A normal-form existence result for minimum-deficiency generalized factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G be a graph and let f,g satisfy f,g\ge 0 and f+g\ge\deg_G pointwise. Then there exists an (f,g)-optimal spanning subgraph H such that \deg_H(v)\le f(v) for every v\in V(G).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonnegative f and g whose sum dominates the vertex degrees of G, some minimum-deficiency spanning subgraph satisfies every f upper bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists H:\ \delta(H;f,g)=\delta(f,g)\ \text{and}\ \deg_H\le f.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Min–Max Formula for \((f,g)\)-Factor Deficiency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Min–max characterization of \((f,g)\)-factor deficiency, using the section's definitions of \(\delta(f,g)\), \(\tau(X,Y)\), and \(\nabla(X,Y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G\) be a graph and let \(f,g:V(G)\to\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) satisfy \(f(v)+g(v)\ge \deg_G(v)\) for every \(v\in V(G)\). Then
\[
\delta(f,g)=\max_{\substack{X,Y\subseteq V(G)\\X\cap Y=\varnothing}}\left\{\tau(X,Y)+|\nabla(X,Y)|-f(X)-g(Y)\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonnegative integer-valued vertex functions f and g whose pointwise sum dominates the vertex degrees, the (f,g)-factor deficiency equals the maximum, over all disjoint vertex sets X and Y, of the number of contextually defined (X,Y)-odd components plus the number of edges between X and Y, minus f(X) and g(Y).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \delta(f,g)=\max_{\substack{X,Y\subseteq V(G)\\X\cap Y=\varnothing}}\left\{\tau(X,Y)+|\nabla(X,Y)|-f(X)-g(Y)\right\}

knowledge_statements.title: Factor Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Barriers witnessing or maximizing violations of Tutte’s prescribed-degree inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the preceding finite-graph and parity conventions, an ordered pair of disjoint sets \((S,T)\) is an \(f\)-barrier if \(\delta_f(S,T)<0\), where \[\delta_f(S,T)=f(S)-f(T)+\sum_{v\in T}d_{G-S}(v)-q_f(S,T).\] It is a maximum \(f\)-barrier if \(-\delta_f(S,T)=\operatorname{def}_f(G)\). Thus every \(f\)-barrier identifies a parity-and-cut obstruction to an \(f\)-factor, while a maximum barrier attains the largest such obstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An f-barrier is a disjoint pair of vertex sets violating a Tutte f-factor inequality; a maximum barrier realizes the graph’s factor deficiency.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_f(S,T)<0\) certifies that \(G\) has no \(f\)-factor.

notation.meaning: Tutte deficiency expression for the ordered pair (S,T).
Number of parity-obstructing components of the remaining graph.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The obstruction implication is mathematically plausible, but the definition of every negatively valued pair as an f-barrier and the maximum-barrier convention require an authoritative locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Odd components relative to disjoint vertex sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the parity-sensitive components counted in lower–upper factor obstruction formulas and records their symmetry and canonical-decomposition specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph, let \(f,g:V(G)\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), and let \(X,Y\subseteq V(G)\) be disjoint. A connected component \(K\) of \(G-X-Y\) is \((X,Y)\)-odd with respect to \((f,g)\) if \[f(v)=\widehat g(v)\quad\text{for every }v\in V(K),\] and \[f(V(K))+|\nabla(V(K),Y)|\equiv1\pmod2.\] This is equivalent to \(K\) being \((Y,X)\)-odd with respect to \((g,f)\). Let \(\tau(X,Y)\) denote the number of \((X,Y)\)-odd components. Every connected component of \(G[D]\) is \((A,B)\)-odd, and hence \[\tau(A,B)=\#\operatorname{comp}(G[D]).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An (X,Y)-odd component is a component outside disjoint sets X and Y on which the bounds are complementary and whose total f-value plus its number of edges to Y is odd. The definition is symmetric under swapping X with Y and f with g. At the canonical pair (A,B), the count equals the number of D-components.
assumptions_latex: K\text{ is a connected component of }G-X-Y
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K\text{ is }(X,Y)\text{-odd w.r.t. }(f,g)\iff\left(\forall v\in V(K),\ f(v)=\widehat g(v)\right)\land\left(f(V(K))+|\nabla(V(K),Y)|\equiv1\pmod2\right);\quad K\text{ is }(X,Y)\text{-odd w.r.t. }(f,g)\iff K\text{ is }(Y,X)\text{-odd w.r.t. }(g,f);\quad \tau(A,B)=\#\operatorname{comp}(G[D])

knowledge_statements.title: Deficiency–Barrier Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infeasibility certificates supplied by violated Tutte inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) and \(f:V\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) satisfy the stated feasibility and parity assumptions. A certificate of nonexistence of an \(f\)-factor is a disjoint pair \((S,T)\) together with the component list defining \(q_f(S,T)\), such that \[q_f(S,T)>f(S)-f(T)+\sum_{v\in T}d_{G-S}(v).\] Every quantity in this inequality is computable directly from \(G,f,S,T\). Tutte’s \(f\)-factor criterion asserts that such a certificate exists exactly when \(G\) has no \(f\)-factor; a maximum certificate has violation \(\operatorname{def}_f(G)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A violated Tutte inequality, with its parity-obstructing components listed, is a directly checkable certificate that no f-factor exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) has an \(f\)-factor if and only if no deficiency–barrier certificate exists.

notation.meaning: Disjoint vertex sets forming the certificate.
Count of components satisfying the defining odd-parity condition.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind fits the leaf, but the asserted equivalence is Tutte's f-factor theorem and requires a source with a specific theorem or section locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Factor Canonical Decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decomposition induced by edges occurring in prescribed-degree factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a finite graph \(G=(V,E)\), a demand \(f:V\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), and the nonempty family \(\mathcal F_f(G)\) of all \(f\)-factors. Call an edge \(f\)-allowed if it belongs to some \(F\in\mathcal F_f(G)\), and let \(G_f=(V,E_f)\) be the spanning subgraph of all allowed edges. The canonical allowed-edge decomposition is the partition of \(V\) into the connected components of \(G_f\). Every \(f\)-factor uses only edges within these components, and each allowed edge is realized by at least one \(f\)-factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The allowed-edge decomposition partitions the vertices into components connected by edges that occur in at least one f-factor.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The connected components of \(G_f\) form a uniquely determined partition associated with \((G,f)\).

notation.meaning: Family of all f-factors of G.
Edges occurring in at least one f-factor.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Allowed-edge connected components give a well-defined factor-component decomposition, but the broad title may denote a finer canonical decomposition. An authoritative definition is needed to resolve the intended local sense.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotonicity of Canonical Classes Under Ordered Parameters
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The sets \(A(f,g),B(f,g),D(f,g)\) retain their source-defined meanings in the canonical structure of (f,g)-optimal subgraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph and let \(f_1,f_2,g_1,g_2:V(G)\to\mathbb Z\). If \(f_1\leq f_2\), \(g_1\leq g_2\), and \(f_1+g_1\geq\deg_G\), then \(A(f_1,g_1)\supseteq A(f_2,g_2)\), \(B(f_1,g_1)\supseteq B(f_2,g_2)\), and \(D(f_1,g_1)\supseteq D(f_2,g_2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When both integer-valued parameter functions increase pointwise and the first pair's sum dominates the vertex degrees, each canonical class A, B, and D can only shrink.

knowledge_statements.title: Tutte Reduction to Perfect Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unweighted gadget reduction from exact prescribed degrees to perfect matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(G=(V,E)\) and \(f:V\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) with \(f(v)\le d_G(v)\), create one incidence vertex \((v,e)\) for every \(e\in\delta_G(v)\). For each \(v\), create \(d_G(v)-f(v)\) dummy vertices and join each to every incidence vertex at \(v\). For every edge \(e=uv\), join \((u,e)\) to \((v,e)\). Compute a perfect matching \(M\) in the resulting graph. Output \[F=\{e=uv:(u,e)(v,e)\in M\}.\] If no perfect matching exists, report that no \(f\)-factor exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An incidence-and-dummy gadget converts f-factor existence into perfect-matching existence, with cross-gadget matching edges selecting the factor.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite undirected loopless graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The auxiliary graph has a perfect matching if and only if \(G\) has an \(f\)-factor, and the displayed extraction maps one to the other.

notation.meaning: Set of edges incident with v.
Perfect matching in the auxiliary graph.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Perfect 2-Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and equivalent spanning-structure descriptions for a finite graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite graph with $p=|V|$, and let $x$ be a $2$-matching. It is perfect if $\sum_{e\ni v}x_e=2$ for every $v\in V$. Equivalently, $x$ is perfect if and only if its size is $p$. Such a perfect $2$-matching exists exactly when $G$ contains vertex-disjoint cycles and edges whose vertex sets cover $V$; this spanning system is also called a $q$-factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a finite graph with p vertices, a 2-matching is perfect when the total edge weight incident with every vertex equals 2. Equivalently, its size is p. Existence of a perfect 2-matching is equivalent to the existence of vertex-disjoint cycles and edges covering every vertex, called a q-factor.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ is perfect}\iff (\forall v\in V)\ \sum_{e\ni v}x_e=2\iff |x|=p;\quad G\text{ has such an }x\iff G\text{ has a spanning vertex-disjoint union of cycles and edges.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Double-subdivision reduction of f-factors to perfect f-matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of f-factor existence to perfect f-matching existence on a twice-subdivided graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph and let \(f:V(G)\to\mathbb Z\). Construct \(G''\) by subdividing each edge of \(G\) with two new vertices, and extend \(f\) to \(V(G'')\) by setting \(f(x)=1\) at every new vertex \(x\). Then \(G''\) has a perfect \(f\)-matching if and only if \(G\) has an \(f\)-factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subdivide every edge of G with two new vertices and assign demand 1 to each new vertex. The resulting graph has a perfect f-matching if and only if the original graph has an f-factor.
assumptions_latex: G''\text{ is obtained by subdividing every edge of }G\text{ with two new vertices}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G''\text{ has a perfect }f\text{-matching}\iff G\text{ has an }f\text{-factor}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clone-expansion reduction of perfect f-matching to perfect matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of perfect f-matching existence to ordinary perfect-matching existence by replacing each vertex with the prescribed number of clones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph and let \(f:V(G)\to\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\). For each \(v\in V(G)\), let \(U_v\) be a set of \(f(v)\) elements, with the sets \(U_v\) pairwise disjoint. Define \(G'\) on \(\bigcup_{v\in V(G)}U_v\) by joining every element of \(U_v\) to every element of \(U_w\) whenever \(vw\in E(G)\). Then \(G'\) has a perfect matching if and only if \(G\) has a perfect \(f\)-matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace every vertex v by f(v) clones and completely join the clone sets corresponding to adjacent vertices. The resulting graph has a perfect matching if and only if the original graph has a perfect f-matching.
assumptions_latex: \text{Every element of }U_v\text{ is adjacent to every element of }U_w\text{ whenever }vw\in E(G)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G'\text{ has a perfect matching}\iff G\text{ has a perfect }f\text{-matching}

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Factor Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weight-preserving extension of the incidence-and-dummy matching reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an edge-weighted instance \((G,f,w)\), construct the Tutte auxiliary graph. Give each cross edge \((u,e)(v,e)\), where \(e=uv\), weight \(w(e)\), and give every incidence-to-dummy edge weight zero. Compute a minimum-weight perfect matching \(M\) and return \[F=\{e=uv:(u,e)(v,e)\in M\}.\] Every perfect matching selects exactly \(f(v)\) cross edges incident with each original vertex \(v\), and \[w(M)=\sum_{e\in F}w(e).\] Infeasibility of perfect matching is equivalent to infeasibility of the \(f\)-factor instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assigning original costs to cross-gadget edges makes the Tutte construction preserve feasibility and total weight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Minimum-weight perfect matchings in the auxiliary graph correspond weight-for-weight to minimum-weight \(f\)-factors of \(G\).

notation.meaning: Perfect matching of the auxiliary graph.

children.title: Direct f-Factor Methods
children.top_down_role: Direct approaches specialized to prescribed-degree f-factor problems.

knowledge_statements.title: Direct f-Factor Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct solution through maximum-cardinality capacitated matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \((G,f)\), run a direct capacitated blossom algorithm for a maximum-cardinality integral \(b\)-matching with vertex capacities \(b(v)=f(v)\) and edge capacities one. Let its output be \(F\subseteq E\). Since \(d_F(v)\le f(v)\), one has \[2|F|=\sum_{v\in V}d_F(v)\le f(V).\] Stop and output \(F\) as an \(f\)-factor exactly when \(|F|=f(V)/2\); otherwise report that no \(f\)-factor exists. For weighted factors, optimize weight subject to this maximum-cardinality requirement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A direct capacitated-blossom method finds a maximum b-matching; it is an f-factor exactly when every vertex capacity is saturated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is an \(f\)-factor if and only if \(|F|=f(V)/2\).

notation.meaning: Vertex capacity, set equal to f(v).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Saturation of all capacities is correctly characterized by cardinality f(V)/2, but the claimed direct capacitated-blossom algorithm and weighted extension require an authoritative locator.

children.title: Degree-Constrained Subgraph Methods
children.top_down_role: Direct approaches for broader degree-constrained subgraph models.

knowledge_statements.title: Degree-Constrained Subgraph Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary formulation of lower–upper degree-constrained spanning subgraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be finite and let \(g,f:V\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) satisfy \(g(v)\le f(v)\le d_G(v)\). A spanning subgraph \(H\) is a \((g,f)\)-factor precisely when its incidence vector \(x\in\{0,1\}^{E}\) satisfies \[g(v)\le\sum_{e\in\delta_G(v)}x_e\le f(v)\qquad(v\in V).\] Thus a degree-constrained subgraph method may optimize \(\sum_{e\in E}w_ex_e\) over these integral constraints, using augmenting-trail or matching-polytope machinery to enforce integrality rather than accepting the bare linear relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lower and upper degree bounds become binary incidence constraints; direct methods optimize over their integral feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible binary vectors are in one-to-one correspondence with spanning \((g,f)\)-factors.

notation.meaning: Indicator that edge e belongs to the chosen subgraph.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The binary formulation correctly represents (g,f)-factors, but the additional assertion about direct augmenting-trail or matching-polytope methods is nontrivial and unsupported.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence of a Forbidden-Degree-Avoiding Subgraph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives a local cardinality condition ensuring that all prescribed forbidden degree sets can be avoided simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected graph and, for each \(v\in V\), let \(F(v)\subseteq\{0,1,\ldots,d_G(v)\}\). If \(|F(v)|\leq\lfloor d_G(v)/2\rfloor\) for every \(v\in V\), then there exists \(E'\subseteq E\) such that \(d_{(V,E')}(v)\notin F(v)\) for every \(v\in V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If each vertex forbids at most half of its possible incident-edge count, rounded down, then the graph has a spanning subgraph whose degree at every vertex avoids the corresponding forbidden set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists E'\subseteq E\quad\forall v\in V:\ d_{(V,E')}(v)\notin F(v)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: (f,g)-factor deficiency and optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines generalized factors through violations of complementary degree bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G be a graph and let f,g:V(G)\to\mathbb{R} satisfy f,g\ge 0 and f+g\ge \deg_G pointwise. For a spanning subgraph H, let \bar H=(V(G),E(G)\setminus E(H)) and define \delta(v;H;f,g)=\max\{0,\deg_H(v)-f(v),\deg_{\bar H}(v)-g(v)\}, \delta(H;f,g)=\sum_{v\in V(G)}\delta(v;H;f,g), and \delta(f,g)=\min_H\delta(H;f,g). An (f,g)-factor is a spanning subgraph satisfying \deg_H\le f and \deg_{\bar H}\le g; equivalently, one exists iff \delta(f,g)=0. Moreover, \delta(H;f,g)=\delta(\bar H;g,f) and \delta(f,g)=\delta(g,f). A spanning subgraph H is (f,g)-optimal when \delta(H;f,g)=\delta(f,g).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonnegative vertex functions f and g whose sum is at least the degree in G, the deficiency of a spanning subgraph is the total positive violation of its f upper bounds and the complementary subgraph's g upper bounds. An (f,g)-factor exists exactly when the minimum deficiency is zero. Deficiency is invariant under exchanging the subgraph with its complement and exchanging f with g. A minimum-deficiency spanning subgraph is called (f,g)-optimal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H\text{ is an }(f,g)\text{-factor}\iff \delta(H;f,g)=0,\qquad \exists H\text{ an }(f,g)\text{-factor}\iff\delta(f,g)=0;\quad \delta(f,g)=\delta(g,f).
